source_lines.57: 1.1 Let $P(x)=\sum_{|k|\le m}a_ke^{2\pi ikx}$ be a trigonometric polynomial. Its Fourier coefficients are a_k: the integral of $e^{2\pi i(k-j)t}$ on [0,1] is one for k=j and zero otherwise, by direct integration for the nonzero integer k-j. For 0<epsilon<1 put $u_\varepsilon(x)=\phi(\varepsilon x)P(x)$, a Schwartz function: the derivatives of P are bounded and the scaled phi and all its derivatives decay to every order, so the Leibniz formula proves every Schwartz seminorm finite. Direct substitution in the absolutely convergent Fourier integral gives $$\widehat{u_\varepsilon}(\xi)=\sum_{|k|\le m}a_k\varepsilon^{-1}\psi((\xi-k)/\varepsilon).$$ The kth summand is supported in $[k-\varepsilon/8,k+\varepsilon/8]$. Thus for every integer N>=0 the interval $[-N-1/2,N+1/2]$ contains exactly the entire summands with |k|<=N and misses the other ones. F4 then gives the exact identity $$T_{N+1/2}u_\varepsilon(x)-T_{-N-1/2}u_\varepsilon(x)=\phi(\varepsilon x)S_NP(x).$$ The half-integer cutoffs avoid every endpoint frequency; no half-weight term occurs. [F1, F2, F3, F4, given]
source_lines.59: 1.2 We prove the precise periodic averaging limit used below. Let w be continuous, nonnegative and bounded by $C(1+|x|)^{-2}$, and let G be continuous and one-periodic. Then $$\varepsilon\int_{\mathbb R}w(\varepsilon x)G(x)dx\longrightarrow\Bigl(\int_{\mathbb R}w\Bigr)\int_0^1G(t)dt.$$ Decomposing the line into n+[0,1) and substituting gives the left side as $\int_0^1G(t)R_\varepsilon(t)dt$, where $R_\varepsilon(t)=\varepsilon\sum_{n\in\mathbb Z}w(\varepsilon(n+t))$. This rearrangement is absolute: $|G|$ is bounded, $\int w<\infty$, and F8 followed by F9 applies. These Riemann sums converge uniformly for t in [0,1] to $\int w$. To verify uniformity, partition the line into cells $[\varepsilon(n+t),\varepsilon(n+t+1))$. For cells meeting [-R,R], the difference between the left-endpoint sum and the integral is at most $(2R+2)\omega_R(\varepsilon)$, where $\omega_R$ is the modulus of continuity of w on [-R-1,R+1], and 0<epsilon<=1. For the remaining cells the sum and integral of the decay majorant are at most C/(1+R), uniformly in t and epsilon, by comparison of the monotone tails of $(1+|x|)^{-2}$ with their integrals. First choose R large and then epsilon small. The resulting uniform convergence allows integration against bounded G and proves the displayed limit. [F8, F9]

source_lines.27: Assume AC. If the uniformly linearised finite model operators are restricted weak type (r,r) and (s,s), with 1<r<p<s<infinity, they are strong type (p,p), uniformly in the selector and finite family.
source_lines.45: **Given:** $1<r<p<s<\infty$ and a finite model A. Restricted weak type means that there are constants $K_r,K_s$ independent of A such that for q=r,s, every measurable E with finite measure and every lambda>0 satisfies $m\{|A\mathbf1_E|>\lambda\}\le K_q^q\lambda^{-q}m(E)$. This interpretation uses only characteristic inputs; the stronger convention allowing bounded supported inputs also suffices.
source_lines.47: 1.1 For q>1 define the testing functional $N_q(h)=\sup_B m(B)^{-1+1/q}\int_B|h|$, where the supremum is over measurable B of finite positive measure. It is homogeneous and subadditive by the integral triangle inequality. If $m\{|h|>t\}\le(K/t)^q$, F1 with exponent one, applied on B, gives $\int_B|h|\le\int_0^\infty\min(m(B),(K/t)^q)dt=\frac q{q-1}K m(B)^{1-1/q}$. For K>0 split the integral at $t=K m(B)^{-1/q}$; for K=0 every positive level set is null and the bound is zero. Thus $N_q(h)\le q'K$, where $q'=q/(q-1)$. Conversely, if $N_q(h)=D<\infty$, apply the definition to $B=\{|h|>t\}\cap[-R,R]$. When its measure is positive, $t m(B)^{1/q}\le D$; when zero the same measure bound holds. Increasing R gives $m\{|h|>t\}\le(D/t)^q$. This proves both comparisons even if the original level set could have infinite measure. [F1, F2, given]
source_lines.49: 2.1 If u is a nonnegative simple function with $0\le u\le a\mathbf1_E$, list its finitely many positive values in increasing order. It is the sum of their successive nonnegative differences times the indicators of the corresponding superlevel sets. Each such set lies in E and the differences sum to at most a. Linearity and step 1.1 therefore give $N_q(Au)\le q'K_q a m(E)^{1/q}$ for q=r,s. A complex simple u with $|u|\le a\mathbf1_E$ is the sum of the positive and negative real parts and i times the positive and negative imaginary parts, each bounded by $a\mathbf1_E$. Hence $N_q(Au)\le4q'K_q a m(E)^{1/q}$. The same result is zero for null E because its indicator has zero output almost everywhere by the assumed restricted bound and linearity of the finite coefficient formula. [F3, step 1.1, given]
source_lines.51: 3.1 Let f be a complex simple function supported on a set of finite measure. Put $E_k=\{2^k<|f|\le2^{k+1}\}$, $m_k=m(E_k)$ and $f_k=f\mathbf1_{E_k}$. There are only finitely many nonempty E_k, they are disjoint, and $f=\sum_k f_k$ almost everywhere. For each integer n, split $f=f^{\rm high}_n+f^{\rm low}_n$ by summing over k>=n and k<n respectively. Subadditivity of the testing functional and step 2.1 give $N_r(Af^{\rm high}_n)\le C_r\sum_{k\ge n}2^k m_k^{1/r}$ and $N_s(Af^{\rm low}_n)\le C_s\sum_{k<n}2^k m_k^{1/s}$, with $C_q=8q'K_q$. Since $|Af|>2^n$ implies that one of the two pieces has magnitude greater than $2^{n-1}$, the converse comparison in step 1.1 bounds its level-set measure by $$m\{|Af|>2^n\}\le(2C_r)^r2^{-nr}\Bigl(\sum_{k\ge n}2^k m_k^{1/r}\Bigr)^r+(2C_s)^s2^{-ns}\Bigl(\sum_{k<n}2^k m_k^{1/s}\Bigr)^s.$$ [F3, step 1.1, step 2.1]
source_lines.53: 4.1 Set $b_k=2^{pk}m_k$. The sum over n of $2^{np}$ times the first term in step 3.1, apart from its constant, is $$\sum_{n\in\mathbb Z}\Bigl(\sum_{j\ge0}2^{-(p-r)j/r}b_{n+j}^{1/r}\Bigr)^r.$$ For nonnegative numbers x_j and summable nonnegative weights w_j, finite Hölder gives $(\sum_j w_jx_j)^r\le(\sum_jw_j)^{r-1}\sum_jw_jx_j^r$. Here $w_j=2^{-(p-r)j/r}$ has finite sum W_r because p>r. Applying this inequality, then summing over n, bounds the display by $W_r^r\sum_k b_k$. One may first use finite sets of n,j and then increase them: every summand is nonnegative and each shifted sum of the finitely supported b is at most $\sum_k b_k$. Likewise the second term gives $$\sum_{n\in\mathbb Z}\Bigl(\sum_{j\ge1}2^{-(s-p)j/s}b_{n-j}^{1/s}\Bigr)^s\le W_s^s\sum_k b_k,$$ where $W_s=\sum_{j\ge1}2^{-(s-p)j/s}<\infty$ since s>p. These are two explicit geometric sums, not an interpolation theorem used as an undeclared supplier. [F4, step 3.1]
source_lines.55: 5.1 Apply F1 to Af and split the positive t-axis into $[2^n,2^{n+1})$. Monotonicity of its level-set measure yields $\|Af\|_p^p\le(2^p-1)\sum_n2^{np}m\{|Af|>2^n\}$. The nonnegative sum is valid whether or not finiteness is known initially. Steps 3.1 and 4.1 bound it by $C\sum_k2^{pk}m_k\le C\int|f|^p$, because $|f|>2^k$ on E_k. Thus the strong bound is established for every finite-support simple f, with C depending only on r,p,s and the two restricted constants, not on the finite family or selector. [F1, step 3.1, step 4.1]
source_lines.57: 6.1 For general $f\in L^p(\mathbb R)$, the same finite model formula makes sense: each packet belongs to $L^{p'}$ and $L^p$ by its Schwartz decay, so F4 makes the coefficients absolute. More explicitly an exponent M with Mp>1 and Mp'>1 gives integrable powers of the packet bound. For every integer $j\ge1$ define $Q_j(t)=\operatorname{sgn}(t)\lfloor j\min(|t|,j)\rfloor/j$, with $\operatorname{sgn}(0)=0$, and put $f_j=\mathbf1_{[-j,j]}(Q_j(\operatorname{Re}f)+iQ_j(\operatorname{Im}f))$. Each component of $f_j$ takes only the $2j^2+1$ values $k/j$ with $|k|\le j^2$, so $f_j$ is a simple measurable function supported on a finite-measure set. Componentwise rounding toward zero gives $|f_j|\le|f|$, while $f_j\to f$ almost everywhere. Hence $|f_j-f|^p\le2^p|f|^p$, and F5 gives $\|f_j-f\|_p\to0$. Hölder gives convergence of every packet coefficient; more strongly, the triangle inequality and selector bound give $$\|Af_j-Af\|_p\le\sum_{u\in S}\|\phi_u\|_p\|\phi_u\|_{p'}\|f_j-f\|_p\longrightarrow0.$$ This finite auxiliary sum may depend on S; it is used only to identify the limit, not in the uniform estimate. Pass to the limit in step 5.1 using Minkowski's norm continuity to obtain the stated uniform strong bound. Empty finite families, zero simple functions and zero endpoint constants are covered without division by them. The strict inequalities r<p<s are exactly what makes the two geometric weights summable; no endpoint weak-to-strong inference is made. AC is inherited as identified in F6. This conditional interpolation proof does not assume that the Hunt restricted estimates have already been proved. [F3, F4, F5, F6, step 5.1] ∎

source_lines.53: 1.1 The proof establishes the stronger sum of absolute tile contributions. Choose complex numbers $\varepsilon_s$ of modulus one so that $\varepsilon_sa_s\langle\mathbf1_{\omega_{s,+}}(N)\phi_s,g\rangle$ is nonnegative real, taking $\varepsilon_s=1$ for a zero product. Finite sesquilinearity bounds that sum by $\int_E|\sum_s\varepsilon_sa_s\mathbf1_{\omega_{s,+}}(N(x))\phi_s(x)|dx$. Write $b_s=\varepsilon_sa_s$. Empty T and sigma=0 give zero. If delta=0, exponent20 packet decay bounds the integral of $|\phi_s|$ on $E\cap N^{-1}(\omega_{s,+})$ by $C\sqrt{|I_s|}\delta=0$ for each s, so all contributions vanish. Hence assume delta,sigma>0. Singletons give $|b_s|\le\sigma\sqrt{|I_s|}$. A possible member s=t contributes at most $C\sigma L\int_{E\cap N^{-1}(\omega_t)}\chi_{J_0}\le C\sigma\delta L$, by packet decay with exponent20. Remove this one member. Each remaining tile has its top frequency contained in exactly one half of its frequency interval. Split them into the strict plus and strict minus trees according as that half is right or left, retaining the same top t and the bounds delta,sigma. [F1, F2, F5, given]
source_lines.55: 1.2 We record a kernel bound. If $K_r$ satisfies $|K_r(z)|\le C r^{-1}(1+|z|/r)^{-20}$ and h is Schwartz, then for every interval J of length j<=r and every x,y in J, $|(K_r*h)(x)|\le C Mh(y)$. Indeed $|x-y|\le r$ makes the displayed weight at x comparable to that at y. On $|z-y|<r$ its integral against |h| is bounded by twice the centered average times a constant. On the annulus $2^nr\le|z-y|<2^{n+1}r$, it is at most $C2^{-19n}Mh(y)$, using the centered interval of radius $2^{n+1}r$. The geometric sum proves the bound uniformly in x,y,r. [F4]

source_lines.39: [L3] **Natural exponents, in a monoid.** Let $(M,\cdot,e)$ be a monoid (def-semigroup-and-monoid) and $g \in M$. By the recursion theorem (thm-recursion), applied with the set $M$, the element $e$ and the function $x \mapsto x \cdot g$ from $M$ to $M$, there is exactly one function $\mathbb{N} \to M$, written $n \mapsto g^{n}$, with $$g^{0} = e, \qquad g^{\sigma(n)} = g^{n} \cdot g \quad (n \in \mathbb{N}).$$ In particular $g^{0} = e$ for **every** $g$, including $g = e$, and $g^{1} = g^{\sigma(0)} = e \cdot g = g$. Since $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$ (def-natural-numbers), the exponent $0$ is a genuine value of the definition and not a separate convention. **Integer exponents, in a group.** Let $G$ be a group (def-group) and $g \in G$. Write $\iota : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{Z}$ for the embedding $k = [(k,0)]$ of lem-nat-embeds-int, which is injective, preserves addition, multiplication and order, and has as image exactly the nonnegative integers. For $x \in \mathbb{Z}$ define - $g^{x} := g^{k}$, the natural power, when $0 \le x$ and $x = k$; - $g^{x} := (g^{k})^{-1}$ when $x < 0$ and $-x = k$. **Why this is well defined.** The order on $\mathbb{Z}$ is total and antisymmetric (thm-int-ordered-ring, def-int-order), so exactly one of $0 \le x$ and $x < 0$ holds and the two clauses never both apply. In the first clause $x$ is nonnegative, so $x = k$ for some $k \in \mathbb{N}$, and $k$ is unique because $\iota$ is injective. In the second clause $x < 0$ gives $0 = x + (-x) < 0 + (-x) = -x$ by compatibility of the order with addition (thm-int-ordered-ring, def-int-operations), so $-x$ is a positive integer and again $-x = k$ for a unique $k$. The inverse $(g^{k})^{-1}$ is a single determined element by lem-inverse-unique and def-invertible-element. Finally the two readings of $g^{k}$, as a natural power and as an integer power, agree by construction, so no ambiguity is introduced. **Abbreviation.** In an exponent we write $k$ for the integer $k$ when a natural number $k$ is used where an integer is expected; this is unambiguous because $\iota$ is injective and preserves the arithmetic and the order, and because the two readings of $g^{k}$ agree as just noted. **Additive notation.** When the group is written additively the same object is written $n g$ or $n \cdot g$ rather than $g^{n}$, with $0 g = 0$ and $\sigma(n) g = n g + g$; the definitions are identical, only the symbols differ. ([[def-group-power]]).

Then $$\langle g \rangle \;=\; \{\, g^{n} \;:\; n \in \mathbb{Z} \,\} ,$$ the cyclic subgroup generated by $g$ (def-generated-subgroup) being exactly the set of integer powers of $g$. source_lines.45: [L6] Let $G$ be a group, $g \in G$, and let orders be as in def-order-in-a-group. Throughout, a natural number written where an integer is expected means its image under the embedding $\iota : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{Z}$ of lem-nat-embeds-int. **Finite order.** Suppose $\operatorname{ord}(g) = n$ with $n \in \mathbb{N}$, $n \ge 1$. Then: 1. for every $k \in \mathbb{Z}$, $g^{k} = e$ if and only if $k = qn$ for some $q \in \mathbb{Z}$, that is, if and only if $n \mid k$ (thm-division-algorithm-in-z); 2. the powers $g^{0}, g^{1}, \dots, g^{n-1}$ are pairwise distinct: if $i, j \in \mathbb{N}$ with $i < n$, $j < n$ and $g^{i} = g^{j}$, then $i = j$; 3. $\langle g \rangle = \{\, g^{s} : s \in \mathbb{N},\ s < n \,\}$ and $\langle g \rangle \approx n$; so $\langle g \rangle$ is finite with $|\langle g \rangle| = n = \operatorname{ord}(g)$. **Infinite order.** If $\operatorname{ord}(g) = \infty$ then for $j, k \in \mathbb{Z}$, $g^{j} = g^{k}$ implies $j = k$; so the integer powers of $g$ are pairwise distinct and $\langle g \rangle$ is not finite. ([[lem-order-characterisation]]).

source_lines.39: [L3] Let $(M,\cdot,e)$ and $(M',\cdot',e')$ be monoids (def-semigroup-and-monoid). A **monoid homomorphism** from $M$ to $M'$ is a function $f : M \to M'$ such that - **(H1)** $f(x \cdot y) = f(x) \cdot' f(y)$ for all $x, y \in M$; - **(H2)** $f(e) = e'$. Let $G$ and $G'$ be groups (def-group). A **group homomorphism** from $G$ to $G'$ is a function $f : G \to G'$ satisfying (H1) alone: $$f(xy) \;=\; f(x)\, f(y) \qquad \text{for all } x, y \in G .$$ Condition (H2) is not imposed for groups because it follows: a group homomorphism automatically satisfies $f(e) = e'$ and $f(x^{-1}) = f(x)^{-1}$ (lem-group-homomorphism-basic-properties). For monoids it does **not** follow and must be assumed, which is why the two definitions differ. A homomorphism from a structure to itself is an **endomorphism**. The identity map of $M$ is a monoid homomorphism, and a composite of monoid homomorphisms is one, since $(g \circ f)(xy) = g(f(x)f(y)) = g(f(x))\,g(f(y))$ and $(g \circ f)(e) = g(e') = e''$; the same computation, without the second clause, shows a composite of group homomorphisms is a group homomorphism. ([[def-group-homomorphism]]).

source_lines.38: [L1] Let $p$ be a prime natural number (def-prime). A finite $p$-group is a finite group $P$ (def-group, def-finite-cardinality) whose order has the form $$|P|=p^n$$ for some $n\in\mathbb N$, with natural exponentiation as in def-nat-power. The case $n=0$ permits the trivial group. A finite $p$-group is nontrivial exactly when $n\ge 1$. ([[def-finite-p-group]]).

source_lines.31: Assume the Axiom of Choice inherited from the named suppliers. Let $k$ be any field and $G=\mathrm{SL}_2$ over $k$ with diagonal torus $T_2=\{\operatorname{diag}(x,x^{-1})\}$, upper triangular Borel $B$, $U^+=\{\binom{1\ a}{0\ 1}\}$ and $U^-=\{\binom{1\ 0}{a\ 1}\}$ ([[def-root-datum-of-a-split-reductive-group]], [[lem-sl2-structure-and-root-coordinates]], [[thm-bruhat-decomposition-for-split-reductive-group]]). The root datum is $X(T_2)=\mathbb Z\chi$ with $\alpha=2\chi$ and $\alpha^\vee=\chi^\vee$, so $\langle\alpha,\alpha^\vee\rangle=2$ and the group is simply connected; the root groups are $U_{\pm\alpha}=U^\pm$, $n_\alpha=\binom{0\ 1}{-1\ 0}$ represents $s_\alpha$, $tu_\alpha(a)t^{-1}=u_\alpha(\alpha(t)a)$, and $\mathfrak{sl}_2=\mathfrak t\oplus\mathfrak g_\alpha\oplus\mathfrak g_{-\alpha}$ with $\dim\mathfrak g_{\pm\alpha}=1$. The Weyl group is $W=\{1,s_\alpha\}\cong\mathbb Z/2$; the Bruhat decomposition is $G=B\sqcup Bn_\alpha B$ with $Bn_\alpha B=U^+n_\alpha B$ the open Bruhat cell, parametrized by $U^+\times B\cong\mathbf A^1\times\mathbf G_m\times\mathbf A^1$; separately $U^-T_2U^+$ is the open Gaussian cell; on $k$-points $\mathrm{SL}_2(k)=B(k)\sqcup B(k)n_\alpha B(k)$, while $G/B\cong\mathbf P^1$ with $G(k)$ acting through $\mathrm{PGL}_2(k)$. The cell $B$ has dimension $2$ and the open Bruhat cell has dimension $3$; the unique longest element $w_0=s_\alpha$ gives this dense open cell, and the opposite Borel is $B^-=U^-T$.

The group scheme $U_n$ of upper unitriangular matrices ([[def-upper-unitriangular-group-scheme]]) is a smooth connected unipotent algebraic group over $k$: it is a closed subgroup of $U_n$ trivially, its coordinate ring $k[X_{ij}\mid i<j]$ is coconnected by the weight filtration, and its central series has additive quotients ([[lem-upper-unitriangular-central-series]]).

source_lines.26: Assume the Axiom of Choice inherited from the named suppliers. Let $k$ be a field and $n\ge1$, $G=\mathrm{GL}_n$ with standard split maximal torus $T=D_n$ of diagonal matrices and standard Borel $B$ of upper triangular matrices ([[def-root-datum-of-a-split-reductive-group]], [[thm-parabolics-and-levi-decomposition]]). The roots are $\alpha_{ij}=\chi_i-\chi_j$ ($i\neq j$) with root groups $U_{ij}=\{I+aE_{ij}\}$, and the base is $\{\alpha_{i,i+1}:1\le i\le n-1\}$, identified with $\{1,\dots,n-1\}$. For $I\subseteq\{1,\dots,n-1\}$ let $\Delta\smallsetminus I=\{a_1,a_1+a_2,\dots,a_1+\cdots+a_{s-1}\}$ with $a_i\ge1$ and $\sum a_i=n$; then $P_I$ consists of the block upper triangular matrices with diagonal blocks of sizes $a_1,\dots,a_s$, arbitrary entries above the block diagonal and zero below, the standard Levi subgroup is $L_I=\prod_i\mathrm{GL}_{a_i}$ (block diagonal) and $R_u(P_I)$ is the block upper unitriangular subgroup, with identity diagonal blocks, zero blocks below them and arbitrary blocks above them; the multiplication $R_u(P_I)\rtimes L_I\to P_I$ is an isomorphism, $I\mapsto P_I$ is a bijection onto the smooth parabolic subgroup varieties containing $B$, and $P_\varnothing=B$, $P_{\Delta}=G$. The maximal proper parabolics $P_{\Delta\smallsetminus\{i\}}$ are the stabilizers of the partial flags with a single subspace of dimension $i$, and the Bruhat cells of the complete flag variety $G/B$ are indexed by $S_n$ with $\dim Y(w)=n(w)=\#\{(i,j):i<j,\ w(i)>w(j)\}$.
source_lines.42: 2.1 Let $I\subseteq\{1,\dots,n-1\}$ and let the complement of $I$ in the ordered set of simple roots be the partial sums listed, so that the integers $a_1,\dots,a_s\ge1$ sum to $n$. Choose a cocharacter with diagonal exponents constant within each block and strictly decreasing between consecutive blocks. Entrywise conjugation scales $x_{ij}$ by the exponent difference, so its limit subgroup is precisely the group with zero blocks below the diagonal and its limit kernel has identity diagonal blocks. By [F2] its zero simple-root pairings recover $I$. Thus $P_I$ is the group of invertible matrices preserving the flag of subspaces $0\subseteq k^{a_1}\subseteq k^{a_1+a_2}\subseteq\cdots\subseteq k^n$, i.e. the block upper triangular matrices with diagonal blocks of sizes $a_1,\dots,a_s$; its unipotent radical $R_u(P_I)$ has identity diagonal blocks, zeros below and arbitrary blocks above and its Levi factor is the block diagonal $\prod_i\mathrm{GL}_{a_i}$; the multiplication map $R_u(P_I)\rtimes L_I\to P_I$ is a group-scheme isomorphism by [F2], and $P_\varnothing=B$ and $P_{\Delta}=G$ because the corresponding flags are the complete flag and the trivial flag. The all-algebra matrix equations verify these stabilizers scheme-theoretically. For $n=1$ the simple-root set is empty, both endpoints are $G=B=\mathbf G_m$, and its unipotent radical is trivial. [F2, step 1.1, algebra]
source_lines.44: 3.1 The maximal proper parabolics correspond to $I=\Delta\smallsetminus\{i\}$, i.e. to the stabilizers of a single subspace of dimension $i$: taking $a_1=i$, $a_2=n-i$ gives the block upper triangular group with two diagonal blocks, which is the stabilizer of $k^i\subseteq k^n$, and the general $P_I$ is the intersection of these stabilizers over the cuts $i\in\Delta\smallsetminus I$, not over $I$. For $n\ge3$, the minimal proper parabolics strictly above $B$ are $P_{\{i\}}$, since singletons are the minimal nonempty proper subsets of the base. For $n\le2$ there is no proper parabolic strictly between $B$ and $G$; in particular, for $n=2$ the singleton gives $G$, rather than a proper parabolic. Finally, the simple-root reflections act on the characters $\chi_i$ by adjacent transpositions. Since they generate the Weyl group, its faithful lattice action is precisely $S_n$. The Bruhat cells of $G/B$ are indexed by $S_n$, and the length $n(w)$ equals the dimension of the cell by the length formula of [F3]. For the roots $\chi_i-\chi_j$ with $i<j$, the count $|\Phi^+\cap w\Phi^-|$ is the inversion number of $w^{-1}$. This equals the inversion number of $w$: $(i,j)\mapsto(w(j),w(i))$ bijects their inversion sets. Thus the count is $\#\{(i,j):i<j,\ w(i)>w(j)\}$ over every field. [F2, F3, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

source_lines.53: [F1] *Root coordinates of $\mathrm{SL}_2$.* $X(T_2)=\mathbb Z\chi$, $\Phi=\{\pm2\chi\}$, $\alpha=2\chi$, $\alpha^\vee=\chi^\vee$ with $\langle\chi,\alpha^\vee\rangle=1$, the Weyl group is $\{1,s_\alpha\}$ acting by $s_\alpha(\chi)=\chi-\langle\chi,\alpha^\vee\rangle\alpha=-\chi$, $u_\alpha(a)=\binom{1\ a}{0\ 1}$, $u_{-\alpha}(a)=\binom{1\ 0}{a\ 1}$, and $\mathrm{SL}_2$ is generated by $U^+$ and $U^-$ ([[lem-sl2-structure-and-root-coordinates|Structure of $\mathrm{SL}_2$ and root coordinates]], [[def-root-datum-of-a-split-reductive-group]]).
source_lines.75: 1.1 With the identification $X(T_2)=\mathbb Z\chi$ of [F1], the fundamental weight is $\omega=\chi$ and $X(T_2)^+=\{m\chi:m\ge0\}$, so [F2] gives the simple modules $L(m)=V(m\chi)$ for $m\ge0$. The trivial representation is one-dimensional hence simple with highest weight $0$, so $L(0)$ is the trivial representation. The standard representation $k^2$ is simple: for any nonzero $v=(a,b)$ one has $\binom{a\ 0}{b\ a^{-1}}e_1=v$ when $a\ne0$ and $\binom{0\ -b^{-1}}{b\ 0}e_1=v$ when $a=0$, so the submodule generated by any nonzero vector is all of $k^2$; moreover $e_1$ is fixed by $U^+$ and is a $T_2$-eigenvector of weight $\chi$, so $e_1$ is primitive of weight $\chi=\omega$ and $k^2\cong L(1)$ by [F2]. [F1, F2]
source_lines.77: 1.2 Fix $m\ge0$ and let $v\in L(m)$ be a primitive vector of weight $m\chi$, which exists and is unique up to scalar by [F3]. By [F4] $L(m)$ is generated as a $U^-$-module by $v$, and $U^-=U_{-\alpha}\cong\mathbf G_a$. By [F5] write $u_{-\alpha}(c)\cdot v=\sum_{i\ge0}c^iv_i$, where $v_0=v$, $v_i\in L(m)_{(m-2i)\chi}$, and only finitely many $v_i$ are nonzero. Let $W=\operatorname{span}_k\{v_i:i\ge0\}$. For every $k$-algebra $R$ and $a\in R$, the group law gives $u_{-\alpha}(a)\cdot(u_{-\alpha}(c)\cdot v)=u_{-\alpha}(a+c)\cdot v$; comparing coefficients of $c^j$ in these polynomial expressions yields $u_{-\alpha}(a)\cdot v_j=\sum_{i\ge j}\binom{i}{j}a^{i-j}v_i$, so $W_R$ is stable under every $U^-(R)$-point. Thus $W$ is a $U^-$-submodule containing $v$, and [F4] implies $L(m)=W$. The weights $(m-2i)\chi$ are distinct, so this is a direct sum of one-dimensional spaces $kv_i$ for the nonzero coefficients; hence every weight space of $L(m)$ has dimension at most one. [F3, F4, F5]
source_lines.90: - The computation $g\cdot e_i^p=(g\cdot e_i)^p$ shows that the $p$-th symmetric power always contains the Frobenius twist $L(1)^{(p)}\cong L(p)$. For $0\le m<p$, $S^m(k^2)$ is simple: a nonzero submodule contains a weight monomial $e_1^ae_2^{m-a}$ by [F6]; the coefficient of $t^{m-a}$ in its universal $U^+$-translate is $e_1^m$, so the submodule contains $e_1^m$. The universal $U^-$-translate of $e_1^m$ has coefficients $\binom mi e_1^{m-i}e_2^i$, all nonzero because $m<p$, so the submodule is the whole symmetric power. Coefficients belong to the submodule by its coaction criterion, rather than by interpolation over $k$.

[F1] *def-axiom-of-choice.* The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement. > Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function > (def-choice-function). Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty, there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for all $S \in \mathcal{F}$. ([[def-axiom-of-choice]])
[F2] *def-dependent-choice.* Let $X$ be a set and let $R \subseteq X \times X$ be a binary relation on $X$. Call $R$ **entire on $X$** when $\text{for every } x \in X \text{ there is } y \in X \text{ with } x \mathbin{R} y .$ The **Axiom of Dependent Choice**, written $\mathrm{DC}$, is the following statement. ([[def-dependent-choice]])

source_lines.36: ## Statement
source_lines.38: Assume AC and DC. A rational Gorenstein normal local surface domain in the permitted canonical-module setting with normal completion is resolved by finitely many ordinary blowups at singular closed points. Every model is normal, its closed local rings are rational, and its canonical module is invertible; the terminal model is regular and projective over the local base. It is unchanged off the original closed point.
source_lines.40: ## Facts & Assumptions
source_lines.48: [F3] *lem-rational-singular-point-blowup-canonical-pullback-surjective.* Assume AC and DC. For a nonregular rational normal local surface domain in the permitted regular-base dualizing setting, let $f:X\to\operatorname{Spec}A$ be its ordinary point blowup, $E$ its exceptional divisor and $I=O_X(1)$. Then $H^1(X,\omega_X\otimes I^n)=0$ for $n\ge0$ and the canonical evaluation $f^*\omega_A\to\omega_X$ is surjective. ([[lem-rational-singular-point-blowup-canonical-pullback-surjective]])
source_lines.50: [F4] *lem-rational-surface-local-rings-propagate-by-point-sequence-spreading.* Assume AC and DC. If a permitted normal local surface domain $A$ is rational and $A\subset B$ is a normal two-dimensional local domain with the same fraction field, essentially of finite type over $A$, then $B$ is rational. ([[lem-rational-surface-local-rings-propagate-by-point-sequence-spreading]])
source_lines.52: [F5] *lem-rational-gorenstein-surface-tangent-conic-and-hilbert-function.* Assume AC and DC. Let $A$ be a nonregular rational normal local surface domain in the permitted canonical-module setting, with $\omega_A\cong A$. Then its point blowup is normal with trivial canonical module. Its exceptional conormal $L$ has degree two and $\dim_\kappa\mathfrak m^n/\mathfrak m^{n+1}=2n+1$. ([[lem-rational-gorenstein-surface-tangent-conic-and-hilbert-function]])
source_lines.54: [F6] *lem-nonsquare-tangent-conic-rational-surface-blowups-terminate.* Assume AC and DC. For a nonregular rational normal local surface domain in the permitted class with invertible canonical module and normal completion, if its tangent-conic quadratic is not a scalar times a square, repeatedly blowing up its singular points terminates in a regular model. ([[lem-nonsquare-tangent-conic-rational-surface-blowups-terminate]])
source_lines.56: [F7] *lem-square-tangent-conic-blowup-singularities-controlled-by-a-cubic.* Assume AC and DC. For a rational Gorenstein normal local surface singularity with square tangent conic, choose $\mathfrak m=(x_1,x_2,z)$ and a relation $z^2=\sum a_{ijk}x_ix_jx_k$. There is a nonzero homogeneous cubic $H\in\kappa[X_1,X_2]$ whose zero scheme on the reduced exceptional line contains all singular successors. ([[lem-square-tangent-conic-blowup-singularities-controlled-by-a-cubic]])
source_lines.58: [F8] *lem-double-plus-simple-cubic-rational-surface-branch-terminates.* Assume AC and DC. Let $A$ be a rational Gorenstein normal local surface in the permitted canonical-module setting, with normal completion and generators $\mathfrak m=(x,y,z)$. If $z^2+a xy^2\in z\mathfrak m^2+(x,y)^4$ for a unit $a$, all its singular point-blowup branches terminate. ([[lem-double-plus-simple-cubic-rational-surface-branch-terminates]])
source_lines.60: [F9] *lem-triple-cubic-rational-surface-branch-reduces-in-two-steps.* Assume AC and DC. For a rational Gorenstein normal local surface in the permitted setting with square tangent conic, if its nonzero controlling cubic is a scalar times a cube, its continuing branch enters the nonsquare case or the double-plus-simple cubic class after at most two successive square successors. This allows every characteristic and residue field. ([[lem-triple-cubic-rational-surface-branch-reduces-in-two-steps]])

The geometric midpoint interpretation of this algebraic component is the claim of the next lemma.

source_lines.60: 2.1 Let β_r:S¹∧T_r→T_{r+1} be the prespectrum structure map, and let b_{r,n} be its induced stabilization map on π_{r+n}. Since m_b is an inverse-limit element, its coordinates satisfy σ⁻¹β_r^* m_{r+1,b}=m_{r,b}. For a based representative α:S^{r+n}→T_r, naturality of the Kronecker pairing gives ⟨m_{r+1,b}, (β_r∘(1∧α))_*[S¹∧S^{r+n}]_{F₂}⟩ =⟨β_r^* m_{r+1,b}, (1∧α)_*[S¹∧S^{r+n}]_{F₂}⟩ =⟨m_{r,b}, α_*[S^{r+n}]_{F₂}⟩. All sphere classes in these pairings are mod-two fundamental classes, not unreduced integral classes. For the second equality, represent the cohomology suspension of m_{r,b} by its external product with the degree-one generator of S¹. Under S¹∧S^{r+n}≅S^{r+n+1}, the mod-two sphere fundamental class is the external product of the two mod-two fundamental classes. Evaluation of external products on product chains is the product of the two evaluations; the S¹ factor evaluates to 1. Naturality of the Kronecker pairing then gives exactly the displayed equality. These are the published suspension, external-product/Künneth, and Kronecker naturality interfaces; coefficients are F₂, so there is no sign ambiguity. Thus $D_{r+1,n}b_{r,n}=D_{r,n}$ coordinate by coordinate, proving the claimed suspension compatibility. [step 1.1, F1, F2, F3] ∎

source_lines.63: 2.1 If n=2m, induction computes the preceding rank as R[p₁,…,p_{m-1}]. All those generators lift, so j* is surjective degreewise. In the published rank-2m Gysin sequence the actual maps, after identifying the sphere total space with BSO(2m−1), are H^{k−2m}(BSO(2m);R) --·e--> H^k(BSO(2m);R) --j*--> H^k(BSO(2m−1);R) --p_!--> H^{k−2m+1}(BSO(2m);R) --·e--> H^{k+1}(BSO(2m);R). Surjectivity of j* in degree k makes every class in its target a pullback. Exactness gives p_!j*=0, so p_! vanishes in degree k. At the following term, exactness therefore makes multiplication by e injective on H^{k−2m+1}(BSO(2m);R). Taking k=a+2m−1 for every integer a proves that e is a non-zero-divisor in each degree a. Exactness at H^k(BSO(2m);R) independently gives ker(j*:H^k(BSO(2m);R)→H^k(BSO(2m−1);R)) =eH^{k−2m}(BSO(2m);R). Negative-degree groups are zero, so the same statement includes the initial degrees. For a class of degree d subtract a polynomial lift of its restriction, then divide the remainder by e; the resulting class has degree d−2m. Induction on d proves polynomial generation. For a polynomial relation Σ_{a=0}^N e^a P_a(p)=0, restriction gives P₀=0 by the preceding rank's polynomial independence. Injectivity of multiplication by e then repeats the argument to show every P_a=0. The published top-class identity gives p_m=e². This proves the even-rank presentation over R. [step 1.1, F2, algebra]

It fixes p and reverses the orientation of the complement plane: the ordered first vector v changes sign while the orientation o stays fixed. Thus cτ=σc, with σ orientation reversal on BSO(2m). Since τ*p*=p*, the image of j* is σ-invariant. The Euler sign formula gives σ*e=−e and σ*p_i=p_i. Every element of the already computed even-rank polynomial ring has a unique expansion Σ e^a P_a(p₁,…,p_{m-1}); since 2 is invertible, its invariants are exactly the polynomials with even a. Since I is a two-sided ideal, J is a two-sided ideal in T⊗T. We have Δ̃(R)∈J for each R∈R₀. Every element of I is a finite sum of terms xRy with x,y∈T and R∈R₀, so multiplicativity gives Δ̃(xRy)=Δ̃(x)Δ̃(R)Δ̃(y)∈J. Therefore Δ̃(I)⊂J, and Δ̃ descends to Δ_A:A→A⊗A. Also ε̃(R)=0 for every R∈R₀ because each generator is homogeneous of positive degree. Since ε̃ is multiplicative, it vanishes on all of I and descends to A. The descended maps remain algebra homomorphisms, coassociative and counital. The basis theorem gives A₀=F₂·1 and A_d=0 for d<0. source_lines.75: 1.1 Proof of the base case. Take K_1=BO(1)=RP∞. Its orientation double cover is BSO(1)=V_1(R∞), contractible by the published stable-Stiefel theorem. The oriented-Grassmannian definition supplies this literal double cover. The covering homotopy lifting and fibration long exact sequence give π₁=Z/2 and no higher homotopy groups. The Schubert CW construction has one cell in each nonnegative degree (rank-one symbol a₁=d+1); thus its integral cellular chains are finite free in each degree. Cellular homology and Noetherian submodules give integral finite generation. The finite-cover transfer, with $d=2$, identifies its F-cohomology with that of its contractible cover, hence it vanishes in positive degrees. Field evaluation UCT identifies cohomology with the dual of homology; a nonzero vector has a nonzero functional under AC, so field homology also vanishes. Marked homotopy uniqueness transports all these facts to any chosen CW model. [given, F1, F5]

source_lines.55: 1.1 For n≥1, forgetting orientation is genuinely a two-sheeted cover BSO(n)=Gr⁺_n(R∞)→BO(n)=Gr_n(R∞) in the chosen model. On a base graph chart, Gram–Schmidt supplies a continuous orthonormal frame of the tautological bundle. Its two possible orientations give two disjoint open subsets of the oriented chart, each mapped homeomorphically to the base chart. These charts cover BO(n). This includes n=1: SO(1) is trivial, Gr⁺_1(R∞)=S∞, and forgetting orientation is v↦Rv from the unit sphere to RP∞; over a chart with a chosen unit representative it has the two sections v and −v. Rank zero is excluded here and treated as a point below. [given, F1]
source_lines.57: 2.1 Lift each Schubert characteristic disk D^d→BO(n) to its two sheets; this is possible because the disk is contractible, and the two lifts restrict to the two lifts over every boundary cell. Choose a label for the two lifts of each cell using AC. Their open interiors map homeomorphically to the underlying Schubert open cell, and the lifted boundary maps into the inverse image of the lower Schubert skeleton. Thus these disks supply attaching maps with finite boundary support. Each finite Schubert skeleton is compact Hausdorff with finitely many cells; its two-sheeted preimage is compact Hausdorff, and the finite attaching quotient maps continuously and bijectively onto that preimage. It is therefore a homeomorphism. [step 1.1, F2, F4]
source_lines.59: 3.1 The infinite topology is the weak topology of these lifted cells. To check the nontrivial direction, let C be a subset whose inverse image in every lifted characteristic disk is closed. Over any evenly covered open set U of BO(n), restrict to one sheet U⁺. On each base characteristic disk, the preimage of U splits into relatively open-and-closed pieces on which a chosen lift lies in U⁺; the lifted-cell test makes the preimage of C∩U⁺ closed on each such piece, hence on the preimage of U. Therefore the preimage of U⁺\C is open relative to the preimage of U. Since that preimage of U is open in each characteristic disk, this restricted preimage is open in the full disk. The base CW weak-topology test makes U⁺\C open in U⁺, hence C∩U⁺ closed there. The same holds on the other sheet, and these sheets cover BSO(n), so C is closed upstairs. Conversely a closed subset has closed inverse image under each characteristic map by continuity. The lift topology is therefore exactly the CW weak topology. Finite cell counts in each dimension and closure finiteness are inherited from the Schubert structure, with two lifts per cell. For n=0, BSO(0) is a point by the published definition. This is the lifted-cover CW prerequisite of the shared MSO prespectrum definition. [step 2.1, F2, F3] ∎

source_lines.60: 1.1 Each simplex is a closed finite-dimensional disk with its usual faces, attached to the previously constructed skeleton. Its boundary has finitely many faces. The finite-boundary-support CW construction gives J(G) and its weak topology, with disjoint simplex interiors. The action preserves faces and their slot ordering, and is free: any occupied slot has label g, and gh=g forces h=1. Distinct vertices of a simplex have different slots, so no nonidentity action identifies two points within one simplex. For B_wG choose one representative for each orbit of simplices, oriented in increasing slot order. Their disks attach by their face orbits, with finite boundary support and disjoint interiors. A set is closed in this cell construction exactly when its inverse image is closed on each simplex of J(G); that is also the orbit-quotient closed-set criterion. Thus the constructed CW topology is exactly the orbit topology. [given, F1, F2, F5]
source_lines.62: 2.1 Let t_s be the weight in slot s. It is continuous by the map-out criterion on each characteristic simplex. On its positive locus the label g_s is continuous into discrete G: the open star of (s,g) is the locus t_s>0, g_s=g, checked on each simplex. Let U_s⊂B_wG be t_s>0. Normalizing a representative by right multiplication by g_s^{-1} defines a section on U_s, since (x h)(g_s h)^{-1}=x g_s^{-1}. source_lines.67: 1.1 A finitely generated subgroup F of T is finite: if its generators have orders d_1,...,d_r, the product of those cyclic groups surjects onto F. For finite F, the covering J(F)→B_wF has |F| sheets. For each singular simplex, sum all its lifts to obtain a chain map τ. Existence and uniqueness of based lifts apply because a simplex is simply connected; restriction to a face bijects its lift set with that face's lift set. Thus ∂τ=τ∂ and p_#τ=|F| id, including degree zero. These are exactly the lift-sum identities proved in the published transfer supplier. On rational homology, τ_* is injective because p_*τ_*=|F| id. The map J(F)→* is a weak equivalence by the weak-join $K(G,1)$ lemma; the published weak-equivalence/homology lemma and the rationalization lemma give zero positive rational homology of J(F). Therefore B_wF has zero positive rational homology. A rational cellular cycle in B_wT has finite support. Row 3 places all its cells in B_wF for one finitely generated, hence finite, subgroup F. The cellular differential agrees with that in B_wF, and the inclusion of cellular chain groups is injective, so the same chain is a cycle in B_wF. It bounds there by the preceding paragraph, hence bounds in B_wT. Cellular/singular comparison proves positive rational acyclicity. Marked CW uniqueness identifies B_wT with every chosen K(T,1), and homotopy invariance transfers the result. [given, F1, F2, F5]

source_lines.45: 1.1 The prespectrum construction constructs T_r as a based CW complex. Over a d-dimensional Schubert cell of BO(r), its Thom attachment contributes cells of dimension d+r, with d≥0; hence every cell outside the basepoint has dimension at least r. Apply the published high-relative-cells lemma to the CW pair (T_r,*): it is (r−1)-connected. In particular T_r is path-connected and simply connected for r≥2. The basepoint is a vertex. [given, F1, F2]

source_lines.87: 4.1 Equivariance of the polynomial lift. The extension $F$ on $X$ is equivariant: for every $g$, the two regular maps expressing equivariance agree on the dense orbit by step 1.3 and therefore on $X$. Let $E_K$ be the finite-dimensional rational module of polynomial maps $operatorname{End}(V)	ooperatorname{End}(V^{otimes d})$ of degree at most $K$, for $KgedegPhi$, with action $(gcdotPsi)(Y)=g^{otimes d}Psi(g^{-1}Yg)(g^{-1})^{otimes d}$. Let $I_Ksubset E_K$ consist of maps vanishing on $X$. Then $I_K$ is stable and the class of the lift from step 3.1 in $E_K/I_K$ is invariant. Scalar matrices act trivially on $E_K$: they conjugate neither the input nor the output. For $Nge2$, Weyl's theorem [F3] applied to the semisimple Lie algebra $mathfrak{sl}(V)$ gives an $mathfrak{sl}(V)$-stable complement to $I_K$. This complement is stable under $mathrm{SL}(V)$, since elementary matrices $exp(tE_{ij})$ generate that group and their rational representation acts by exponentiating the differential; together with scalar matrices they generate $mathrm{GL}(V)$ over $mathbb C$. For $N=1$ the whole group acts trivially, so any vector-space complement suffices. The quotient map restricted to this complement is thus a $mathrm{GL}(V)$-isomorphism and lifts the invariant class to an invariant $Phi'in E_K$. It agrees with $F$ on $X$ and satisfies $Phi'(e)=B$, proving (1). [F3, step 1.3, step 3.1, algebra]

source_lines.135: 1.1 Let U=U(m), I=I_chi. Replace x by y=x−chi(x). These shifted generators have the original brackets, because chi vanishes on brackets. Choose a basis adapted to the lower-central filtration, with weight w_i the largest lower-central index containing its basis vector. PBW reordering and the commutator formula show that I^n is spanned by ordered monomials of total lower-central weight≥n: one inclusion follows from reordering n factors, while the reverse follows because each basis vector of weight w lies in I^w, being a linear combination of iterated brackets of length w. [F1, F2, F5, construct, algebra]
source_lines.137: 1.2 The Rees algebra R=⊕_(n≥0) I^n t^n is generated by y_i t^r, 0≤r≤w_i. Their span is a finite-dimensional Lie algebra: a nonzero bracket component y_k has w_k≥w_i+w_j, so r+s≤w_k. PBW gives its enveloping algebra a polynomial associated graded. For any left ideal, Hilbert basis gives finitely many generators of its homogeneous leading ideal; lift them and subtract matching highest-degree terms until the nonnegative degree decreases to zero. The lifts generate the original ideal. Thus the enveloping algebra is left noetherian, and its surjection onto R makes R left noetherian. For a left ideal J⊂U, ⊕(J∩I^n)t^n is a graded left ideal of R and has finitely many homogeneous generators. For fixed k, choosing n greater than k plus their largest degrees gives J∩I^n⊂I^k J. This is the precise Artin–Rees consequence needed here. [F1, F2, F5, construct, algebra]
source_lines.139: 1.3 Set E_chi=∪_(n≥0)(U/I^n)^*, with left action (x f)(r)=f(r x). To prove injectivity, take a U-linear map phi:J→E_chi. U is noetherian, so choose finitely many generators of J. A common I^k kills their images and hence all images, since I is two-sided. The scalar functional lambda(j)=phi(j)(1) kills I^k J. Choose n with J∩I^n⊂I^k J, extend lambda from J/(J∩I^n) to U/I^n, and call the extension a∈E_chi. The map U→E_chi, u↦u a, extends phi, because at r its value on j is a(rj)=phi(rj)(1)=phi(j)(r). Baer's criterion gives injectivity. This supplies the injective-continuous-dual assertion cited without proof in BK Lemma8.20. [F1, F2, F5, construct, algebra]

source_lines.147: 1.7 The right action preserves continuity. For a fixed u∈U(g), the finite PBW subspace generated by all iterated ad m on u is finite-dimensional and its negative-column action is nilpotent; sufficiently long products of ad m vanish. Moving u past a product of sufficiently many shifted m generators therefore leaves at least n of them on the left. Equivalently u I^(n+C)⊂I^n U(g) for some C=C(u). Thus lambda u kills I^(n+C)X. On this continuous-dual module the right shifted m-action is locally nilpotent. Injectivity of E_chi makes Hom_m(−,E_chi) exact, and right Skryabin makes its Whittaker vectors exact. These Whittaker vectors are precisely Hom_m(X,C_chi). Dualizing this finite-dimensional vector space gives an exact covariant functor. [F1, F2, F5, construct, algebra]
source_lines.149: 1.8 The restricted dual uses the row-sum torus a=span{Σ_(row(j)=r)E_jj}, not the full Cartan and not the column-origin vector c. Every e-adjacent pair lies in one row, so chi has a-weight0. If X is generated over U(m) by finitely many a-weight spaces, an m-linear functional into C_chi vanishes outside those finitely many weights: lambda(uv)=chi(u)lambda(v), and chi(u)=0 in every nonzero a-weight. Thus the restricted-dual definition agrees with the entire finite-dimensional Hom space. Generalized parabolic Vermas are U(m)-free on a finite-dimensional Levi module by PBW; their finite projective flags/presentations from the repaired parabolic highest-weight supplier make every genuine parabolic O object finitely generated over U(m). This establishes exactness on precisely that category. [F1, F2, F5, construct, algebra]

source_lines.201: 5.1 Let $Z$ be a finite-dimensional Cartan-semisimple $\mathfrak g$-module. Then $N\otimes Z$ is again a genuine parabolic object: its weights are sums of weights of $N$ and $Z$, and local finiteness for $\mathfrak p$ follows from $U(\mathfrak p)n\otimes Z$ being finite-dimensional for each $n$. It is finitely generated over $U(\mathfrak m)$ by tensors of generators of $N$ with a basis of $Z$: induction on word length uses $xn\otimes z=x(n\otimes z)-n\otimes xz$. Thus its $V$ image is defined on the stated domain. Apply the original-head right Skryabin counit $H_N\otimes_W Q_{\chi,\mathrm{right}}\to D_\chi N$, $f\otimes\overline a\mapsto fa$. Tensor it with $Z^\vee$, apply right Wh and use step 2.3 to obtain $H_N\circledast_{\mathrm{right}}Z^\vee\cong H_{N\otimes Z}$. Combine this actual counit with the module pairing of step 4.1 and take finite duals. This gives the natural $W$ isomorphism $\nu_{N,Z}:V(N\otimes Z)\to V(N)\circledast Z$ for EVERY genuine parabolic object $N$, including objects without an induced-module realization. Coassociativity, counit associativity and the inverse product formulas of step 3.2 make its two iterated tensor constructions agree under transported associativity. Naturality in a map of finite tensor factors follows from its ordinary dual map and the basis-independent evaluation pairing; hence adjacent flips are intertwined. [F2, F6, step 2.3, step 4.1, construct, algebra]
source_lines.203: 6.1 Compute the actual Casimir coefficients in ordinary box matrix units. On the LEFT lift, the coefficient at $v_k$ after $\Omega=\sum E_{ab}\otimes E_{ba}$ is $\sum_hE_{h,k}\eta_{\mathrm{tail}}X_{hj}$. Positive matrices give $(E_{h,k}-\delta_{hk}\rho_k^{\mathrm{tail}})X_{hj}$ after undoing the shift. Negative matrices give $\chi(E_{h,k})X_{hj}-X_{kj}$ by step 1.9. Their total scalar is $-\rho_k^{\mathrm{tail}}-\sum_{b>\operatorname{col}(k)}q_b=q_{\operatorname{col}(k)}-n$. On the RIGHT lift the coefficient at $v^h$ is $\sum_k\eta_{\mathrm{head}}Y_{ik}E_{h,k}$; step 2.2 moves negative matrices left, giving $\chi(E_{h,k})Y_{ik}-Y_{ih}$, and the total scalar is $-\rho_h^{\mathrm{head}}-\sum_{b<\operatorname{col}(h)}q_b=q_{\operatorname{col}(h)}-n$. Multiplying by $Y$ on the left or $X$ on the right therefore gives the SAME entries $C_{j,i}=\sum_{\operatorname{col}(h)\le\operatorname{col}(k)}Y_{i,k}E_{h,k}X_{h,j}+\sum_k(q_{\operatorname{col}(k)}-n)Y_{i,k}X_{k,j}+\sum_{\operatorname{row}(h)=\operatorname{row}(k),\,\operatorname{col}(h)=\operatorname{col}(k)-1}Y_{i,h}X_{k,j}$. There is no extra displacement sign on the ordinary $E_{h,k}$; signs are already in $X,Y$. The entries lie in $W$ because the Casimir preserves the actual Whittaker subspace. The module pairing now intertwines the two transported Casimirs, while the continuous tensor pairing transposes the source Casimir term by term. Hence $\nu$ intertwines the source and target Casimir maps. With flip compatibility this also intertwines their polynomial and generalized-eigenspace residue projections, with the usual contragredient retained for reverse translation. [F2, F3, F6, step 1.9, step 2.2, step 4.1, step 5.1, construct, algebra]

source_lines.25: Assume the Axiom of Choice inherited from the supplied injective-resolution six-functor construction. Let $f:Y\to X$ be a proper surjective morphism of finite-type complex algebraic varieties, and let $F\in D^b_c(X;k)$ for a field $k$. Write $Y_p=Y\times_X\cdots\times_XY$ with $p+1$ factors, $f_p:Y_p\to X$, and $F_p=f_p^*F$. In the analytic topology of [[def-analytic-topology-and-finite-smooth-algebraic-stratifications]] the natural augmented derived Cech map is a quasi-isomorphism:
source_lines.26: $$F\xrightarrow{\sim}\operatorname{Tot}_{p\geq0}Rf_{p*}F_p.$$
source_lines.27: Here totalization is the normalized or unnormalized alternating-face total supplied by the simplicial-derived construction. There is one fixed lower cochain bound; consequently its diagonals are finite in every degree. The claim commutes with arbitrary algebraic base change and coefficient morphisms. In particular $R\Gamma(X,F)\simeq\operatorname{Tot}_pR\Gamma(Y_p,F_p)$. Individual fibers of $f$ need not be cohomologically acyclic, connected, or smooth.

By the proper base change and fiber-pullback clauses of [F1], the stalk at $x$ of $Rf_{p*}F_p$ is $R\Gamma(S^{p+1},K)$ with $K$ the constant derived pullback, and these identifications are natural for all face and degeneracy maps, so the first page of the stalk row in internal degree $q$ is
source_lines.48: $$H^q(K)\xrightarrow{\delta_{-1}}H^q(S,K)\xrightarrow{\delta_0}H^q(S^2,K)\xrightarrow{\delta_1}\cdots,$$

source_lines.51: 2.1 Explicit contraction of every augmented row. For $r\geq0$ let $\mathrm{ins}_r:S^r\to S^{r+1}$ insert $y$ as first coordinate, with $S^0=\mathrm{pt}$; so $\mathrm{ins}_0$ is the point $y$ itself. The deletion and insertion maps satisfy $d_0\,\mathrm{ins}_{r+1}=\mathrm{id}$ and $d_i\,\mathrm{ins}_{r+1}=\mathrm{ins}_r\,d_{i-1}$ for $i>0$. Put $h_{p+1}:=\mathrm{ins}_{p+1}^*:H^q(S^{p+2},K)\to H^q(S^{p+1},K)$ and $h_0:=\mathrm{ins}_0^*:H^q(S,K)\to H^q(K)$, with $\delta_{-1}$ the constant pullback of the projection $S\to\mathrm{pt}$. Applying the two identities termwise gives $h_{p+1}\delta_p+\delta_{p-1}h_p=\mathrm{id}$ for every $p\geq0$: the $i=0$ term of $h_{p+1}\delta_p$ is the identity, and the terms $i>0$ are the negatives of $\delta_{p-1}h_p$; moreover $h_0\delta_{-1}=\mathrm{id}$, because the projection followed by the chosen point is the identity of $\mathrm{pt}$. Hence every augmented horizontal row is contractible, in particular exact, in every internal degree $q$, using only functorial pullback on cohomology. [step 1.2, algebra]

source_lines.30: For a bicosimplicial complex $K^{p,r,q}$ of modules over a commutative ring, with $p,r\geq0$ and one fixed lower bound $q\geq a$, the alternating-face total complex and the diagonal alternating-face total complex are naturally chain-homotopy equivalent:
source_lines.31: $$\operatorname{Tot}_{p,r,q}K^{p,r,q}\simeq\operatorname{Tot}_{n,q}K^{n,n,q}.$$
source_lines.32: On the left total degree is $p+r+q$ and differential is $\delta_h+(-1)^p\delta_v+(-1)^{p+r}d$; on the right total degree is $n+q$ and differential is $\delta_{\mathrm{diag}}+(-1)^nd$. These comparisons preserve augmentation and apply to coherent derived diagrams after a supplied functorial strict resolution. They require no dimensional finiteness of the coefficient modules and no choice principle. Normalization can be applied on either side without changing the conclusion.
source_lines.34: ## Facts & Assumptions
source_lines.36: **Given:** $K^{p,r,q}=0$ unless $p,r\geq0$ and $q\geq a$. Horizontal cofaces $d_h^i:K^{p,r,q}\to K^{p+1,r,q}$ and codegeneracies $s_h^i:K^{p,r,q}\to K^{p-1,r,q}$, and the analogous vertical operators, satisfy the cosimplicial identities and commute between directions. The internal differential raises $q$ by one, squares to zero and commutes with these operators. The three $\delta$'s are the corresponding alternating coface sums. The auxiliary bisimplicial modules in steps 1.1–4.1 instead have faces lowering degree and degeneracies raising it; step 5.1 reverses their universal operator formulas.
source_lines.50: 1.1 Universal models and contractions. For a bisimplicial $R$-module $M$, let $Q_{p,r}$ have value $R[\Delta([u],[p])\times\Delta([v],[r])]$ at $(u,v)$. An element $x\in M_{p,r}$ determines the unique map $Q_{p,r}\to M$ sending the universal generator to $x$. The diagonal chain complex of $Q_{p,r}$ consists of pairs of monotone vertex strings; define $h$ on each basis string by prepending $(0,0)$. Deleting the first vertex gives the original string, and every other deletion commutes with prepending with its index reduced by one. Thus $\partial h+h\partial=1-e$, where $e$ sends every degree-zero vertex to $(0,0)$ and is zero in positive degrees. On the double total, identified with $C_*(\Delta[p];R)\otimes_R C_*(\Delta[r];R)$, use the separate prepend-zero contractions $h_p,h_r$ and projectors $e_p,e_r$. For homogeneous $x$, set $H(x\otimes y)=h_p(x)\otimes y+(-1)^{|x|}e_p(x)\otimes h_r(y)$. The Koszul differential gives $\partial H+H\partial=(1-e_p)\otimes1+e_p\otimes(1-e_r)=1-e_p\otimes e_r$. These contractions fill every positive-degree cycle and every augmentation-zero degree-zero cycle by specified finite chains. Unlike a constant simplicial map on unnormalized chains, $e$ is supported only in degree zero. [F3, F4, construct, algebra]
source_lines.52: 2.1 Diagonal-to-total comparison. Put $\operatorname{Diag}_m(M)=M_{m,m}$ and $\operatorname{Tot}_m(M)=\bigoplus_{p+r=m}M_{p,r}$ with the Koszul boundary. Set $\varphi_0=1$. Inductively evaluate $\varphi_{m-1}\partial z$ on the universal generator $z$ of $Q_{m,m}$, and fill it using the total contraction of step 1.1. It is a cycle because $\partial\varphi_{m-1}=\varphi_{m-2}\partial$; when $m=1$, it is the difference of the two endpoint vertices and has augmentation zero. Evaluate that specified filling under the representing map for each $x\in M_{m,m}$ to define $\varphi_m(x)$. This is linear and natural, and its boundary is $\varphi_{m-1}\partial x$. Thus $\varphi$ is a natural chain map, given degreewise by finite linear combinations of structure operators. [step 1.1, construct]
source_lines.54: 3.1 Total-to-diagonal comparison. Set $\psi_0=1$. For each summand $M_{p,r}$ in total degree $m=p+r>0$, evaluate $\psi_{m-1}\partial z$ on the universal generator of $Q_{p,r}$ and fill it with the diagonal contraction of step 1.1. The induction hypothesis makes it a cycle; in degree $m=1$ its two endpoint coefficients cancel. Evaluate the filling under the representing map of each element of $M_{p,r}$ and sum over $p+r=m$. This defines a linear natural chain map $\psi$, again by specified finite operator formulas. [step 1.1, step 2.1, construct]
source_lines.56: 4.1 Homotopy inverses. Let $C,C'$ each be the diagonal or total chain functor, and let $f,g:C\to C'$ be natural chain maps with $f_0=g_0$. Set $h_0=0$. For $m\geq1$, on a universal generator $z$ of a representing summand of $C_m$, put $\beta_m=(f_m-g_m)(z)-h_{m-1}(\partial z)$. The previously established equation $\partial h_{m-1}+h_{m-2}\partial=f_{m-1}-g_{m-1}$ makes $\partial\beta_m=0$. This cycle has positive degree, so its specified model contraction gives $h_m(z)$ with $\partial h_m(z)=\beta_m$. Extend by representing maps. Then $\partial h+h\partial=f-g$. Apply this to $\psi\varphi$ and $1$ on the diagonal, and to $\varphi\psi$ and $1$ on the total; both composites are the identity in degree zero. The resulting natural homotopies have finite operator formulas. [step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, construct]
source_lines.58: 5.1 Cosimplicial variance and the internal differential. The maps and homotopies of steps 2.1–4.1 are finite linear combinations of morphisms in the simplex categories. Their identities can be tested on the free representables of step 1.1, so they are universal additive operator identities. Reverse every operator and every composition to obtain cochain maps in the opposite directions and cochain homotopies lowering simplicial total degree by one. This reverses the two homotopy-inverse identities, without taking algebraic duals. Apply these formulas in each internal degree $q$. Naturality makes them commute with $d$. A comparison preserves simplicial total degree $t=p+r=n$, so it commutes with the signed internal differential $(-1)^td$. For a homotopy $H$ lowering $t$ by one, the internal terms in $DH+HD$ are $(-1)^{t-1}dH+(-1)^tHd=0$. Hence the comparisons and homotopies apply to precisely the two cochain differentials in the Statement. [step 2.1, step 3.1, step 4.1, algebra]

source_lines.126: 1.1 The orbit map $G\to N$, $g\mapsto\operatorname{Ad}(g)e$, has irreducible image closure. By [F1] its image has dimension $\dim\mathfrak g-\dim Z_{\mathfrak g}(e)=2|\Phi^+|=\dim N$; by [F6] the constructible image is dense and therefore contains a nonempty open subset of the irreducible variety $N$. The orbit is $G$-stable, so its translates of this open subset cover the orbit; consequently $G\cdot e$ is open in $N$. [F1, F6, algebra]
source_lines.128: 1.2 The Springer map is $$\mu:G\times^B\mathfrak n^+\longrightarrow N,\qquad[g,x]\longmapsto\operatorname{Ad}(g)x.$$ Its graph is the incidence subvariety $$\{(gB,y)\in X\times N:y\in\operatorname{Ad}(g)\mathfrak n^+\},$$ which is closed because the spaces $\operatorname{Ad}(g)\mathfrak n^+$ form a vector subbundle of $X\times\mathfrak g$. The projection $X\times N\to N$ is projective by [F4], so $\mu$ is proper by the projective-morphism theorem included in [F4]. Surjectivity follows from the last clause of [F1]. [F1, F4]
source_lines.132: 3.1 The fiber over $e$ is a single point. Indeed, if $e\in\operatorname{Ad}(g)\mathfrak n^+$, write $g=b_1n_wb_2$ by [F3]. The element $x=\operatorname{Ad}(b_1^{-1})e$ still has every simple coefficient nonzero by [F2]. Since $\operatorname{Ad}(n_w^{-1})x\in\mathfrak n^+$, each nonzero simple-root component of $x$ must map to a positive root space; distinct root spaces cannot cancel. Therefore $w^{-1}$ sends every positive simple root to a positive root, so $w=1$ by [F3], and $gB=B$. This algebraic argument holds after every algebraically closed extension of $\mathbb C$ as well. Equivariance gives a singleton geometric fiber over every point of $O=G\cdot e$. The restriction $\mu_O:\mu^{-1}(O)\to O$ is proper by base change. Its fibers are finite type and their geometric point sets are singletons, so each fiber point is isolated and has residue field finite over the base residue field; the finite-fiber criterion in [F8] makes $\mu_O$ quasi-finite, and proper quasi-finite finiteness in [F8] makes it finite. Both source and target are integral of dimension $2|\Phi^+|$, so the induced function-field extension is finite. It is separable in characteristic zero, and by [F9] has a primitive element $\theta$. After replacing an affine open $\operatorname{Spec}A\subseteq O$ by a smaller nonempty principal open, its finite preimage is $\operatorname{Spec}B$ with $B$ finite over $A$, $\theta$ lies in $B$, and $B=A[\theta]\cong A[T]/(f)$ for the monic minimal polynomial $f$ of $\theta$: first clear denominators to place $\theta$ in $B$, then localize to kill the finite torsion quotient $B/A[\theta]$ and to put the coefficients of $f$ in $A$. The discriminant of $f$ is nonzero by separability, so after inverting it this finite map is étale of rank $d=[\operatorname{Frac}B:\operatorname{Frac}A]$. Every geometric closed fiber in this open then has $d$ distinct points, but every geometric fiber over $O$ is a singleton; therefore $d=1$. This proves birationality without inferring degree from a closed-point count alone. [F2, F3, F8, F9, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 1.2]

source_lines.59: In $S_4$, written in one-line notation, let $b:=s_2=1324$ and $w:=s_2s_1s_3s_2=3412$ (a reduced word of length $4$; the two middle generators commute). (a) The interval $[b,w]$ has exactly ten elements: $1324$; $1342,1423,2314,3124$; $1432,2413,3142,3214$; and $3412$. (b) For comparable pairs in this interval the only Kazhdan–Lusztig polynomial different from $1$ is $P_{b,w}(q)=1+q$; so $\mu(b,w)=1$, and $(b,w)$ is a $\mu$-pair with $\ell(w)-\ell(b)=3>1$: $\mu$-pairs need not be covers. All other $\mu$-pairs inside the interval are covers, and all $r_{y,z}$ for $y,z\in[b,w]$ are the corresponding Laurent polynomials read off from [[thm-r-polynomial-recursion-and-degree-bounds]]. (c) The descent recursion of [[thm-kazhdan-lusztig-polynomial-recursion]] at $y=b$, $w$ and $s=s_2$ (a left descent of $w$, with $sw=2413$ and $sb=1234=\mathrm{id}$, so $c=1$) reads $$P_{b,w}(q)=P_{\mathrm{id},2413}(q)+qP_{b,2413}(q)-\!\!\!\sum_{\substack{b\le z\le 2413\\ s_2z<z,\ \mu(z,2413)\ne0}}\!\!\!\mu(z,2413)\,q^{(4-\ell(z))/2}P_{b,z}(q);$$ the sum is empty because $[b,2413]=\{1324,1423,2314,2413\}$ and its only element with $s_2z<z$ is $1324$, for which $\mu(1324,2413)=0$; since $P_{\mathrm{id},2413}=P_{b,2413}=1$, the recursion returns $P_{b,w}=1+q$, in agreement with (b). (d) The inverse Kazhdan–Lusztig polynomial of [[def-inverse-kazhdan-lusztig-polynomials]] is $q'_{b,w}=-v-v^3$, while $q'_{b,1342}=q'_{b,1423}=q'_{b,2314}=q'_{b,3124}=-v$ and $q'_{b,1432}=q'_{b,2413}=q'_{b,3142}=q'_{b,3214}=v^2$; the matrix identity $\sum_zq'_{x,z}p_{z,w}=\delta_{x,w}$ of [[thm-kazhdan-lusztig-inversion-formula]] holds on the ten-point interval. In particular the inverse coefficients are not all nonnegative even though all $p_{y,z}$ are.

For a dualizing class $c:k_S\to\omega_S[-n]$, compose $c\circ g_F$ and use $\theta_*\dashv\theta^!$ and $\theta^!\omega_S=\omega_T$. The resulting map $k_T\to\omega_T[2d-n]$ is a Borel–Moore class of degree $n-2d$ on $T$. This defines the supported cap operation even if $T$ is singular or has excess dimension; no purity of $\theta$ is asserted. The external product uses $\omega_A\boxtimes\omega_B=\omega_S$: on the supplied finite local product cochain models, compact-support cochains tensor, and their finite-dimensional duals tensor as well, giving this canonical comparison and its restriction compatibility. For a constructible $C$ on $M$, the mate is the adjoint of $b_!a^*q^!C\xrightarrow{\mathrm{BC}^{-1}}u^*q_!q^!C\xrightarrow{u^*\epsilon_q}u^*C$, where the arbitrary-map proper-support exchange of [F1] supplies $\mathrm{BC}:u^*q_!\xrightarrow{\sim}b_!a^*$ and $\epsilon_q$ is the exceptional counit. To identify its dualizing evaluation with step 2.1, factor $q$ as its graph $\Gamma_q:A\hookrightarrow A\times M$ followed by the second projection. The graph is the pullback of $\Delta$ along $(q,\operatorname{id}_M):A\times M\to M\times M$; its supported orientation map is that pullback of $g_\Delta$. Base change of the graph along $\operatorname{id}_A\times u$ is exactly $\theta$, so its supported orientation map after this second pullback is $g_F$. For the product projection, tensor–Hom evaluation with the relative dualizing factor $\omega_A$ computes the counit; this is the finite product cochain evaluation of step 2.1. Composing the graph counit and that evaluation gives $\epsilon_q$ by the composition-of-counits identity in [F1]. source_lines.87: 1.1 The geometry and the cohomology of the projective line. The fiber products are $Z_{12}=Z_{21}=\mathbb P^1$. By [F3] its Schubert CW structure has one $0$-cell and one $2$-cell, so the cellular cochain complex is $k\oplus k[-2]$. By [F4] it computes singular cohomology, and [F6] identifies this with constant-sheaf cohomology. Choosing cocycles representing the two generators gives a quasi-isomorphism $k\oplus k[-2]\to R\Gamma(\mathbb P^1,k)$. Hence $L_2\simeq k[1]\oplus k[-1]$ and $L_1=k$. [F3, F4, F6, algebra]
source_lines.89: 2.1 The two classes and their composites. The unit $\alpha:k\to R\Gamma(\mathbb P^1,k)$ includes the degree-zero summand, generating $\operatorname{Ext}^{-1}(L_1,L_2)=k$. Evaluation at a point projects to that summand; its shift $\beta:L_2\to k[1]$ generates $\operatorname{Ext}^1(L_2,L_1)=k$, since $\operatorname{Hom}(k[-2],k)=0$. Therefore $\beta[-1]\circ\alpha=\operatorname{id}_k$. The reverse composite $\alpha[1]\circ\beta$ is also nonzero: it is the projector of $L_2=k[1]\oplus k[-1]$ onto $k[1]$, and is neither zero nor $\operatorname{id}_{L_2}$. [step 1.1, algebra]
source_lines.91: 3.1 The convolution check. The corner degrees are $d_1+d_2-r=2$ for $\alpha$ and $d_2+d_1-s=0$ for $\beta$. [F1, F2, step 1.1, step 2.1]
source_lines.93: 4.1 The geometric product. The adjunction chain of [F1] sends $\alpha$ to $\operatorname{id}_{k_{\mathbb P^1}}$, hence to the positive fundamental class $[\mathbb P^1]$. Write $i:\mathrm{pt}\hookrightarrow\mathbb P^1$ for the evaluation point. Evaluation is the global-sections image of $k_{\mathbb P^1}\to i_*k$, and its adjoint under $R\Gamma\dashv a^!$, $a:\mathbb P^1\to\mathrm{pt}$, is the composite $k_{\mathbb P^1}\to i_*k=i_*i^!\omega_{\mathbb P^1}\to\omega_{\mathbb P^1}$, with the last arrow the proper trace. Thus $\Phi_{21}^{1}(\beta)=i_*[\mathrm{pt}]$ with coefficient $+1$. Geometrically $\mathbb P^1\times\{i\}$ meets the middle diagonal of $\mathbb P^1\times\mathbb P^1$ transversely at $(i,i)$; the map from its tangent line to the complex normal line of the diagonal is an isomorphism, preserving the real orientation. The positive Thom cap of [F5] therefore gives that point with multiplicity $+1$, and proper pushforward to $Z_{11}=\mathrm{pt}$ gives $[\mathrm{pt}]$. This computes $[\mathbb P^1]*[\mathrm{pt}]=[\mathrm{pt}]$, with middle degree drop $2$ and no permutation sign, agreeing with step 3.1. It verifies a transverse instance of the calculus, not its general nontransverse case. AC is inherited through [A1]. [A1, F1, F2, F5, step 2.1, step 3.1] ∎

source_lines.87: 4.1 The diagram chase. Let $I\subseteq R$ be a finitely generated ideal and let $K:=\ker(I\otimes_RM\to M)$. For every $n$ the sequence $0\to I\cap\mathfrak m^n\to I\oplus\mathfrak m^n\to I+\mathfrak m^n\to0$, with maps $x\mapsto(x,-x)$ and $(a,b)\mapsto a+b$, is exact, so after tensoring with $M$ and using [F20] the sequence $(I\cap\mathfrak m^n)\otimes_RM\to I\otimes_RM\oplus\mathfrak m^n\otimes_RM\to(I+\mathfrak m^n)\otimes_RM\to0$ is exact; the vertical maps to $M$ are the multiplication maps, which are injective on $\mathfrak m^n\otimes_RM$ and on $(I+\mathfrak m^n)\otimes_RM$ because both ideals contain $\mathfrak m^n$ and step 3.1 applies. Given $k\in K$, its image $(k,0)$ in the middle maps to zero in $(I+\mathfrak m^n)\otimes_RM$ and hence, by exactness at the middle, equals $(x,-x)$ for some $x\in(I\cap\mathfrak m^n)\otimes_RM$; then $x$ maps to $k$ in $I\otimes_RM$ and to $0$ in $\mathfrak m^n\otimes_RM$, so $x\in\ker((I\cap\mathfrak m^n)\otimes_RM\to M)$ and $K$ lies in the image of $(I\cap\mathfrak m^n)\otimes_RM\to I\otimes_RM$. [step 3.1, F20]

source_lines.108: 4.1 Base change and finite flat normalization. Consider a cartesian square with $f:X\to Y$ proper and $g:Y'\to Y$ flat of pure relative dimension $n$, and write $f':X'=X\times_Y Y'\to Y'$ and $g':X'\to X$. For an integral $d$-dimensional $V\subseteq X$, put $W=\overline{f(V)}$ and $e=\dim V-\dim W$. If $e>0$, both $g^*f_*[V]$ and $f'_*g'^*[V]$ are zero: every component of the flat pullback of $V$ has dimension $d+n$, while its image has dimension at most $\dim W+n<d+n$. If $e=0$, set $m=[k(V):k(W)]$. For each component $W_i$ of $g^{-1}(W)$, let $C_i$ be the Artinian local ring of $W\times_Y Y'$ at its generic point. Flat pullback gives coefficient $\ell(C_i)$ on $[W_i]$. The generic algebra of $V\times_Y Y'$ over $C_i$ is $C_i\otimes_{k(W)}k(V)$, a free $C_i$-module of rank $m$. Decomposing it into its Artinian local factors shows that the sum of the generic lengths of the components above $W_i$, weighted by their function-field degrees over $k(W_i)$, is $m\ell(C_i)$. These are precisely the coefficients of $[W_i]$ in $f'_*g'^*[V]$ and $g^*f_*[V]$, respectively. Hence the base-change identity holds on cycles and therefore on Chow groups. Finally, if $f$ is finite flat of constant degree $n$ between integral schemes of the same dimension, then $f$ is dominant and $[k(X):k(Y)]=n$, so $f_*[X]=n[Y]$ by step 1.1. [F1, step 1.1, given, algebra] ∎

source_lines.49: 1.1 On a finite affine cover with affine intersections, quasi-coherent sections on each intersection are module localizations. A short exact sequence therefore gives a termwise exact sequence of Čech complexes, hence a long exact sequence of their cohomology by the elementary kernel/image diagram chase. The localization Čech complex for a principal cover of an affine scheme is exact in positive degrees: localizing it at any prime, one covering function is a unit and insertion of its index is a contracting homotopy. Its cohomology modules thus vanish at every prime, and vanish globally. Refining finite affine covers by principal covers and using this contraction in the rows or columns of the double Čech complex preserves their cohomology. In particular the standard cover may be used consistently for sheaves, exact sequences and closed-immersion pushforwards. Its complex has length $N$, so its cohomology vanishes above $N$. [F1, algebra]
source_lines.53: 2.1 For $N>0$, the Čech complex of $\mathcal O(d)$ on $\mathbb P_A^N$ decomposes into complexes indexed by Laurent monomials $T_0^{e_0}\cdots T_N^{e_N}$ with $\sum e_i=d$. Such a monomial appears on precisely the intersections whose index set contains $J=\{i:e_i<0\}$. If $J$ is empty, the simplex complex has one copy of $A$ in degree-zero cohomology. If $J$ is the full index set, it has one copy of $A$ in degree $N$. In every other case choose an index outside $J$; insertion of that index with the usual alternating sign is a contracting homotopy, so the complex is acyclic. Thus $H^0(\mathcal O(d))$ has the finite basis of monomials with all $e_i\ge0$, $H^N(\mathcal O(d))$ has the finite basis with all $e_i<0$, and all intermediate groups vanish. The top group is zero for $d\ge-N$. For $N=0$ the space is affine, its sole group is $A$ in degree zero for every twist, and the assertions follow directly. [step 1.1, algebra]

source_lines.90: 1.1 (Actual cosimplicial Hodge complexes.) Choose the smooth projective proper hypercover $a:Y_\bullet\to Y$ of [F1]. For sheaves of rational or complex vector spaces, construct the Godement resolution of [F10]. Its first functor $C^0$ is exact because stalks are exact and products of surjective linear maps are surjective under AC. In a short exact sequence of sheaves, the corresponding germ embeddings into $C^0$ form a diagram with exact rows and columns; the kernel-cokernel exact sequence makes the three cokernels short exact. Iteration proves that every successive cokernel functor, every $C^t$ and every $\Gamma C^t$ is exact, the last again being a product of stalks. In particular resolutions and global sections preserve filtration levels, their finite intersections and associated gradings. Their first-quadrant totals compute derived global sections: termwise flasque acyclicity from [F10] applies to each sheaf of the bounded de Rham complex, and each total diagonal is finite. Apply this construction on every $Y_p$ and put $K_{\mathbb Q}^{p,q}=\Gamma(Y_p,C^q(\mathbb Q_{Y_p}))$ and $K_{\mathbb C}^{p,q}=\bigoplus_{k+t=q}\Gamma(Y_p,C^t(\Omega^k_{Y_p}))$, for $p,q\ge0$, with $F^b$ given by $k\ge b$. These are the resolved global de Rham complexes, not the complex of global holomorphic forms. Godement pullback along each face is induced by pulling a germ collection at a point to the stalk over its image; the successive cokernels preserve these maps, so their composites obey the simplicial identities and preserve $F$. The constant inclusion $\mathbb Q\otimes\mathbb C\to\Omega^0$ gives the functorial rational comparison; on cohomology it is the scalar-extension comparison of [F4]. Exactness and acyclicity of the resolution show $H^q(K_{\mathbb C}^p)=H^q(Y_p;\mathbb C)$, with the holomorphic-degree image filtration, and $H^q(K_{\mathbb Q}^p)=H^q(Y_p;\mathbb Q)$. The compact Hodge theorem [F4] gives pure weight $q$ and Hodge-de Rham $E_1$ degeneration on each smooth projective component. The latter makes the actual internal differential $F$-strict: if $dx\in F^b$, degeneration lifts the leading lower-filtration class of $x$ to a cycle up to a higher-filtration term and a boundary; subtracting the cycle and boundary raises the preimage filtration without changing $dx$, and finite induction supplies a preimage in $F^b$. This proves differential strictness directly. Thus every level is an actual weight-zero rational Hodge complex. Each internal total diagonal is finite, and $F^{q+1}K^{p,q}=0$, so [F3] applies to its first-quadrant simple complex, giving the mixed Hodge structure and $E_1^{p,q}=H^q(Y_p;\mathbb Q)$, $E_2$ degeneration and $\operatorname{Gr}^W_qH^n(sK)=E_2^{n-q,q}$. The terms have $p=n-q\ge0$, so weights are at most $n$, and the finitely many $E_1^{p,q}$ entries on every total diagonal are finite-dimensional by [F4]. Descent [F2] identifies the rational simple cohomology naturally with $H^n(Y;\mathbb Q)$, carrying this structure. [F1, F2, F3, F4, F9, F10, construct, algebra]

source_lines.124: 1.1 The ideal $I$ of $p$ is a nonzero coherent ideal on the integral regular projective surface $X$. Thus the blowup is integral, regular and pure of dimension two; $E$ is effective Cartier, isomorphic to $\mathbb P^1_{\kappa(p)}$, with normal line bundle $\mathcal O(-1)$. The residue degree $r$ is finite. To apply the intersection theory, we also verify absolute projectivity. Choose $X\hookrightarrow\mathbb P^n_k$ and its ample hyperplane bundle $H$. For some $s$, $I\otimes L$, $L=H^{\otimes s}$, is globally generated. A finite set of its global sections generates it: choose finitely many sections spanning each of finitely many affine neighborhoods, possible since $X$ is quasi-compact and the sheaf is of finite type. [F1, F2, F3]
source_lines.126: 2.1 Put $S=\bigoplus_{d\ge0}I^d\otimes L^{\otimes d}$. The preceding sections yield a graded surjection $\mathcal O_X[z_0,\ldots,z_N]\to S$, since $S$ is generated in degree one. Its relative Proj is canonically $X'$ by invertible rescaling; the twist need not be an ordinary ideal. Hence $X'$ is a closed subscheme of $\mathbb P^N_X$. Base change of $X\hookrightarrow\mathbb P^n_k$ embeds the latter as a closed subscheme of $\mathbb P^N_k\times_k\mathbb P^n_k$. [F3, step 1.1]
source_lines.128: 3.1 The product has a closed Segre embedding into $\mathbb P^{(N+1)(n+1)-1}_k$: its coordinates are $z_{ab}=u_av_b$, and the defining equations are all rank-one minors $z_{ab}z_{ij}-z_{aj}z_{ib}$. On $D_+(z_{ij})$, these equations identify its coordinate ring with the polynomial ring on $z_{aj}/z_{ij}$ ($a\ne i$) and $z_{ib}/z_{ij}$ ($b\ne j$); all other coordinates are their products. This is exactly the product of the affine charts $D_+(u_i)$ and $D_+(v_j)$, and the identifications respect their ratio transitions. They glue to the closed embedding. Thus $X'$ is projective over $k$, and all intersection and proper-cohomology hypotheses are satisfied. [F3, F7, step 2.1]
source_lines.130: 4.1 By the exceptional-curve Euler formula, $\chi_k(E,\mathcal O_E)=r$ and $\chi_k(E,\mathcal O_E(E))=0$, so its degree over $k$ is $-r$. Restriction of the intersection product to the effective curve $E$ gives $E^2=-r$. For any Cartier divisor $D$ on $X$, $\pi|_E$ factors through $\operatorname{Spec}\kappa(p)$, since the pulled-back point ideal vanishes on $E$. The restriction of $\pi^*\mathcal O_X(D)$ is therefore trivial. Its degree is zero, and the restriction formula gives $E\cdot\pi^*D=0$. This formula allows arbitrary $D$; only $E$ must be effective. [F1, F4, F6, F7, step 3.1]
source_lines.132: 4.2 Pushforward vanishing and the projection formula give $\chi(X',\pi^*\mathcal N)=\chi(X,\mathcal N)$ for every invertible $\mathcal N$. Pullback respects tensor products and duals. Apply this equality to the four sheaves $\mathcal O_X$, $\mathcal O_X(D)^\vee$, $\mathcal O_X(D')^\vee$, and their tensor product in the defining Euler-characteristic expression for intersection. The result is $\pi^*D\cdot\pi^*D'=D\cdot D'$, including the self-intersection case. [F5, F6, F7, step 3.1]
source_lines.134: 5.1 For the reduced curve through $p$, the proved point formula gives $\pi^*C=C'+mE$. Orthogonality and symmetry imply $0=E\cdot C'+mE^2$, hence $C'\cdot E=mr$. Bilinearity and step 4.2 give $C^2=(C'+mE)^2=(C')^2+2m^2r-m^2r$, so $(C')^2=C^2-m^2r$. If $p\notin C$, a local equation is a unit near $p$; its pullback misses $E$, and the off-center isomorphism gives $\pi^*C=C'$. The same pullback identity yields $(C')^2=C^2$. Choice enters only through the recorded suppliers. [F1, F6, F7, F8, step 4.1, step 4.2] ∎
