source_lines.27: For a nonzero finite-dimensional standard homogeneous cyclotomic KLR module M over any field, choose a word by successive maximal last-color blocks i_1^{r_1}...i_s^{r_s}. Among the simple shift orbits occurring as constituents of M, exactly one normalized orbit S_c contributes to that word; its right crystal label is c=tilde f_{i_s}^{r_s}...tilde f_{i_1}^{r_1}u_Lambda. Its word graded dimension is product_a [r_a]_{i_a}!, and [M:S_c]_v equals gdim e(word)M divided by that product. All other simple orbits occurring in M have zero space at this word; simple orbits absent from M may have nonzero space there. The zero module has zero character and requires no extremal-word selection. Consequently graded word characters are injective on G0. If two fields have modules with the same word character, their extremal words and detected canonical B(Lambda) labels coincide. No one-dimensional word-space assertion is made. Choice is inherited only through the existing abstract crystal identification.
source_lines.39: 1.1 Let M be a nonzero finite-dimensional standard homogeneous cyclotomic module. Choose a nonzero word by successively maximizing the last constant-color block, then the preceding block after restricting that maximum, until the vacuum is reached. Write the resulting word as i_1^{r_1}...i_s^{r_s}, adjacent colors distinct. Restriction to a word idempotent is exact. Every simple constituent of M with nonzero word space must have precisely the same first maximal last-block length: a shorter length gives zero, a longer length would contradict maximality for M. The actual maximal-tail supplier identifies the full maximal restriction of this simple with N tensor L(i_s^{r_s}), where N is simple with zero residual i_s-tail. Repeat on N and on the corresponding exact restriction of M. At the end N is the unique vacuum simple. Reconstruct using the actual unique-head induction supplier. Hence exactly one simple shift orbit among the constituents of M can contribute at the chosen word. Its crystal label is obtained by the same successive right-induction powers from the vacuum, so is field independent under the native11 canonical B(Lambda) identification. [F1, F2, algebra]

source_lines.32: The hypothesis $e>n$ in [[thm-separated-hecke-residues-give-seminormal-idempotents-and-bases]] cannot be dropped. Take $F=\mathbb C$, $q=-1$ (so $e=e(\mathbb C,-1)=2$, [[def-quantum-characteristic-of-an-invertible-hecke-parameter]]), $n=3$ and $\lambda=(2,1)$. The two distinct standard tableaux $s=\begin{smallmatrix}1&2\\3\end{smallmatrix}$ and $t=\begin{smallmatrix}1&3\\2\end{smallmatrix}$ have contents $\operatorname{content}_s(1),\operatorname{content}_s(2),\operatorname{content}_s(3)=0,1,-1$ and $\operatorname{content}_t(1),\operatorname{content}_t(2),\operatorname{content}_t(3)=0,-1,1$, and the extended quantum-integer identity gives $[1]_{-1}=1=[-1]_{-1}$, since $[-1]_{-1}=-(-1)^{-1}[1]_{-1}=1$. Hence $$([\operatorname{content}_s(k)]_q)_{k=1,2,3}=(0,1,1)=([\operatorname{content}_t(k)]_q)_{k=1,2,3}\quad(q=-1):$$ the q-content sequences collide although $s\ne t$, so the separation conclusion of the theorem fails. The difference of the two putative separating eigenvalues at $k=2$ is $[-1]_{-1}-[1]_{-1}=0$. Thus interpolation cannot distinguish the two tableaux: a formula that excludes equal values may still define a polynomial, but it is not a separating projector for these two labels. The attempted generator formula has axial distance $\rho=2$ and $[\rho]_{-1}=0$. In fact $L_2$ has a nontrivial Jordan block on this cell, so this cell has no simultaneous JM-eigenbasis. This explicit example shows that the uniform separation hypothesis $e>n$ cannot be dropped; it does not claim that every individual cell at every parameter with $e\le n$ lacks a seminormal basis. At the boundary $e=n=2$, still over $\mathbb C$ with $q=-1$, the row and column tableaux both have tuple $(0,1)$. The global Lagrange products in the theorem are consequently $1$ for both labels, so they are not orthogonal. Thus even the proposed replacement $e\ge n$ fails for the full global-idempotent statement.

source_lines.157: 5.1 **The vertical terminal alternatives.** Let $\mu$ be a multipartition and $r\downarrow_Tr+1$ at $(a,b,n)$, so the two nodes are vertically adjacent. Use the following precise tests: (a) an incoming edge $t$ with $|t-r|>1$; (b) $r\nearrow_Tr+2$ or $r+1$ is in a later component than $r+2$; (c) $r-1\nearrow_Tr+1$ or $r-1$ is in a later component than $r$. Test (a) gives $s_tT\xrightarrow{t}T$ and preserves the vertical pair. In test (b), standardness and the consecutiveness of the three entries force $s_{r+1}T$ and $s_rs_{r+1}T$ to be standard: the node of $r+2$ is above and right of $r$, hence above and right of the node of $r+1$, and after the first swap the nodes of $r,r+1$ are incomparable. Thus $s_rs_{r+1}T\xrightarrow{r}s_{r+1}T\xrightarrow{r+1}T$, while $r+1,r+2$ occupy the original vertical pair in $s_rs_{r+1}T$. The different-component case uses the same two swaps without any within-component inequality. Test (c) gives the analogous $s_rs_{r-1}T\xrightarrow{r}s_{r-1}T\xrightarrow{r-1}T$, with $r-1,r$ in the original vertical pair. If none of the tests holds, labels other than the triple adjacent to $r$ cannot have an inversion between consecutive row-reading positions: any such inverse-order consecutive pair is in incomparable nodes or distinct components and is exactly an incoming edge. Reading $r-1,r-2,\ldots,1$ backwards and $r+2,r+3,\ldots,d$ forwards consequently places them in row-reading order except for the lower-row prefix before the vertical pair and the upper-row tail after it; tests (c) and (b) exclude any further excursion. More explicitly, if $L$ is the initial label at $(a,b,n)$ and $U$ the initial label at $(a+1,b,n)$, the forced belt filling is $L,\ldots,L+b-2$ in the first $b-1$ lower-row positions, $r=L+b-1$ in $(a,b,n)$, $r+1=L+b$ in $(a+1,b,n)$, and $L+b+1,\ldots,U$ in the remaining upper-row tail; all outside entries are unchanged. Among standard belt fillings this is Bruhat-maximal: the $b$ lower-row entries are the lexicographically smallest possible increasing subset, namely $L,\ldots,L+b-2,L+b$, because choosing the $b$ smallest would violate column $b$. Every other valid subset has no smaller prefix counts in the upper row, hence is below it by step 2.1. This is exactly the Garnir tableau, including $b=1=\mu_a$. A horizontal brick is a consecutive same-row string. All selections, chains and comparisons are finite, so no choice principle is used. [F3, F4, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, algebra] ∎

source_lines.74: 1.3 Cores and their height matrices. For a componentwise $e$-core let $b_{ia}$ be the largest bead on runner $i$ ($0\le i<e$) and $t_{ia}=(b_{ia}-i)/e$, so the packed beta set on runner $i$ is $\{i+ek:k\le t_{ia}\}$. Counting beads $\ge-eL$ for large $L$ gives the column sums $\sum_i t_{ia}=c_a-e$. Writing $R_i=\sum_at_{ia}$, the hub satisfies $\delta_i=R_i-R_{i-1}$ for $1\le i<e$ and $\delta_0=R_0-R_{e-1}-\ell$; since $\sum_iR_i=\sum_ac_a-e\ell$ is fixed, equal hub is equivalent to equal row sums. Hence cores of a fixed hub and fixed charges are exactly the integer $e\times\ell$ matrices $T=(t_{ia})$ with fixed row sums $R_i$ and column sums $c_a-e$. [F1, F2, algebra]
source_lines.80: 2.2 The size formula. If $T(\kappa),T(\eta)$ are the height matrices of two such cores, then $|\eta|-|\kappa|=\frac e2\Bigl(\sum_{i,a}t_{ia}(\eta)^2-\sum_{i,a}t_{ia}(\kappa)^2\Bigr).$ Indeed, count the beta numbers $\ge-eL$ in a component: their number is $eL+c_a$, the same for both cores, while their sum changes by $\sum_i i\,\Delta t_{ia}+\frac e2\sum_i\Delta(t_{ia}^2+t_{ia})$; from $\beta_j=\lambda_j+c_a-j$ the change in that sum equals the change in the partition size, and summing over $a$ the equal row sums kill $\sum_i i\sum_a\Delta t_{ia}$ while the equal column sums kill the linear $\sum\Delta t_{ia}$ term. In particular the squared-norm difference is even, so the displayed size difference is an integer multiple of $e$. [F1, step 1.3, algebra]

source_lines.86: 1.2 Equalizing the component weights with charged runners. Choose a component $a$ whose weight exceeds its target and a component $b$ whose weight is deficient. A positive-weight component has a removable rim $e$-hook by [F5]. For each component $c$ use the charged infinite beta set $B_c=\{\lambda_j^{(c)}+c_c-j:j\ge1\}$. This is the ordinary beta display shifted to charge $c_c$, with all sufficiently negative positions occupied and all sufficiently positive positions vacant. A removable hook is a bead move $u\mapsto u-e$ to a gap, and its charged foot residue is $u-e+1$ modulo $e$. To see the foot formula, order the beta positions before and after the move: the affected consecutive rows form the boundary strip between the starting and ending positions, and the leftmost removed box in the last affected row has charged content one more than the ending position. The inverse move wraps a hook whose foot has charged residue one more than its starting position. Let $f$ be the charged foot residue of the hook removed from $a$. In $B_b$, choose the largest occupied integer $v\equiv f-1\pmod e$; it exists by the two tail conditions, and $v+e$ is vacant by maximality. Move $v$ to $v+e$ in component $b$. Its new hook has charged foot residue $v+1=f$. Equivalently, in an uncharged display for component $b$ the runner to use is $f-c_b-1$ modulo $e$, so different component charges cannot be ignored. Both moves stay on their own runners and preserve the component cores and total rank. The earlier of $a,b$ determines the strict dominance orientation: removing boxes there and adding them later decreases every intervening prefix sum; adding boxes there reverses the inequality. In that orientation the equal-remainder hook pair is unique, since the two changed components determine both strips. Its charged foot residues agree, so the foot difference evaluates to zero at $t=1$; it is nonzero over $F(t)$ by [F2], and consequently has a finite positive valuation. Thus the single signed contribution is nonzero, giving a Jantzen edge. If $\delta_c$ is the current component weight minus its target, then $\delta_a\ge1$, $\delta_b\le-1$, and this transfer changes $\sum_c\delta_c^2$ by $-2\delta_a+2\delta_b+2\le-2$. Finitely many such transfers therefore equalize all component weights. [F2, F5, algebra]
source_lines.88: 2.1 Fixed component sizes. For two full multipartitions that differ only in component $a$, every contributing equal-remainder hook pair in $J$ lies in $a$: the other components are unchanged on both sides and cancelling hooks between two unchanged components would return the same multipartition. The common residue factor $Q_at^{na}$ is a unit of $\mathcal O$, and replacing it by the level-one factor $Q_at^m$ multiplies each foot difference by a Laurent unit, so the valuation is unchanged and the full-level $J$ coefficient equals the level-one coefficient of [F2]. Inserting the level-one paths of step 1.1 in component $a$ and leaving the other components fixed connects all multipartitions with equal component sizes and the same component cores. [F1, F2, step 1.1]
source_lines.90: 3.1 Conclusion. Steps 1.2 equalize component sizes along Jantzen edges from any starting multipartition, and step 2.1 connects all multipartitions of fixed component sizes with equal component cores. Composing the two finite chains connects any two multipartitions of rank $n$ with equal componentwise $e$-cores, proving that they are $J$-equivalent; the fixed-size comparison of coefficients is step 2.1. [F1, F2, step 2.1, step 1.2] ∎

source_lines.97: 6.1 The graph, the basic lower bound, and the case of no path. Draw a directed graph $G$ on $\{1,\dots,r\}$ with an arrow $k\to l$ if and only if some $y\in X$ satisfies $y_k-y_l=a_{kl}-1$. First we note that $x_k-x_r\ge a_{kr}+1\qquad\text{for every }k<r:$ for $k=u\ge t+1$ this is the equality $x_u-x_r=a_{ur}+1$ of step 5.1, for $k=t$ it follows from $x_t-x_r\ge a_{tr}+2$, and for $k<t$ it follows from $x_k-x_r=(x_k-x_t)+(x_t-x_r)\ge (a_{kt}-1)+(a_{tr}+2)=a_{kr}+1$ using the known bound for the pair $(k,t)$ with $k,t\le r-1$. Suppose first that $G$ contains no directed path from $t$ to $r$. Let $T$ be the set of vertices reachable from $t$ (so $t\in T$, $r\notin T$) and let $R$ be its complement; there is no arrow from $T$ to $R$, since such an arrow would put its target in $T$. Define new potentials $\hat s_k:=s_k+1$ for $k\in T$ and $\hat s_k:=s_k$ for $k\in R$, and set $\hat a_{kl}:=\hat s_k-\hat s_l$. Then $\hat a_{tr}=a_{tr}+1,\qquad \hat a_{kl}\in\{a_{kl}-1,a_{kl},a_{kl}+1\},$ and $\hat a_{kl}=a_{kl}-1$ occurs exactly for $k\in R$, $l\in T$. The new $(t,r)$ bound follows from the sandwich of step 5.1: $\hat a_{tr}-1=a_{tr}\le y_t-y_r\le a_{tr}+2=\hat a_{tr}+1$ for all $y\in X$. For any other pair the bound is immediate if $\hat a_{kl}\ge a_{kl}$, since the old upper bound $y_k-y_l\le a_{kl}+1\le\hat a_{kl}+1$ survives. If $\hat a_{kl}=a_{kl}-1$, then $k\in R$, $l\in T$; the absence of an arrow from $T$ to $R$ says no $y$ has $y_l-y_k=a_{lk}-1$, so the old lower bound $y_l-y_k\ge a_{lk}-1$ improves to $y_l-y_k\ge a_{lk}$ for all $y$, i.e. $y_k-y_l\le -a_{lk}=a_{kl}=\hat a_{kl}+1$. Thus the bounds hold for all pairs with both entries in $\{t,\dots,r\}$, as required, and stage $t$ is complete in the no-path case. [step 5.1, algebra]
source_lines.99: 7.1 The case of a path: the witnesses. Now suppose $G$ contains a directed path from $t$ to $r$, and let $t=k_1\to k_2\to\cdots\to k_h=r$ be one of minimal length (so $k_1,\dots,k_h$ are pairwise distinct by [F2]). For each $m=1,\dots,h-1$ choose an occurrence $y_m\in X$ witnessing the arrow $k_m\to k_{m+1}$, i.e. $y_{m,k_m}-y_{m,k_{m+1}}=a_{k_mk_{m+1}}-1$, Distinct edges have distinct witnessing occurrences. Indeed, for any witness put $z=y-s$. The first $r-1$ coordinates have spread at most one. A witness for two edges ending before $r$ would have the same low value at both starts and the same high value at both ends, giving a shortcut from the earlier start to the later end. For a last-edge witness, $z_{k_{h-1}}=z_r-1$; tightness against the chosen $x$ and step 6.1 give $z_k-z_r\ge-1$ for $k<r$, and the old spread bound gives $z_k-z_r\le0$. If it also witnessed an earlier edge, that edge would start at $z_r-1$, giving a shortcut directly to $r$. Both contradict shortestness. Now put $x^{(m)}:=x-e_{k_{m+1}}+e_r\qquad(1\le m<h),$ so that $x^{(h-1)}=x$ because $k_h=r$. We shall prove by downward induction on $m$ that there is a multiset $Y_m\equiv X$ (in the equivalence relation generated by zero exchanges) containing $x^{(m)}$ and every occurrence among $y_1,\dots,y_m$ other than the chosen moving occurrence $x$, and that the following two statements hold: $B_m:\quad (x^{(m)}_{k_m}-x^{(m)}_{k_{m+1}})-(y_{m,k_m}-y_{m,k_{m+1}})=2, \qquad C_m:\quad x_{k_m}-x_r=a_{k_m r}+1 .$ Reading $C_1$ together with step 4.1 (which gives $x_{k_1}-x_r=x_t-x_r\ge a_{tr}+2$) will then contradict the choice of $x$; the contradiction is completed below. We record $B_{h-1}$ and $C_{h-1}$: by the basic lower bound of step 6.1, $(x_{k_{h-1}}-x_r)-(y_{h-1,k_{h-1}}-y_{h-1,r})\ge(a_{k_{h-1}r}+1)-(a_{k_{h-1}r}-1)=2$, while tightness of $Y_{h-1}:=X$ gives $\le2$; hence equality holds, which is $B_{h-1}$, and then $C_{h-1}$ follows because $y_{h-1,k_{h-1}}-y_{h-1,r}=a_{k_{h-1}r}-1$ and $(x_{k_{h-1}}-x_r)-(y_{h-1,k_{h-1}}-y_{h-1,r})=2$. [step 6.1, given]

source_lines.46: 1.1 Every right coset of $W_P$ has a minimal-length representative $w$; minimality gives $w(P)\subset R_L^+$, since otherwise right multiplication by a corresponding simple reflection decreases its inversion number. Such a $w$ sends all positive subsystem roots to positive roots. Along a reduced word for $v\in W_P$, inversion numbers therefore increase at each step of $wv$, giving $\ell(wv)=\ell(w)+\ell(v)$. Conversely this equality shows $w$ is the unique minimum in its coset: if $u=wv$ were another minimum its length would be $\ell(w)+\ell(v)$, forcing $v=1$. Thus $W^P$ is exactly this set of representatives. Applying [F1] to finite products and the cross-relations shows $H_P$ has basis $N_v\theta_\ell$ for $v\in W_P$, $\ell\in L$: these elements span the subalgebra because cross-relations and finite Hecke multiplication keep all finite Weyl indices in $W_P$, and are independent as a subset of the PBW basis of $H$. The length-additive factorization $N_{wv}=N_wN_v$ now proves $H=\bigoplus_{w\in W^P}N_wH_P$. Tensoring gives $I_P(V)=\bigoplus_{w\in W^P}N_w\otimes V$, including the injected identity summand, which is $H_P$-stable. [F1, F2, algebra]
source_lines.48: 2.1 Repeatedly move $f\in A$ through a reduced word for $N_w$ using [F1]. The leading term is $N_w w^{-1}(f)$; each correction omits at least one generator, so after finite Hecke multiplication it is a linear combination of $N_vg_v$ with $\ell(v)<\ell(w)$ and $g_v\in A$. Factoring each $v=up$ with $u\in W^P$, $p\in W_P$, gives $\ell(u)\le\ell(v)<\ell(w)$. The subspaces of $I_P(V)$ spanned by summands with representative length at most $k$ are therefore $A$-stable. Their successive quotients are direct sums indexed by the representatives of length $k$, with $f$ acting on the $w$-summand as $w^{-1}(f)$ on $V$. Commuting invertible operators $\theta_\ell$ can be simultaneously decomposed into generalized eigenspaces: take one lattice basis, split into generalized eigenspaces of the first operator, and successively split each stable summand for the remaining finitely many operators. In an invariant-subspace exact sequence the generalized $t$-weight spaces form an exact sequence, since their projections are polynomials in these commuting operators (finite-dimensional polynomial interpolation). This proves the multiset formula, including multiplicities and exactness under submodules and quotients. [F1, F3, step 1.1, algebra]

source_lines.24: Let $f^\lambda=|\operatorname{Std}(\lambda)|$ for an $r$-multipartition $\lambda$ of $n$. There is an explicit bijection between **$r$-colored permutations** $(\sigma,\kappa)\in S_n\times\{1,\ldots,r\}^n$ and pairs $(P,Q)$ of standard multitableaux of a common shape. Its forward map scans positions $i=1,\ldots,n$: if $\kappa_i=c$, row-insert the value $\sigma(i)$ into component $c$ of $P$ and place the recording label $i$ in the new box of component $c$ of $Q$. Its inverse scans $i=n,n-1,\ldots,1$: find the unique component whose recording tableau contains $i$, delete that recording corner, and reverse-row-delete the corresponding box of its insertion tableau to recover $\sigma(i)$; the component is $\kappa_i$. Consequently,
source_lines.40: 1.1 For each color $c$, take the subsequence of values $\sigma(i)$ with $\kappa_i=c$, in increasing order of their positions $i$. If its values are not $1,\ldots,m$ in that order, replace them by their increasing ranks before applying ordinary row insertion. The insertion and reverse-deletion routes use only comparisons, so this order-preserving relabelling leaves every bumping position unchanged; after reverse deletion, replace ranks by the original values in the same order. Thus [F1] gives standard insertion and recording tableaux of the same shape for every color subsequence, including an arbitrary subset of $\{1,\ldots,n\}$. At the step for position $i$, record $i$ in the new box of $Q^{(c)}$. Their entries across components are the values $1,\ldots,n$ once in $P$, and the positions $1,\ldots,n$ once in $Q$, so $P,Q$ are standard multitableaux of the same multipartition. This is the stated forward map. [F1, F2]
source_lines.42: 1.2 To invert, begin with standard multitableaux $(P,Q)$ of common shape. At global step $i=n,n-1,\ldots,1$, there is exactly one component $c$ with recording entry $i$. Since every recording component is standard and all larger global labels have already been removed, $i$ is the largest entry in the current $Q^{(c)}$ and occupies a removable corner. Remove that box from $Q^{(c)}$. In $P^{(c)}$, replace the current set of distinct values by their increasing ranks, reverse-row-delete the same corner, and replace the expelled rank by the corresponding original value; this works because both bumping and reverse deletion use only comparisons. Define that value to be $\sigma(i)$ and set $\kappa_i=c$. The process is defined at every step and ends with empty tableaux. [F1, F2]

source_lines.29: A **finite two-way relay channel** is the three-node DMN of [[def-finite-discrete-memoryless-network-and-code]] with terminal inputs $X_1,X_2$, relay input $X_r$, terminal outputs $Y_1,Y_2$, relay observation $Y_r$, and transition law $W(y_1,y_2,y_r\mid x_1,x_2,x_r)$. Terminals 1 and 2 have independent uniform messages $M_1$ and $M_2$ and wish to exchange them. A causal code uses $X_{1,i}=f_{1,i}(M_1,Y_1^{i-1})$, $X_{2,i}=f_{2,i}(M_2,Y_2^{i-1})$, and $X_{r,i}=f_{r,i}(Y_r^{i-1})$; terminal 1 estimates $M_2$ from $(M_1,Y_1^n)$ and terminal 2 estimates $M_1$ from $(M_2,Y_2^n)$. The probability of error is the probability either estimate is wrong. This is a full-duplex model: all three nodes choose an input at every use, and each input depends only on that node's message and past observations.

Write $H(P_S):=-\sum_{s:P_S(s)>0}P_S(s)\ln P_S(s)$ for source entropy in nats. Fix positive integers $n_k$ with $n_k/k\to\rho\in(0,\infty)$. A deterministic $(k,n_k)$ joint code is as in [[def-it-point-to-point-joint-source-channel-code]]. If $H(P_S)=0$, a zero-error code sequence exists for every such $W$. If $H(P_S)<\rho C(W)$, there are codes with block error tending to zero. Conversely, every code sequence with block error tending to zero satisfies $H(P_S)\le\rho C(W)$. Thus strict violation $H(P_S)>\rho C(W)$ rules out reliable transmission; the positive-entropy equality boundary is not asserted.

source_lines.40: Let $(M_0,g_0)$ be a compact connected smooth Riemannian manifold with smooth boundary. A geodesic segment in $M_0$ satisfies the geodesic equation for the Levi-Civita connection of $g_0$ on $(0,L)$ and extends smoothly to its endpoints, where derivatives are interpreted one-sided. A nontangential maximal geodesic segment is a unit-speed geodesic $\gamma:[0,L]\to M_0$, with $L>0$, whose initial velocity points strictly inward at $\partial M_0$, whose terminal velocity points strictly outward at $\partial M_0$, and whose points for $0<t<L$ lie in $M_0^\circ$. For $f\in C_c^\infty(M_0^\circ,\mathbb R)$ define its geodesic ray transform by $I_{g_0}f(\gamma)=\int_0^L f(\gamma(t))\,dt$. The unweighted scalar ray transform is called injective on compactly supported smooth functions if $I_{g_0}f(\gamma)=0$ for every such segment implies $f=0$. For complex-valued $f$, injectivity means injectivity of its real and imaginary parts separately.

source_lines.42: For a boundary chart $\phi:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb H^2$, let $o_\phi(x)$ be the ray obtained by applying $\det(d\phi_x^{-1})$ to the standard positive ray in $\det\mathbb R^2$. Give $\widetilde M$ the smooth boundary-chart structure whose two local sheets over $U$ are $\{(x,o_\phi(x)):x\in U\}$ and $\{(x,-o_\phi(x)):x\in U\}$, each with coordinate map $(x,\pm o_\phi(x))\mapsto\phi(x)$. On an overlap with a second chart $\psi$, the sheet sign changes by $\operatorname{sgn}\det D(\psi\circ\phi^{-1})$; this sign is locally constant, so the sheet transitions are smooth half-space transitions. Thus $\pi$ is the associated two-sheeted smooth covering map, including over the boundary. The involution $\tau(x,o_x)=(x,-o_x)$ exchanges the sheets. The canonical orientation of $\widetilde M$ at $(x,o_x)$ is the ray $(\det d\pi_{(x,o_x)})^{-1}(o_x)$ in $\det T_{(x,o_x)}\widetilde M$.

In the standard solid torus $V=S^1\times D^2$, let $P_{2,1}$ be the oriented curve $s\mapsto(e^{4\pi i s},r e^{2\pi i s})$ on an interior parallel torus, where $0<r<1$. Let $K=T(2,3)$ be the right trefoil and use the companion embedding that matches the product meridian and longitude of $V$ to the positive meridian and preferred longitude of $K$. The outer torus of $X_{P_{2,1}}$ is incompressible, and $X_{P_{2,1}}$ is not a product $T^2\times[0,1]$ with its outer and inner tori as ends. The companion torus $T_c$ is essential; both pieces of $E_{P_{2,1}(K)}$ cut along $T_c$ are Seifert-fibered, while the whole satellite exterior is neither atoroidal nor Seifert-fibered. Let $M=H_-\cup_\varphi H_+$ be a Heegaard splitting of a closed oriented smooth $3$-manifold, let $\Sigma=\partial H_-=\partial H_+$, and let $c\subset\Sigma$ be an embedded circle with a chosen annular neighbourhood. If $\varphi$ is replaced by $\varphi\circ\tau_c$ or $\varphi\circ\tau_c^{-1}$, where $\tau_c$ is a Dehn twist in the chosen annular coordinates, the resulting oriented $3$-manifold is obtained from $M$ by one surgery on a knot $K$ obtained by pushing $c$ into the interior of $H_-$. The annulus between $c$ and the boundary of a tubular neighbourhood of $K$ supplies a framing; the surgery meridian is identified with $\mu+ \lambda_A$ or $\mu-\lambda_A$, according to the twist direction, where $\mu$ is the meridian of $K$ and $\lambda_A$ is the parallel determined by that annulus. Thus the surgery coefficient relative to this framing is integral with absolute value $1$.

source_lines.88: 1.2 Let $M=E_K(p/q)$ and choose a bicollar of the gluing torus. Thickening the exterior and attached solid torus across this collar gives an open cover of $M$ whose two sets retract to the pieces and whose intersection retracts to $T_K$. Write $\alpha=p\mu+q\lambda$, and choose $\beta=r\mu+s\lambda$ with $ps-qr=1$, so $\alpha,\beta$ form a basis of $H_1(T_K;\mathbb Z)$. In the Mayer–Vietoris map, $\alpha$ maps to $(p[\mu],0)$ because it bounds the attached solid-torus meridian disk, and $\beta$ maps to $(r[\mu],\pm v)$ where $v$ generates the first homology of the attached solid torus; the coefficient is $\pm1$ because $\beta$ intersects $\alpha$ once. The pieces and their overlap are path-connected: the exterior is a connected manifold and hence path-connected, and the solid torus and boundary torus are path-connected. By [F6], the following $H_0$ map sends $1$ to $(1,-1)$ and is injective. Exactness therefore identifies $H_1(M;\mathbb Z)$ with the cokernel of the $H_1$ map. source_lines.78: 1.2 Choose a minimum genus surface $F$ for $K\#J$ and, among such surfaces transverse to the standard sum sphere $S$, one minimizing the finite number of circular components of $F\cap S$. Such a surface exists by [F1], [F3], and well-ordering of the nonnegative integers. The intersection is a compact one-manifold whose boundary is the two points $(K\#J)\cap S$, hence consists of one arc $\alpha$ and finitely many circles. [given, F1, F3, F5, A1, choose]
source_lines.84: 3.2 If $c$ separates $F$, cutting gives a component $F_K$ containing the knot boundary and a component $F_0$ with boundary $c$. Let their genera be $h_K,h_0$. Since $F_K$ has two boundary components and $F_0$ has one, Euler characteristic additivity along the cut and [F2] give $g(F)=h_K+h_0$. Cap $F_K$ by a parallel copy of $D$ and discard $F_0$. If $h_0>0$ this is a lower genus spanning surface, contradiction; if $h_0=0$, it is another minimum genus surface with fewer intersection circles, contradicting the choice in step 1.2. The cap is embedded after rounding in the local product neighbourhood from step 2.1. Thus no circle can occur. [given, F2, step 1.2, step 2.1, construct, algebra]
source_lines.86: 4.1 With no circles, $F\cap S=\alpha$. Since $S$ separates the two knot pieces in the standard sum model, the proper arc $\alpha$ separates $F$ into two connected surfaces $F_1,F_2$, each with one boundary component. Cutting along an arc increases total Euler characteristic by $1$, so [F2] gives $g(F)=g(F_1)+g(F_2)$. The two surfaces are connected because any component of either side not incident to $\alpha$ would already be a separate component of $F$; the sole arc has just one collar on each side. Their boundary circles consist of the corresponding knot subarc and $\alpha\subset S$, and hence represent $K$ and $J$ by [L1] and the original connected-sum datum. Thus $g(K)+g(J)\le g(F_1)+g(F_2)=g(F)=g(K\#J)$. Together with step 1.1 this proves the full equality. [given, F2, F5, L1, step 1.1, step 3.1, step 3.2, algebra] ∎

source_lines.43: 1.1 For $A_2$ take $\Phi_A=\{u_0,\ldots,u_5\}$. This finite set spans the plane, is reduced, and each root reflection is a symmetry of the regular hexagon. Its Cartan integers are $2\cos\theta\in\{0,\pm1,\pm2\}$. Put $\alpha=u_0$ and $\beta=u_2$; then $\Phi_A^+=\{\alpha,\beta,\alpha+\beta\}$ is a positive system with base $(\alpha,\beta)$, and $(\alpha,\beta)=-1/2$. Thus its Cartan matrix is $\begin{pmatrix}2&-1\\-1&2\end{pmatrix}$ and its off-diagonal Cartan product is $1$. [L2, algebra]
source_lines.45: 1.2 For $B_2$ take $\Phi_B=\{\pm e_1,\pm e_2,\pm e_1\pm e_2\}$. This finite set spans the plane, omits zero, and is reduced. The reflections in the coordinate roots change one sign, while those in $e_1\pm e_2$ interchange the coordinates with possible sign changes, so every root reflection preserves $\Phi_B$; direct pairings give Cartan integers in $\{0,\pm1,\pm2\}$. The roots $\alpha=e_1-e_2$ and $\beta=e_2$ form a base, since the positive roots are $\alpha,\beta,\alpha+\beta,\alpha+2\beta$. Moreover $(\alpha,\alpha)=2$, $(\beta,\beta)=1$, and $(\alpha,\beta)=-1$, so the Cartan matrix for $(\alpha,\beta)$ is $\begin{pmatrix}2&-1\\-2&2\end{pmatrix}$ and its off-diagonal Cartan product is $2$. [L2, algebra]
source_lines.47: 1.3 For $G_2$, choose $\alpha,\beta$ with $(\alpha,\alpha)=6$, $(\beta,\beta)=2$, $(\alpha,\beta)=-3$ and put $$\Phi_G=\{\pm\alpha,\pm\beta,\pm(\alpha+\beta),\pm(\alpha+2\beta),\pm(\alpha+3\beta),\pm(2\alpha+3\beta)\}.$$ The Gram determinant is positive, so $\alpha,\beta$ form a basis; the displayed coefficient pairs then show that $\Phi_G$ is finite, spans the plane, omits zero, and is reduced. The reflection $s_\alpha$ interchanges $\beta$ with $\alpha+\beta$ and $\alpha+3\beta$ with $2\alpha+3\beta$, and fixes $\alpha+2\beta$; the reflection $s_\beta$ interchanges $\alpha$ with $\alpha+3\beta$ and $\alpha+\beta$ with $\alpha+2\beta$, and fixes $2\alpha+3\beta$. Together with the images of $\alpha$ and $\beta$, these permutations show that the long and short roots are the two orbits of the simple reflections. Conjugating $s_\alpha$ or $s_\beta$ therefore proves reflection closure for every root. Direct pairings give integral Cartan integers in $\{0,\pm1,\pm2,\pm3\}$. The six displayed unnegated roots are positive and have base $(\alpha,\beta)$, whose Cartan matrix is $\begin{pmatrix}2&-1\\-3&2\end{pmatrix}$ and whose off-diagonal Cartan product is $3$. [L2, algebra]

source_lines.32: ideals.
source_lines.40: [L1] A finite-dimensional complex semisimple Lie algebra is a finite direct sum of simple ideals ([[thm-semisimple-lie-algebras-decompose-as-direct-sums-of-simple-ideals]]).
source_lines.44: [L3] Relative to any decomposition of a semisimple algebra into simple ideals, every ideal is the sum of a subfamily of the simple factors ([[prop-ideals-and-quotients-of-semisimple-lie-algebras]]).
source_lines.50: 1.1 The simple-ideal decomposition is unique up to order. Indeed, given decompositions $\mathfrak g=\bigoplus_{i=1}^m\mathfrak g_i=\bigoplus_{j=1}^n\mathfrak h_j$, [L3] writes each ideal $\mathfrak g_i$ as a sum of a subfamily of the $\mathfrak h_j$. Simplicity and nonzeroness force that subfamily to consist of exactly one factor, so $\mathfrak g_i=\mathfrak h_j$ for a unique $j$. Distinct $i$ give distinct $j$, and every $\mathfrak h_j$ occurs because the $\mathfrak g_i$ span $\mathfrak g$. Thus $m=n$ and the two families agree after a permutation. [L1, L3, algebra]
source_lines.54: 2.1 By [L1] write $\mathfrak g=\mathfrak g_1\oplus\cdots\oplus\mathfrak g_m$ as a direct sum of simple ideals. Each $\mathfrak g_j$ is a finite-dimensional complex simple Lie algebra, so by [L2] it has a connected finite-type Dynkin diagram, well defined up to isomorphism, and step 1.1 makes the resulting multiset depend only on the isomorphism class of $\mathfrak g$. [L1, L2, step 1.1, algebra]

source_lines.27: Let $\lambda$ be regular dominant integral in type $A_2$. The six distinct weights $w\mathbin\cdot\lambda$ are indexed by $W=S_3$, and there is an embedding $M(w\mathbin\cdot\lambda)\hookrightarrow M(v\mathbin\cdot\lambda)$ exactly when $v\le w$ in Bruhat order. Thus the directed Hasse diagram runs from the longest element's Verma module down through the two length-two, two length-one, and identity vertices as inclusions into $M(\lambda)$.
source_lines.37: 1.1 Put $p=\langle\lambda+\rho,\alpha_1^\vee\rangle$ and $q=\langle\lambda+\rho,\alpha_2^\vee\rangle$. Both are positive integers. Write $s=s_{\alpha_1}$, $t=s_{\alpha_2}$, and $w_0=sts=tst$. In the simple-root basis, the displacements $\lambda-w\cdot\lambda$ for $w=e,s,t,st,ts,w_0$ are respectively $$ (0,0),\quad(p,0),\quad(0,q),\quad(p+q,q),\quad(p,p+q),\quad(p+q,p+q). $$ These are six distinct points. Their coordinatewise order is exactly Bruhat comparability: $e$ is below all, $s,t$ are incomparable, $st,ts$ are incomparable, and each length-one vertex lies below each length-two vertex, with $w_0$ above all. [given, algebra]
source_lines.39: 2.1 The simple-root singular-vector theorem gives embeddings for six of the eight Bruhat covers: $e<s$, $e<t$, $s<ts$, $t<st$, $st<w_0$, and $ts<w_0$. Their positive integral exponents are respectively $p,q,p+q,p+q,p,q$. The two remaining covers are $s<st$ and $t<ts$, each a reflection in $\alpha_1+\alpha_2$. [step 1.1, given, algebra]
source_lines.43: 3.1 Composing the eight cover embeddings from steps 2.1 and 2.2 gives an embedding whenever $v\le w$ in Bruhat order. Conversely, any nonzero map $M(w\cdot\lambda)\to M(v\cdot\lambda)$ sends its highest vector to a nonzero vector of weight $w\cdot\lambda$ in the target. The PBW weight model therefore requires $v\cdot\lambda-w\cdot\lambda\in Q^+$, which by the six displacements in step 1.1 is equivalent to $v\le w$. This proves the exact embedding poset. [step 1.1, step 2.1, step 2.2, given] ∎

source_lines.36: 1.1 Direct composition gives $1=123$, $a=213$, $b=132$, $ab=231$, $ba=312$, and $aba=bab=321$. No word of length at most two represents $321$: after canceling $aa=bb=1$, the list of such words is $1,a,b,ab,ba$. Thus these six words have lengths $0,1,1,2,2,3$ respectively. At lengths one and two the indicated reduced words are unique. At length three any adjacent repetition cancels, so the only reduced words are $aba$ and $bab$, both for $321$. This enumerates every reduced expression of every element. [given]
source_lines.40: 3.1 Its covers are $1\to a,b$; $a\to ab,ba$ and $b\to ab,ba$; and $ab,ba\to321$. Each is left multiplication by a transposition. For the middle four covers, compute $(ab)a^{-1}=aba=(13)$, $(ba)a^{-1}=b$, $(ab)b^{-1}=a$, and $(ba)b^{-1}=bab=(13)$. For the last two use $321=bab$ to get $321(ab)^{-1}=b$, and $321=aba$ to get $321(ba)^{-1}=a$. The first two use $a,b$ themselves. Each cover raises length by one. Conversely any transposition multiplication raising length by one must connect adjacent ranks, and the displayed list includes every possible pair of adjacent ranks. Thus chains of such multiplications give exactly the subword order computed in 2.1; both usual strong Bruhat conventions agree here. [step 1.1, step 2.1]

In the A2 setting of [[ex-the-a2-bgg-resolution-with-six-verma-summands]], the interval $[e,s_1s_2]$ has exactly two saturated paths $s_1s_2\rhd s_1\rhd e$ and $s_1s_2\rhd s_2\rhd e$, and the interval $[s_1,w_0]$ has exactly two saturated paths $w_0\rhd s_1s_2\rhd s_1$ and $w_0\rhd s_2s_1\rhd s_1$. In each case the two composites of canonical inclusions $M(x\circ\lambda)\to M(y\circ\lambda)$ coincide, while the two products of signs are opposite, so the corresponding component of $d^2$ vanishes: for the $(w_0,s_1)$-component of the composite of the last two differentials one computes

source_lines.49: [F1] In type A2 the interval $\{e,s_1,s_2,s_1s_2\}$ has $\ell(s_1s_2)=2$ and $\ell(e)=0$, and both $s_1$ and $s_2$ lie strictly between because each is a reduced subword of $s_1s_2$ and covers $e$; hence its two intermediate elements are $s_1,s_2$ and the two saturated paths are $s_1s_2\rhd s_1\rhd e$ and $s_1s_2\rhd s_2\rhd e$. Likewise $\{s_1,s_1s_2,s_2s_1,w_0\}$ has $\ell(w_0)=3$, $\ell(s_1)=1$, and both $s_1s_2$ and $s_2s_1$ lie strictly between because $w_0=s_2s_1s_2$ contains $s_2s_1$ as a subword and $s_1$ is a subword of both $s_1s_2$ and $s_2s_1$; hence its two saturated paths are $w_0\rhd s_1s_2\rhd s_1$ and $w_0\rhd s_2s_1\rhd s_1$. The diamond lemma identifies these as the only saturated paths of the two intervals ([[lem-bruhat-rank-two-intervals-are-diamonds]], [[lem-bruhat-covers-are-reflection-covers]], [[def-bgg-bruhat-verma-sum-in-degree-k]]).

source_lines.62: 1.1 Suppose first that all edges of $\Gamma$ are simple and there is no trivalent vertex. Then by [L1] the graph is a path on $n\ge1$ vertices, and the Cartan matrix is the $A_n$ matrix $a_{ii}=2$, $a_{i,i+1}=a_{i+1,i}=-1$, $a_{ij}=0$ for $|i-j|\ge2$; the corresponding root system is $A_n$. [L1, L2, algebra]
source_lines.68: 1.4 The diagram types are distinguished by rank, edge multiplicities and positions, and, for a simply-laced branch, the unordered arm lengths. At rank $n\ge4$ the $D_n$ arms $(1,1,n-3)$ differ from the exceptional arms, which all have just one arm of length $1$. Reversing the path interchanges the two orientations for $F_4$ and for $G_2$, so these introduce no extra types. To check unbased uniqueness it remains to explain why isomorphisms preserve diagram types. In particular $B_n$ and $C_n$ for $n\ge3$ are non-isomorphic even as unbased root systems. If an isomorphism $\varphi:B_n\to C_n$ existed, the image of a chosen base $\Delta_B$ would be a base. Indeed it is a basis of roots, every root has integral coefficients of one sign relative to it because this is true relative to $\Delta_B$ and $\varphi$ is linear, and a vector pairing positively with every member of $\varphi(\Delta_B)$ therefore defines the corresponding positive system, whose indecomposable roots are precisely those basis vectors. By [L4] a Weyl element of $C_n$ carries $\varphi(\Delta_B)$ to the standard base $\Delta_C$. After ordering the bases, the composite based isomorphism would identify their Cartan matrices up to a simultaneous row-and-column permutation, because it preserves every Cartan integer. But for $n\ge3$ the $B_n$ and $C_n$ matrices are transposes and no vertex permutation identifies them: the unique double edge fixes its end of the path, while its arrow is reversed. This contradiction proves non-isomorphism. For $n=2$ the two orientations of the single double edge are interchanged by permuting the two vertices, so [L2] gives $B_2\cong C_2$; and for $n=1$ the unique reduced rank-one system $\{\pm\alpha\}$ is simultaneously $A_1$, $B_1$ and $C_1$. [L2, L3, L4, algebra]
source_lines.70: 1.5 For the low-rank $D$ coincidences, use the coordinate set $D_n=\{\pm e_i\pm e_j:i<j\}$ at $n=2,3$. These are root systems: a reflection in $e_i-e_j$ exchanges coordinates $i,j$, and one in $e_i+e_j$ exchanges them and negates both, preserving this set. Every root has squared norm $2$, pairwise inner products are integers, reducedness is immediate, and the displayed roots span. For $D_3$ put $a=e_1-e_2$, $b=e_2-e_3$, $c=e_2+e_3$. Its roots are exactly the positives and negatives of $$a,\ b,\ c,\ a+b,\ a+c,\ a+b+c.$$ The vector $(2,1,0)$ pairs positively with all three basis vectors, and this list shows they are exactly the simple positive roots. Their squared lengths are $2$, with $(a,b)=(a,c)=-1$ and $(b,c)=0$, so the diagram is the three-vertex path $b-a-c$, giving $D_3\cong A_3$ by [L2]. In $D_2$, the two root lines generated by $e_1+e_2$ and $e_1-e_2$ are orthogonal, each containing just a pair of opposite roots, giving $A_1\sqcup A_1$. In particular arms $(1,1,1)$ describe $D_4$, not $D_3$. [L2, L5, algebra]

source_lines.41: Assume the general DQM density-version convention uses AC and the mean-zero Hilbert-space convention uses Countable Choice; the two-point densities below are explicit, so this proof itself makes no choice. Let $\mathcal X=\{-1,+1\}$ with all subsets measurable and let $P_\theta\{x\}=(1+\theta x)/2$ for $\theta\in[0,1]$. At the boundary law $P_0$, consider allowed one-sided paths $t\mapsto P_{\theta(t)}$ with $\theta(0)=0$, $\theta(t)\in[0,1]$, and an existing right derivative at zero. Their DQM score set is the cone $\{aX:a\ge0\}$, while its closed linear tangent space is all of $L^2_0(P_0)=\{bX:b\in\mathbb R\}$. Thus the score set and its linear tangent space are distinct.
source_lines.69: **Proof technique:** Identify every one-sided score and compare its cone with its real linear span.
source_lines.75: 2.2 Conversely, for each $a\ge0$, take $\theta(t)=at$ for sufficiently small $t\ge0$. The two-coordinate counting-measure $L^2$ remainder is $o(t)$, so this path has score $aX$. Its densities are explicit, so [A1] requires no selection in this construction. Thus every vector on the nonnegative ray is an allowed score. [given, A1, F1, F7, step 1.1, algebra]

The constraints $\theta(t)\ge0$ and $t>0$ force the limit $a:=s(+1)$ to be nonnegative, and $s(-1)=-a$; hence every score is $s(x)=ax$ with $a\ge0$. [step 2.1, F2, algebra]

source_lines.43: Take two independent Bernoulli samples of sizes $n_1,n_2\ge1$ and test the one-sided alternative that the first success probability exceeds the second. Under the null, all $N=n_1+n_2$ trials have a common success probability $p\in[0,1]$. Let $K$ be the number of successes in the first sample and $S$ the total number in both samples. For every integer margin $s\in\{0,\ldots,N\}$, define the supplied conditional-law kernel $Q$ by
source_lines.45: and set $Q(s,\{k\})=0$ outside the displayed range. For each $s$, these weights sum to one because they count all $\binom Ns$ ways to choose the $s$ success positions according to how many lie in the first sample. At margins of positive probability this is the conditional law and it does not depend on $p$; at endpoint nulls $p=0,1$, the formula also supplies a version at the other, probability-zero margins. Large values of $K$ support the one-sided alternative that the first sample has a larger success probability. For $n_1=n_2=2$ and $s=2$, the conditional masses at $k=0,1,2$ are $1/6,4/6,1/6$; the inclusive upper-tail p-values are $1,5/6,1/6$.
source_lines.67: 2.1 There are $\binom{N}{s}$ sequences with $s$ successes. Exactly $\binom{n_1}{k}\binom{n_2}{s-k}$ of them have $K=k$: choose $k$ of the first $n_1$ positions and $s-k$ of the other $n_2$. These counts partition all size-$s$ subsets, so the displayed kernel weights sum to one for every $s$, and when $P_p(S=s)>0$, dividing by the total count using [F3] gives the conditional mass; the feasible range is precisely where both binomial coefficients are nonzero. At $p=0$ only $S=0$ occurs and $K=0$; at $p=1$ only $S=N$ occurs and $K=n_1$, so the supplied kernel has the required conditional law on the realized margin. At the other, probability-zero margins the same formula is simply the chosen kernel extension. [F1, F3, step 1.1, given, construct, algebra]
source_lines.69: 3.1 For $n_1=n_2=2$ and $s=2$, the feasible values are $k=0,1,2$, with counts $1,4,1$ among the six two-success sequences. Their probabilities are therefore $1/6,4/6,1/6$. Summing the masses at or above each observed value gives inclusive p-values $1,5/6,1/6$. The strict-tail-plus-tie formulas are respectively $5/6+U/6$, $1/6+2U/3$, and $U/6$; their intervals $[5/6,1]$, $[1/6,5/6]$, and $[0,1/6]$ have lengths matching the three conditional masses. source_lines.53: Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $X_i$ be iid $N(\mu,1)$, let the full parameter space be $\Theta=\mathbb R$, and test $H_0:\mu\le0$ against the full model at the boundary value $\mu=0$. The likelihood-ratio statistic converges to $(G\vee0)^2$, where $G\sim N(0,1)$; by [[def-chi-square-law]] this is $\tfrac12\chi_0^2+\tfrac12\chi_1^2$, not the ordinary $\chi_1^2$ law.
source_lines.103: 4.1 Under $\mu=0$, the local sets are $C_n=\mathbb R$ and $C_{0n}=(-\infty,0]$ for every $n$, so they are already their limiting closed convex cones. Direct expansion gives $\ell_n(h/\sqrt n)-\ell_n(0)=hZ_n-h^2/2$ with $Z_n=\sqrt n\bar X_n$ and zero remainder. The full and null local maximizers are $Z_n$ and $\min(0,Z_n)$. By [F4] and the mean and variance from step 1.1, $Z_n\Rightarrow G\sim N(0,1)$. Choose a large $R$ with $P(|G|\ge R)$ small and apply [F5] to the closed tails to see that both maximizer sequences are tight. Thus all hypotheses of [F3] hold with $I=1$. [A1, F3, F4, F5, given, step 1.1, choose, algebra, step 3.1]
source_lines.105: 5.1 Completing the square in $\ell_n(\mu)$ gives the full MLE $\bar X_n$ and the constrained MLE $\min(0,\bar X_n)$. Hence the finite-sample likelihood-ratio statistic is $T_n=2[\ell_n(\bar X_n)-\ell_n(\min(0,\bar X_n))]=n(\bar X_n\vee0)^2=(Z_n\vee0)^2$. By [F5], $T_n\Rightarrow(G\vee0)^2$. Its CDF is $0$ for $t<0$ and $P(G\le\sqrt t)=\Phi(\sqrt t)$ for $t\ge0$, so it has mass $1/2$ at zero. By symmetry, $P(G^2\le t)=2\Phi(\sqrt t)-1$ for $t\ge0$, while [F1] gives $P(G=0)=0$; hence $(G\vee0)^2$ has the mixture law $\tfrac12\delta_0+\tfrac12\mathcal L(G^2)=\tfrac12\chi_0^2+\tfrac12\chi_1^2$, not $\chi_1^2$. [A1, F1, F2, F5, step 4.1, given, algebra] ∎

source_lines.55: Thus $m\ge2$. Write $[m]=\{0,1,\ldots,m-1\}$ and give $[m]^k$ the Hamming

source_lines.58: satisfy $d_H(\omega,\omega')>r$ and

source_lines.84: 1.1 Put $\mathcal W=[m]^k$ and fix a bijection from the finite initial segment of size $m^k$ onto $\mathcal W$, whose existence is [F2]. Scan that finite segment in its natural order, retaining a word exactly when its Hamming distance from every previously retained word is greater than $r$. The scan terminates; its retained set $\mathcal C$ has pairwise distances greater than $r$, and every word not retained lies in a radius-$r$ ball about an earlier retained word. [F2, given, construct]
source_lines.86: 1.2 A Hamming ball of radius $r$ has cardinality $B=\sum_{j=0}^r\binom{k}{j}(m-1)^j$: choose the $j$ coordinates that differ and then one of the other $m-1$ symbols at each such coordinate; different values of $j$ give disjoint sets, so [F3] counts the union. [F3, given, algebra]
source_lines.96: 6.1 Steps 3.1, 4.1, and 5.1 prove the claimed cardinality bound. Index the coordinates by $[d]=\{0,1,\ldots,d-1\}$ and map each word to the vector specified in the Statement; the first $km$ coordinates contain the $k$ blocks because $km\le d$ by [F1]. Each word gives one nonzero coordinate in each block, so $u^\omega$ has exactly $k$ ones. If two words differ in $s$ blocks, their vectors differ in exactly two coordinates per such block. Since $s>r$, discreteness of $\mathbb N$ gives $s\ge r+1$, and [F1] gives $k<4(r+1)$; after applying the order-preserving map in [F2], $\iota_{\mathbb R}(s)\ge\iota_{\mathbb R}(r)+1>\iota_{\mathbb R}(k)/4$. Therefore $\|u^\omega-u^{\omega'}\|_2^2=2\iota_{\mathbb R}(s)>\iota_{\mathbb R}(k)/2$. [step 1.1, step 3.1, step 4.1, step 5.1, F1, F2, algebra] ∎

source_lines.33: Let $d\ge1$, $a>0$, and consider the finite experiment indexed by
source_lines.38: $$v:=\max_{\omega\in\{0,1\}^d,\ 1\le i\le d} \|P_\omega-P_{\omega^{(i)}}\|_{\rm TV}.$$
source_lines.40: $$\max_{\omega}R_\omega(K)\ge\frac{a^2d}{8}(1-v),$$
source_lines.60: 1.1 For each coordinate $i$, define $\phi_i(x)=K(x,\{z\in\mathbb R^d:z_i\ge a/2\})$. This is a measurable $[0,1]$-valued function by [F2]. If the true bit is $0$, an action counted by $\phi_i$ has coordinate squared error at least $a^2/4$; if the true bit is $1$, an action outside that event has coordinate squared error at least $a^2/4$. Thus $R_\omega(K)\ge\frac{a^2}{4}\sum_{i=1}^d \bigl[(1-\omega_i)\,P_\omega\phi_i+\omega_i\,P_\omega(1-\phi_i)\bigr],$ where $P f:=\int f\,dP$. [F1, F2, F3, given, algebra]
source_lines.62: 2.1 For any two probability laws $P,Q$ and measurable $\phi:\mathcal X\to[0,1]$, the finite approximants $\phi_N=N^{-1}\sum_{r=1}^N\mathbf1_{\{\phi\ge r/N\}}$ satisfy $0\le\phi-\phi_N\le1/N$. By [F4], $\int\phi_NdP-\int\phi_NdQ\le\|P-Q\|_{\rm TV}$, and the replacement error is at most $2/N$. Letting $N\to\infty$ gives $\int\phi dP-\int\phi dQ\le\|P-Q\|_{\rm TV}$. Applying the same result to $1-\phi$ gives $P\phi+Q(1-\phi)\ge1-\|P-Q\|_{\rm TV}.$ For each coordinate, pair every hypercube vertex with bit $i=0$ to the unique neighbor with bit $i=1$. There are $2^{d-1}$ such pairs, and each pair's two testing errors in step 1.1 sum to at least $1-v$. Averaging over all $2^d$ vertices therefore gives average coordinate error at least $(1-v)/2$. This establishes the coordinate error bound. [F4, step 1.1, algebra]

source_lines.49: Assume the Axiom of Choice. Fix a deterministic matrix $X\in\mathbb R^{n\times p}$ with $n>p\ge1$ whose $p$ columns are linearly independent. Use the experiment on $(\mathbb R^n,\mathcal B(\mathbb R^n))$ indexed by $(\beta,\sigma^2)\in\mathbb R^p\times(0,\infty)$, with observation $Y=X\beta+\varepsilon$ and independent errors $\varepsilon_i\sim N(0,\sigma^2)$. Define the least-squares statistic and residual sum of squares by
source_lines.50: $$\widehat\beta=(X^TX)^{-1}X^TY,\qquad P_X=X(X^TX)^{-1}X^T,\qquad RSS_X=\|(I_n-P_X)Y\|^2,\qquad S^2=\frac{RSS_X}{n-p},\qquad S=\sqrt{S^2}.$$
source_lines.52: $$\widetilde T_c:=\begin{cases} \dfrac{c^T\widehat\beta-c^T\beta}{S\sqrt{c^T(X^TX)^{-1}c}},&S>0,\\ 0,&S=0 \end{cases} \sim t_{n-p},\qquad \frac{RSS_X}{\sigma^2}\sim\chi_{n-p}^2,$$
source_lines.55: For nested deterministic full and reduced design spaces $W_R\subset W_U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ of dimensions $p-q$ and $p$, where $q$ is an integer and $1\le q\le p<n$, let $P_R,P_U$ be the orthogonal projections onto these spaces and define $RSS_R=\|(I-P_R)Y\|^2$ and $RSS_U=\|(I-P_U)Y\|^2$. Under the null hypothesis that the mean vector belongs to $W_R$,
source_lines.56: $$\widetilde F:=\begin{cases} \dfrac{(RSS_R-RSS_U)/q}{RSS_U/(n-p)},&RSS_U>0,\\ 0,&RSS_U=0 \end{cases} \sim F_{q,n-p}.$$
source_lines.94: 1.1 By full column rank, the columns of $X$ are linearly independent. Apply [F2] to obtain orthonormal columns of $Q\in\mathbb R^{n\times p}$ with the same successive spans. Expressing each column of $X$ in this basis gives $X=QR$, where $R$ is upper triangular; its diagonal entries are the nonzero Gram–Schmidt residual norms, so $R$ is invertible. Let $W=\operatorname{col}X$. The columns of $X$ form a basis of $W$, so $\dim W=p$. By [F3], $\mathbb R^n=W\oplus W^\perp$. The subspace $W^\perp$ is finite-dimensional by [F10], and direct-sum dimension additivity in [F10] gives $n=p+\dim W^\perp$, hence $\dim W^\perp=n-p$. By [F3], choose an orthonormal basis of this complement with exactly $n-p$ vectors as the columns of $Q_0$; together with $Q$ it forms an orthonormal basis $[Q\ Q_0]$ of $\mathbb R^n$. [F2, F3, F10, choose, algebra]
source_lines.96: 2.1 Set $U=[Q\ Q_0]$. Then $U$ is orthogonal. Standardizing the independent errors gives $\eta=\varepsilon/\sigma$ with independent standard-normal coordinates, so [F4] makes $U^T\eta=(Z_Q,Z_0)$ a standard-normal product vector with independent coordinate blocks. Since $X=QR$ and $X^TX=R^TR$, the normal-equation solution in [F1] is $\widehat\beta=R^{-1}Q^TY=\beta+\sigma R^{-1}Z_Q$. Substituting $X=QR$ and $(R^TR)^{-1}=R^{-1}R^{-T}$ gives $P_X=Q R(R^TR)^{-1}R^TQ^T=Q[RR^{-1}R^{-T}R^T]Q^T=QQ^T$, because $RR^{-1}=I_p$ and $R^{-T}R^T=I_p$. Since $U$ is orthogonal, $I_n-P_X=Q_0Q_0^T$. Thus $(I_n-P_X)Y=\sigma Q_0Z_0$, so $RSS_X/\sigma^2=\|Z_0\|^2\sim\chi_{n-p}^2$ by [F5]. By [A2] and [F7], the linear maps defining $\widehat\beta$ and $Q_0Z_0$, and the squared-norm map defining $RSS_X$, are Borel; hence these quantities are measurable functions of the independent coordinate blocks and $\widehat\beta$ is independent of $RSS_X$ by [F4]. The map defining $\widehat\beta$ is linear and Borel, so it is a statistic for the stated experiment. The residual map and squared norm are continuous, so $RSS_X$ and $S$ are continuous. The piecewise t version in the Statement is Borel: its quotient is continuous on the Borel set $S>0$ and its value on $S=0$ is constant. Its denominator has positive degree $n-p$, hence $S>0$ almost surely by [F5]. [A1, A2, F1, F4, F5, F7, step 1.1, algebra]
source_lines.100: 4.1 For the nested models, let $W_D=W_U\cap W_R^\perp$. For $u\in W_U$, its orthogonal decomposition relative to $W_R$ has a $W_R$ component and a remaining component in $W_U\cap W_R^\perp=W_D$, because $W_R\subseteq W_U$. Thus [F3] gives $W_U=W_R\oplus W_D$ and $\mathbb R^n=W_U\oplus W_U^\perp$. All these subspaces are finite-dimensional by [F10]. Applying direct-sum dimension additivity in [F10] to the two decompositions gives $p=(p-q)+\dim W_D$ and $n=p+\dim W_U^\perp$, hence $\dim W_D=q$ and $\dim W_U^\perp=n-p$. Combining the orthogonal decompositions gives $\mathbb R^n=W_R\oplus W_D\oplus W_U^\perp$, including the zero-dimensional $W_R$ case $q=p$. Choose orthonormal bases in these three spaces and concatenate them into an orthogonal matrix $V$. By [F4], the coordinates of $V^T\varepsilon/\sigma$ in the three blocks are independent standard normals. Under the null, $P_R(X\beta)=P_U(X\beta)=X\beta$, so $(I-P_R)Y=(I-P_R)\varepsilon=P_{W_D}\varepsilon+P_{W_U^\perp}\varepsilon$ and $(I-P_U)Y=(I-P_U)\varepsilon=P_{W_U^\perp}\varepsilon$: here [F8] identifies $I-P_R=P_{W_R^\perp}$ and $I-P_U=P_{W_U^\perp}$, while the direct sum in [F3] splits the first projection into the two orthogonal components. The coordinate-block maps and the linear projections are continuous, and squared norms are continuous, so [A2] and [F7] make all these random vectors and real variables measurable. Orthogonality and [F9] give $RSS_R-RSS_U=\sigma^2\sum_{j=1}^{q}G_j^2$ and $RSS_U=\sigma^2\sum_{j=1}^{n-p}H_j^2$, where the $G$ and $H$ coordinate blocks are independent standard-normal blocks. By [F5] these sums are independent $\sigma^2\chi_q^2$ and $\sigma^2\chi_{n-p}^2$ variables; both degrees are positive. The piecewise ratio $\widetilde F$ is Borel, since it is continuous on the Borel set $RSS_U>0$ and constant on $RSS_U=0$. Its value is the scaled ratio on $Q_H:=\sum_{j=1}^{n-p}H_j^2>0$ and $0$ when $Q_H=0$; by [F6] this is exactly the defined $F_{q,n-p}$ version. The F denominator is positive almost surely by [F5], so $\widetilde F\sim F_{q,n-p}$. [A1, A2, F3, F4, F5, F6, F7, F8, F9, F10, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

source_lines.22: Let $p\in\mathbb N_0$ and let $\xi$ be a clamped knot vector as in [[def-b-spline-space-and-basis]]. The recursively defined degree-$p$ B-splines are nonnegative, are supported on $[\xi_j,\xi_{j+p+1}]$, and are piecewise polynomials of degree at most $p$. At a knot of multiplicity $\mu\le p$, each B-spline is $C^{p-\mu}$; multiplicity $p+1$ imposes no continuity requirement. On every nonempty knot interval $[\xi_m,\xi_{m+1})$, the active functions $B_{m-p,p,\xi},\ldots,B_{m,p,\xi}$ form a basis of $\mathcal P_p$ and sum to one. Globally, the $n$ B-splines form a basis of $S_{p,\xi}$. In particular, every $q\in\mathcal P_p$ has a unique expansion $q=\sum_{j=1}^n c_jB_{j,p,\xi}$ on $[a,b]$.
source_lines.36: 1.1 For $p=0$, support, piecewise degree, and nonnegativity follow from the indicator definition in [F1]. Inductively, each degree-$p$ term is a lower-degree spline multiplied by an affine factor; on the lower-degree spline's support that factor is nonnegative, and the two supports lie inside $[\xi_j, \xi_{j+p+1}]$. Thus support, degree at most $p$, and nonnegativity hold for every $p$. [A1, F1, algebra]
source_lines.40: 2.1 Define $\psi_{j,0}(y)=1$ and $\psi_{j,d}(y)=\prod_{r=1}^{d}(y-\xi_{j+r})$. When $\xi_{j+d}>\xi_j$, factoring $\psi_{j,d-1}$ gives $(y-x)\psi_{j,d-1}(y)=\frac{x-\xi_j}{\xi_{j+d}-\xi_j}\psi_{j,d}(y)+\frac{\xi_{j+d}-x}{\xi_{j+d}-\xi_j}\psi_{j-1,d}(y)$. Fix a nonempty cell $[\xi_m,\xi_{m+1})$. At degree zero its sole nonzero indicator is $B_{m,0,\xi}$, so the local identity holds. Inductively, the degree-$(d-1)$ local sum has indices $m-d+1\le j\le m$. For every such index, $\xi_j\le\xi_m<\xi_{m+1}\le\xi_{j+d}$, so the displayed identity has a strictly positive denominator. Multiply that local sum by $y-x$, apply the identity, and regroup with [F1]. The two extra lower-degree functions $B_{m-d,d-1,\xi}$ and $B_{m+1,d-1,\xi}$ vanish on the cell by support, even when their supports are empty; their recurrence terms are zero under [F1]. Thus $(y-x)^d=\sum_{i=m-d}^{m}\psi_{i,d}(y)B_{i,d,\xi}(x)$ for $0\le d\le p$, and in particular for $d=p$. [F1, given, step 1.1, algebra]
source_lines.44: 3.2 Fix an open nonempty knot interval $(\xi_m,\xi_{m+1})$ and $p\ge1$. The $p+1$ dual polynomials $\psi_{i,p}$, $m-p\le i\le m$, form a basis of $\mathcal P_p$ in $y$: differentiating the identity of step 2.1 in $x$ at an interior point $x_0$ shows that their span contains $(y-x_0)^k$ for every $0\le k\le p$. For $m-p+1\le i\le m$, the span $\xi_{i+p}-\xi_i$ is strictly positive and factoring gives $\psi_{i,p}-\psi_{i-1,p}=-(\xi_{i+p}-\xi_i)\psi_{i,p-1}$. Differentiate the degree-$p$ local identity in $x$ and use the degree-$(p-1)$ identity and this difference formula to obtain $\sum_{i=m-p}^{m}B'_{i,p,\xi}\psi_{i,p}=p\sum_{i=m-p+1}^{m}\frac{B_{i,p-1,\xi}}{\xi_{i+p}-\xi_i}(\psi_{i,p}-\psi_{i-1,p})$. Comparison in the dual basis yields $B'_{j,p,\xi}=p\left(\frac{B_{j,p-1,\xi}}{\xi_{j+p}-\xi_j}-\frac{B_{j+1,p-1,\xi}}{\xi_{j+p+1}-\xi_{j+1}}\right)$ on this interval. The boundary lower-degree terms vanish by support; any zero denominator corresponds to an identically zero lower-degree spline and its term is zero. For indices outside the active range both sides vanish by support. [A1, F1, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra]
source_lines.46: 4.1 Taking $k=0$ in step 3.1 gives $\sum_{i=m-p}^{m}B_{i,p,\xi}(x)=1$. Step 3.1 also shows that these $p+1$ active functions span $\mathcal P_p$ on the interval. Because $\dim\mathcal P_p=p+1$, they are linearly independent there and are a local basis. [A1, step 3.1, algebra]
source_lines.48: 4.2 Induct on $p$. If the knot multiplicity $\mu\le p-1$, the lower-degree splines in the recurrence are continuous there by induction, so the recurrence makes $B_{j,p,\xi}$ continuous; the derivative formula then makes its derivative $C^{p-1-\mu}$, hence $B_{j,p,\xi}\in C^{p-\mu}$. If $\mu=p$, a B-spline whose support crosses the repeated knot has one nonzero piece on either side, namely $(x-\xi_j)^p/(\xi_{j+p}-\xi_j)^p$ and $(\xi_{j+p+1}-x)^p/(\xi_{j+p+1}-\xi_{j+1})^p$; both one-sided limits equal $1$, while any B-spline not crossing it has zero endpoint value there. If $\mu=p+1$, the required order is $C^{-1}$ and no matching is asserted. [A1, step 3.2, F1, algebra]

source_lines.24: For a nonnegative integer $q$, let $M=2^q$, set $\omega=1$ when $M=1$ and $\omega=e^{-2\pi i/M}$ when $M>1$, and let $a=(a_0,\ldots,a_{M-1})\in\mathbb C^M$. The forward discrete Fourier transform (DFT) is the vector $\widehat a\in\mathbb C^M$ with $\widehat a_k=\sum_{j=0}^{M-1}a_j\omega^{jk}$. The radix-two procedure returns this vector by the following exact recursion. If $M=1$, return $(a_0)$. If $M>1$, recursively compute the length-$M/2$ DFTs $E$ and $O$ of $(a_0,a_2,\ldots,a_{M-2})$ and $(a_1,a_3,\ldots,a_{M-1})$, using the primitive root $\omega^2$. For $0\le k<M/2$, return $\widehat a_k=E_k+\omega^k O_k$ and $\widehat a_{k+M/2}=E_k-\omega^kO_k$. The inverse transform is obtained by running the same procedure with $\overline\omega$ and dividing every output by $M$.

source_lines.31: Let $D,O\subseteq\mathbb Z^2$ be input and output index sets, let $C_{\rm in},C_{\rm out}$ be positive integers, and let $x:D\to\mathbb R^{C_{\rm in}}$ assign a row vector of input channels to each input site. A boundary extension is a function $\widetilde x:\mathbb Z^2\to\mathbb R^{C_{\rm in}}$ whose restriction to $D$ is $x$; zero padding is the extension that is zero off $D$. Choose a finite receptive-field offset set $K\subseteq\mathbb Z^2$, a positive integer stride vector $s\in\mathbb Z_{>0}^2$, an origin $a\in\mathbb Z^2$, one matrix $W_\delta\in\mathbb R^{C_{\rm in}\times C_{\rm out}}$ for each $\delta\in K$, and an output bias row vector $b\in\mathbb R^{C_{\rm out}}$. The discrete convolutional layer is the map $y:O\to\mathbb R^{C_{\rm out}}$ given by
source_lines.34: y(p)=b+\sum_{\delta\in K}\widetilde x(a+s\odot p+\delta)W_\delta\qquad(p\in O),
source_lines.37: where $s\odot p$ is coordinatewise multiplication. Thus each output uses only the input sites in its receptive field, mixes input channels by matrix multiplication, and uses the same weights and bias at every output site. With unit stride on the full lattice and no boundary truncation, this formula is a discrete cross-correlation; many machine-learning software packages call it convolution. Mathematical convolution instead reverses the kernel offsets. The choices of $O$, the extension $\widetilde x$, and the stride specify cropping, padding, and subsampling, and need not preserve a symmetry of the full lattice.

A fixed shared input map gives $y_i^{(0)}=f_{\rm in}(v_{x_i},p_i)$. For each layer $k=1,\ldots,L$ and head $h=1,\ldots,H$, a fixed score map $s_{k,h}:\mathbb R^d\times\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$ gives scores $a_{i,j}^{(k,h)}=s_{k,h}(y_i^{(k-1)},y_j^{(k-1)})$ for every query position $i$ and key position $j$. In the soft model, $\widehat a_{i,\cdot}^{(k,h)}=\operatorname{softmax}(a_{i,\cdot}^{(k,h)})$. In the hard model, $\widehat a_{i,j}^{(k,h)}=1$ at the smallest index $j$ attaining $\max_{r\le n}a_{i,r}^{(k,h)}$ and is $0$ at other indices. source_lines.28: Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice, so the usual Lebesgue-measurable sets on $\mathbb R$ form a complete measure space with Lebesgue measure $\lambda$. Every bounded interval is Lebesgue measurable, and any interval is the countable union of its bounded intersections with $[-n,n]$; since the Lebesgue-measurable sets form a sigma-algebra, $I$ is measurable and $\lambda$ restricts to $I$. Let $\mathbb F$ be $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval with $t_0\in I$, and let $N,m,p\ge1$ be finite. A continuous-time linear state-space model consists of matrices $A\in\mathbb F^{N\times N}$, $B\in\mathbb F^{N\times m}$, $C\in\mathbb F^{p\times N}$, $D\in\mathbb F^{p\times m}$, an initial value $x_0\in\mathbb F^N$, and an input $u:I\to\mathbb F^m$ whose real and imaginary coordinates are Lebesgue measurable and integrable on every compact subinterval of $I$. A state trajectory is a function $x:I\to\mathbb F^N$ whose real and imaginary coordinates are absolutely continuous on every compact subinterval of $I$ (with absolute continuity defined by the $\varepsilon$–$\delta$ condition on finite families of disjoint subintervals), with $x(t_0)=x_0$ and $x'(t)=Ax(t)+Bu(t)$ outside a Lebesgue-null subset of $I$. Its output is $y(t)=Cx(t)+Du(t)$. The term $Du(t)$ is the direct input-to-output term and is separate from the state contribution $Cx(t)$.

source_lines.39: Let $G,H$ be finite vertex-labeled simple undirected graphs with labels in a common set, and let a depth-$K$ aggregation-based message-passing graph neural network use the same initial embedding, layer maps, and graph readout on both graphs. If one-dimensional Weisfeiler–Leman color refinement has equal graph color multisets on $G$ and $H$ at every round $0,\ldots,K$, then the network gives the same graph output on $G$ and $H$. Equivalently, whenever this network distinguishes the pair, one-dimensional Weisfeiler–Leman distinguishes the pair at some round at most $K$.

source_lines.71: 1.1 By induction on $t=0,\ldots,K$, equal round-$t$ WL colors of vertices from either graph imply equal GNN states after $t$ layers. At $t=0$, the shared initial embedding gives this implication. If it holds at $t$ and two vertices have equal round-$(t+1)$ colors, [F2] says their center colors and neighbor-color multisets agree. By the induction hypothesis, equal neighbor colors have equal GNN states; applying this correspondence occurrence by occurrence gives equal neighbor-state multisets. The shared aggregation and update functions in [F1] therefore give equal next-layer states. Thus a well-defined map from each round-$t$ color occurring in either graph to its common GNN state exists. Define $h_0=h_0(\theta)$, $h_t=\Phi_t(\theta,h_{t-1})$, and $J(\theta)=\ell(\theta,h_T)$. source_lines.40: Input a finite horizon $T>0$, a time step $\Delta t>0$, an age cutoff $A>0$, bounded nonnegative rates $\mu,\beta$ on $[0,A]$, and a finite positive initial quadrature $(a_i,m_i^0)_{i=1}^I$ supported in $[0,A)$ for the initial age measure on that interval. source_lines.27: **Graph convention.** For any finite real column-stochastic matrix $P$ on $S=\{1,\ldots,n\}$, the positive-transition graph has a directed edge $j\to i$ exactly when $P_{ij}>0$. This defines the communicating classes and closed classes for real matrices, whether or not their entries can be computed exactly.
source_lines.31: **Output.** A partition of $S$ into the strongly connected components of the directed graph of positive transitions, the list of closed communicating classes, and the remaining transient states.
source_lines.33: **Procedure.** Form the usual row-transition matrix $K=P^{\mathsf T}$. Initialize a Boolean relation $R_{ij}$ to true exactly when $i=j$ or $K_{ij}>0$. For $k=1,\ldots,n$, and then for every $i,j$, replace $R_{ij}$ by $R_{ij}\lor(R_{ik}\land R_{kj})$. Place $i,j$ in the same component exactly when both $R_{ij}$ and $R_{ji}$ are true. Mark a component $C$ closed exactly when $K_{ij}=0$ for every $i\in C$ and $j\notin C$. Return the closed components, the nonclosed components, and their state labels in increasing order. The procedure uses finitely many exact comparisons and Boolean updates; no sparse storage format or cost bound is asserted. It is a graph computation under the exact-comparison interface, not a claim that positivity of arbitrary unrepresented real numbers can be decided from rounded approximations.

source_lines.38: **Inputs.** A finite state set $E\subseteq\mathbb Z^d$, a finite-channel reaction propensity system from [[def-reaction-network-propensity-system-and-generator]], an initial state $x_0\in E$, a horizon $T>0$, and an optional event budget $B\in\mathbb N_0\cup\{\infty\}$, defaulting to $\infty$, where $\mathbb N_0:=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}$. The random source is a sequence $(E_n,U_n)_{n\ge1}$ with $E_n\sim\operatorname{Exp}(1)$ and $U_n$ uniform on $[0,1]$, all coordinates mutually independent. The countable product construction for these input laws uses Countable Choice and Dependent Choice by [[thm-countable-product-of-probability-spaces]]; the exponential law uses Countable Choice by [[thm-exponential-and-weibull-survival-laws]]. For the uniform law, [[thm-lebesgue-measure-is-a-complete-measure]] makes the set function in [[def-lebesgue-measure-and-the-lebesgue-sigma-algebra]] a measure, and [[thm-lebesgue-measure-of-a-box-of-every-kind]] gives its restriction to $[0,1]$ mass one and interval probabilities equal to interval lengths.
source_lines.40: **Procedure.** Set $t=0$, $x=x_0$, $n=0$, and record the initial state. While $t<T$:
source_lines.42: 1. Compute $\lambda(x)=\sum_{j=1}^R a_j(x)$. If $\lambda(x)=0$, keep the state equal to $x$ through $T$ and return status absorbed.
source_lines.43: 2. If $n=B$, return the path prefix through $(t,x)$ with status budget-exhausted; this status does not assert that the horizon was reached.
source_lines.44: 3. Set $\tau=E_{n+1}/\lambda(x)$. If $t+\tau\ge T$, keep the state equal to $x$ through $T$ and return status horizon.
source_lines.45: 4. Set $J$ to the least index with $U_{n+1}<\lambda(x)^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^J a_j(x)$. If the null event $U_{n+1}=1$ occurs, use the largest index with $a_j(x)>0$. This rule never selects a zero-rate channel.
source_lines.46: 5. Set $t\leftarrow t+\tau$, $x\leftarrow x+\nu_J$, append the marked event $(t,J,x)$, and set $n\leftarrow n+1$.
source_lines.48: If the loop reaches $t=T$, return the path through $T$ with status horizon. Each event uses a linear scan of the $R$ propensities and a linear cumulative channel search; no update-tree acceleration is part of this procedure. If $B<\infty$ and the budget expires before $T$, the returned prefix is incomplete.

source_lines.35: For a step size $h>0$ and an admitted base pair $(t,y)\in D$, the **stage graph** consists of the finite tuples satisfying
source_lines.36: $$Y_i=y+h\sum_{j<i}a_{ij}K_j,\qquad t_i=t+c_i h,\qquad K_i=f(t_i,Y_i)\quad(i=1,\ldots,s).$$
source_lines.37: These equations characterize each stage from the preceding slopes because $a_{ij}=0$ for $j\ge i$. For a complete stage tuple, the candidate endpoint is
source_lines.38: $$y^+=y+h\sum_{i=1}^s b_iK_i.$$
source_lines.40: To include unavailable evaluations, let $(E_i)_{i=1}^s$ be evaluator response functions on $D$: at each point $E_i$ has value either $f(\tau,u)$ or the symbol evaluation-failure for stage $i$. Stage-dependent responses allow availability to differ between repeated inputs. A **successful prefix of length $r$**, $0\le r\le s$, is a stage tuple through index $r$ whose stage pairs lie in $D$ and whose responses under $E_i$ equal the corresponding slopes $K_i$. The empty prefix is allowed. For any prefix of length $r<s$, the next pair $(t_{r+1},Y_{r+1})$ is characterized by the same displayed equations using its already specified slopes. There is a unique maximal successful prefix, since every admissible successful extension has the uniquely specified slope $f(t_i,Y_i)$.
source_lines.42: The **status-labelled stage map** is the following mathematical map. For a maximal prefix of length $r<s$, its value is domain-failure with index $r+1$ when the next pair is outside $D$, and evaluation-failure with index $r+1$ when that pair lies in $D$ and its response under $E_{r+1}$ is evaluation-failure. For a complete prefix its value is domain-failure at output when $(t+h,y^+)\notin D$, and success with $(t+h,y^+)$ otherwise. Thus no slope at an inadmissible pair is part of the stage graph. In the exact mathematical model $E_i=f$ on $D$ for every $i$; evaluation-failure represents only an unavailable numerical evaluation. On its success domain the state component $y^+$ defines a one-step map in the sense of [[def-one-step-ode-method-local-defect-order-and-stability]].

source_lines.29: A **smooth hybrid ODE system** on a finite horizon $[0,T]$, with $T\ge0$ and positive integer state dimension $d\ge1$, consists of a finite mode set $M$, an open state-time domain $D_m\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^d$ and a $C^1$ vector field $f_m:D_m\to\mathbb R^d$ for each $m\in M$, a finite set of directed transitions $(m,n)$, and for each transition a $C^1$ scalar guard $g_{mn}:D_m\to\mathbb R$, a declared crossing orientation $\sigma_{mn}\in\{-1,+1\}$, and a $C^1$ reset map $R_{mn}:U_{mn}\to\mathbb R^d$ on an open neighborhood $U_{mn}\subseteq D_m$ of the guard zero set, satisfying $(t,R_{mn}(t,x))\in D_n$ for every $(t,x)\in U_{mn}$. Here $C^1$ has the meaning in [[def-c-one-map-and-local-inverse]]. In mode $m$, a trajectory is a solution of the first-order initial-value problem $y'=f_m(t,y)$ in the sense of [[def-first-order-ode-initial-value-problem-and-solution]]. It follows that mode only until the selected event time.
source_lines.33: A hybrid trajectory has a **finite separated event list** on $[0,T]$ when it has finitely many event times $0<\tau_1<\cdots<\tau_N<T$ and some $\delta>0$ with $\tau_{j+1}-\tau_j\ge\delta$ for each adjacent pair. The definition does not assert that a solution exists, that an event is detected, or that the event list is finite. Those are separate hypotheses or conclusions.

source_lines.35: Let $d,N\ge1$, let $X=\mathbb R^d$, and fix macro times $t_0<t_1<\cdots<t_N$. A **fine/coarse propagator pair** is a pair of deterministic maps $F_n:D_n^F\to X$ and $G_n:D_n^G\to X$, for each $0\le n<N$, where $D_n^F,D_n^G\subseteq X$ are their admitted input sets. Both maps advance a state across the same interval $[t_n,t_{n+1}]$. The labels fine and coarse identify the two roles chosen by the user; they assert no accuracy, stability, cost, or convergence property.
source_lines.37: For an initial state $x_0\in X$, whenever every call succeeds, the **sequential fine trajectory** is the finite sequence $x_{n+1}=F_n(x_n)$, and the **sequential coarse trajectory** is defined by replacing each $F_n$ with $G_n$. A partially defined map is unavailable outside its admitted set; a failed stage evaluation or an unavailable implicit branch is a propagation failure, not a numerical value.
source_lines.39: A canonical ODE instantiation uses the explicit Runge–Kutta stage map of [[def-explicit-runge-kutta-tableau-and-stage-map]] for $r\ge1$ fine substeps of size $(t_{n+1}-t_n)/r$, composed in order to form $F_n$. A coarse backward Euler value is an endpoint $z$ satisfying the equation in [[def-backward-euler-step-equation]] over the full macro interval. Its branch selector is part of the input and must select exactly one admissible root for each admitted start state; if no such selected root exists, the coarse map is unavailable. The backward Euler definition alone asserts neither root existence nor uniqueness.

source_lines.32: Fix a finite horizon $T>0$ and a nondegenerate fixed size interval $[0,X]$ with $X>0$. Let $g,\mu,\gamma:[0,X]\to[0,\infty)$ be bounded Lipschitz functions, with $g(x)\ge g_{\min}>0$. Here $g$ is size growth, $\mu$ is ordinary mortality, and $\gamma$ is the rate at which a dividing parent is removed. For each parent size $y\in[0,X]$, let $K_y$ be a finite nonnegative Borel measure of daughter sizes, supported on $[0,y]$. Assume $y\mapsto K_y(E)$ is measurable for every Borel set $E\subseteq[0,X]$, and that the number moment $k_0(y):=K_y([0,y])$ is uniformly bounded; the size moment $k_1(y):=\int_{[0,y]}x\,K_y(dx)$ is then finite.
source_lines.34:
Because $K_y$ may have atoms, represent the population by a finite nonnegative Borel measure $
u_t$ on $[0,X)$ rather than requiring a density. Given an initial measure $
u_0$, a weak solution is a curve $t\mapsto
u_t$ that is continuous when tested against continuous functions on $[0,X]$ vanishing at $X$ and satisfies, for every $\phi\in C^1([0,T]	imes[0,X])$ with $\phi(t,X)=0$,
source_lines.36:
$$\int_{[0,X)}\phi(T,x)\,
u_T(dx)-\int_{[0,X)}\phi(0,x)\,
u_0(dx)=\int_0^T\!\int_{[0,X)}(\phi_t+g\phi_x-(\mu+\gamma)\phi)(t,x)\,
u_t(dx)\,dt+\int_0^T\!\int_{[0,X)}\!\left(\int_{[0,y]}\phi(t,x)\,K_y(dx)ight)
u_t(dy)\,dt.$$
source_lines.38: This is the measure-valued transport equation with daughter production $\int_{[0,X)}K_y(dx)\,\nu_t(dy)$, no incoming source at $x=0$, and absorbing outflow at $x=X$. The test condition $\phi(t,X)=0$ encodes removal when a characteristic reaches the upper boundary.
source_lines.40: Let $\Pi_{[0,X]}(x):=\min\{X,\max\{0,x\}\}$ and extend the growth field to $\widetilde g(x):=g(\Pi_{[0,X]}(x))$ on $\mathbb R$. This is a bounded globally Lipschitz vector field. By [[thm-size-structured-positivity-number-and-weighted-moment-identities]], its IVP has a unique solution $\chi_y$ on $[0,T]$ from every initial size $y\in[0,X]$. A model characteristic is $\chi_y$ restricted to $[0,\min\{T,\tau_y\}]$, where $\tau_y$ is its first hitting time of $X$ (taking $\tau_y=+\infty$ if there is no hit on $[0,T]$, and $\tau_y=0$ if $y=X$). On this restricted interval, $\widetilde g=g$. For $y<X$ the restricted interval is nondegenerate, and the characteristic is a first-order IVP solution in the sense of [[def-first-order-ode-initial-value-problem-and-solution]]. For $y=X$ the restriction is only the stopped path on $\{0\}$; no derivative on that singleton is asserted, while the extended path $\chi_X$ remains an IVP solution on $[0,T]$. The interval is fixed; moving boundaries, zero growth and discontinuous coefficients are outside this definition.

source_lines.38: The unit circle is an orbitally asymptotically stable periodic orbit of period $2\pi$. At $x_*=(1,0)$ the affine phase $\psi_b(x,y)=x-1$ has a singular phase-bordered shooting Jacobian, while $\psi_g(x,y)=y$ is transverse and gives an invertible phase-bordered shooting Jacobian.
source_lines.50: 1.1 The identities $\dot r=(xx'+yy')/r$ and $\dot\vartheta=(xy'-yx')/r^2$ give $\dot r=r(1-r)$ and $\dot\vartheta=1$. Thus $r=1$ is invariant and $\vartheta(t)=\vartheta(0)+t$, so the least period is $2\pi$. Differentiating $r(1-r)$ at $r=1$ gives the radial variational equation $\dot\rho=-\rho$, whose multiplier is $e^{-2\pi}<1$; the angular variational equation is $\dot\alpha=0$, whose multiplier is $1$. Because the polar-coordinate Jacobian at times $0$ and $2\pi$ is the same invertible matrix, the Cartesian monodromy is conjugate to $\operatorname{diag}(e^{-2\pi},1)$. For $r<1$ the radial derivative is positive, and for $r>1$ it is negative, so each nearby radius moves monotonically toward $1$ and remains between its initial value and $1$. It has a limit $\bar r$; if $\bar r(1-\bar r)\ne0$, then $\dot r=r(1-r)$ is eventually bounded away from zero, contradicting convergence. Hence $\bar r$ is an equilibrium, and the interval between the initial radius and $1$ contains only the equilibrium $1$, so $r(t)\to1$. These bounds also give Lyapunov stability of the unit circle. Thus the orbit is orbitally asymptotically stable and its neutral multiplier is simple. [given, algebra]
source_lines.52: 2.1 At $(1,0)$ the vector field is $(0,1)$. For $\psi_b=x-1$, $c_b=(1,0)$ and $c_b^\top f(x_*)=0$, so [F2] gives a singular shooting Jacobian. For $\psi_g=y$, $c_g=(0,1)$ and $c_g^\top f(x_*)=1$; the phase multiplier is simple by step 1.1, so [F2] gives an invertible Jacobian. [F1, F2, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

source_lines.63: 1.1 On the first block $0\le t\le\tau$, the delayed value is $1$, so $y(t)=1+at$. On the second block, writing $s=t-\tau\in[0,\tau]$, the delayed value is $y(s)=1+as$, hence $y'(\tau+s)=a+a^2s$ and $y(2\tau)=1+2a\tau+a^2\tau^2/2$. [F1, given, algebra]
source_lines.65: 1.2 The first Euler block gives $Y_j=1+ajh$ for $0\le j\le m$. On the second block, [F2] gives $Y_{m+j+1}=Y_{m+j}+ahY_j$ for $0\le j<m$. Summing yields $Y_{2m}=1+a\tau+a h\sum_{j=0}^{m-1}(1+ajh)$. Pairing the terms $j$ and $m-1-j$ (and retaining the middle term when $m$ is odd) gives $\sum_{j=0}^{m-1}j=m(m-1)/2$, so $Y_{2m}=1+2a\tau+a^2h^2m(m-1)/2$. [F2, given, algebra]
source_lines.67: 2.1 Subtracting step 1.2 from step 1.1 and using $\tau=mh$ gives $y(2\tau)-Y_{2m}=a^2h^2m/2=a^2\tau h/2$. Since this is nonnegative, its absolute value is the claimed error, including $a=0$. On the first Euler block, $|Y_j|\le1+|a|\tau$; on the second, $|Y_{m+j}|\le1+|a|\tau+|a|\tau(1+|a|\tau)$ for $0\le j\le m$. The exact solution is polynomial on each of the first three delay blocks: besides step 1.1, on $[2\tau,3\tau]$ it is $y(2\tau+s)=y(2\tau)+(a+a^2\tau)s+(a^2/2)s^2+(a^3/6)s^3$. These formulas give a common bounded tube independent of $h$. The data therefore satisfy [F3] with $\eta=h_0=\tau$, because $f(t,x,z)=az$ is time-independent, the history has zero second derivative, and the tube is compact. Thus the exact error formula is consistent with the first-order guarantee. [F1, F2, F3, step 1.1, step 1.2, given, algebra] ∎
