source_lines.33: Let $v_0,\ldots,v_{m-1}\in\mathbb Q+i\mathbb Q$, $m\ge3$, be the cyclically ordered vertices of a simple strictly convex polygon whose edges are traversed counterclockwise. Let $P$ be its filled convex hull and let $\Gamma$ be the concatenation of its oriented edges. For every $z\notin\Gamma$, the winding number $n(\Gamma,z)$ is $1$ if $z\in\operatorname{int}P$ and $0$ if $z\notin P$.
source_lines.45: [F4] At a single regular arc traversed with positive real tangent, the index on the left side minus the index on the right side is one ([[lem-winding-number-jumps-by-one-across-a-regular-planar-arc]]).
source_lines.53: 3.1 Fix $z\in\operatorname{int}P$. Choose a ray from $z$ whose direction is not aimed at a vertex. Its intersection with the convex polygon is a bounded interval starting at $z$, so the ray exits at the interior $p$ of a single edge with directed tangent $v\ne0$. The polygon interior lies locally to the left of this positively oriented edge. Apply the orientation-preserving similarity $\rho(w)=\overline v(w-p)/|v|$, which sends $p$ to $0$ and the edge tangent to the positive real direction. For every $a\notin\Gamma$, put $c=\overline v/|v|$. Parametrizing the transformed contour and using [F1] gives $\int_{\rho\circ\Gamma}\frac{d\zeta}{\zeta-\rho(a)}=\int_\Gamma\frac{c\,dw}{c(w-a)}=\int_\Gamma\frac{dw}{w-a}$, so $n(\rho\circ\Gamma,\rho(a))=n(\Gamma,a)$. For sufficiently small $\varepsilon>0$, the points $\rho^{-1}(i\varepsilon)$ and $\rho^{-1}(-i\varepsilon)$ lie respectively on the interior and exterior local sides of the edge. Applying [F4] to $\rho\circ\Gamma$ gives $n(\rho\circ\Gamma,i\varepsilon)-n(\rho\circ\Gamma,-i\varepsilon)=1$; the just-proved invariance rewrites this as $n(\Gamma,\rho^{-1}(i\varepsilon))-n(\Gamma,\rho^{-1}(-i\varepsilon))=1$. source_lines.31: Consider a transition in [[def-hybrid-mode-guard-reset-system]] with state dimension $d\ge1$, from mode $m^-$ to mode $m^+$ at $(\tau,x^-)$. Let $g(t,x)=0$ be its $C^1$ guard, let $R(t,x)$ be its $C^1$ reset, and write $f^-=f_{m^-}(\tau,x^-)$ and $f^+=f_{m^+}(\tau,R(\tau,x^-))$. For each incoming and outgoing mode, assume its IVPs initialized at time $\tau$ from states near $x^-$ and $R(\tau,x^-)$, respectively, have unique solutions on a common finite interval and remain in a bounded convex open tube whose compact closure lies inside the open ODE domain. Use the initial state as the parameter and the identity as its $C^1$ initial map in [[lem-parameter-ode-flow-tangent-on-common-tube]]. For event-time variations to the left of $\tau$, impose the same tube hypothesis on the time-reversed incoming field. Thus the relevant mode flows are $C^1$ in initial state, and the incoming flow is jointly $C^1$ in time and initial state near $(\tau,x^-)$. Assume also that
source_lines.32: $$\kappa:=\partial_tg(\tau,x^-)+D_xg(\tau,x^-)f^-\ne0,$$
source_lines.33: and the nominal event crosses in its declared orientation. For every sufficiently small incoming perturbation $\delta x^-$ at the common pre-event time $\tau$, initialize the perturbed incoming mode at $x^-+\delta x^-$, and let $\tau_\delta$ be its local guard root near $\tau$; assume this root is the selected transition. Put $t_0=\max\{\tau,\tau_\delta\}$, and define $\delta x^+$ as the right-limit difference $\lim_{t\downarrow t_0}(x_\delta^+(t)-x^+(t))$, with both outgoing trajectories evaluated at the same clock time $t>t_0$. Then
source_lines.34: $$\delta x^+=S\,\delta x^-+o(\|\delta x^-\|_2),\qquad S=D_xR+\frac{(f^+-D_xR f^- -\partial_tR)D_xg}{\partial_tg+D_xg f^-},$$
source_lines.35: where all derivatives and vector fields are evaluated at the nominal event and the matrix product in the numerator is a column times a row. No claim is made when the crossing derivative vanishes or a nearby trajectory follows a different transition.
source_lines.53: 1.1 Let $H(s,x)=g(s,\phi^-(s;\tau,x))$, where $\phi^-$ is the incoming mode flow initialized at the nominal pre-event time. The stated common-tube hypothesis and [F4], applied to the field and to its time reversal on the left interval, give the required $C^1$ flow dependence near $(\tau,x^-)$. By [F5], $H$ is $C^1$. At $(s,x)=(\tau,x^-)$, [F2] gives $\partial_sH=\kappa\ne0$. By [F3], the nearby event time $s=\tau(x)$ is $C^1$. Since $\phi^-(\tau;\tau,x)=x$, its initial-state derivative at $s=\tau$ is the identity. Implicit differentiation gives $D\tau(x^-)=-D_xg/\kappa$. Thus the actual shift $\delta\tau:=\tau_\delta-\tau$ satisfies $\delta\tau=-D_xg\,\delta x^-/\kappa+o(\|\delta x^-\|_2)$. [given, F2, F3, F4, F5, algebra]
source_lines.55: 2.1 At the perturbed event, [F4] gives incoming state $x^-+\delta x^-+f^-\delta\tau+o(\|\delta x^-\|_2)$. By [F5], the reset-state variation is $D_xR\,\delta x^-+(D_xR f^-+\partial_tR)\delta\tau+o(\|\delta x^-\|_2)$. Compare at $t_0=\max\{\tau,\tau+\delta\tau\}$. If $\delta\tau\ge0$, the nominal outgoing state advances from $\tau$ to $t_0$ by $f^+\delta\tau+o(|\delta\tau|)$, while the perturbed state has just reset. If $\delta\tau<0$, the perturbed outgoing state advances from its reset at $\tau+\delta\tau$ to $t_0=\tau$ by $f^+(-\delta\tau)+o(\|\delta x^-\|_2)$, while the nominal state has just reset. In both cases the same-clock difference is $D_xR\,\delta x^-+(D_xR f^-+\partial_tR-f^+)\delta\tau+o(\|\delta x^-\|_2)$, since step 1.1 gives $\delta\tau=O(\|\delta x^-\|_2)$. [given, F1, F4, F5, step 1.1, algebra]
source_lines.57: 3.1 Substitute the expression for $\delta\tau$ from step 1.1 into step 2.1 and factor $\delta x^-$. The resulting linear map is $D_xR+(f^+-D_xR f^- -\partial_tR)D_xg/\kappa$, which is the stated matrix $S$. The remainder remains $o(\|\delta x^-\|_2)$ because the event-time variation is linear to first order by step 1.1. [step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

source_lines.31: Input an integer $k\ge1$ and dimension $d\in\{2,3\}$. The coordinate vertices are $\{0,\ldots,k-1\}^d$. Identify them with the zero-based matrix indices $0,\ldots,k^d-1$ by the lexicographic bijection $q(i_1,\ldots,i_d)=\sum_{a=1}^d i_a k^{d-a}$. The grid graph has an edge between two coordinate vertices exactly when they differ by $1$ in one coordinate and agree in all others. Use the graph and ordering conventions of [[def-symmetric-structural-elimination-graph-and-ordering]] on these indices. Thus $d=2$ gives the five-point graph and $d=3$ the seven-point graph.
source_lines.33: Order a rectangular coordinate subbox recursively as follows. For each coordinate whose side length is at least $2$, choose its lower median coordinate, namely the coordinate with $\lfloor(m-1)/2\rfloor$ positions below it in a side of length $m$. Let $S$ be the union of the coordinate hyperplanes at those selected medians. Delete $S$, obtaining at most $2^d$ nonempty rectangular child boxes. Recursively order the child boxes in lexicographic order of their lower corners, then append the vertices of $S$ in lexicographic order. If no coordinate has side length at least $2$, append the remaining vertex as a terminal separator. Apply this rule first to the whole grid. The resulting order is the **coordinate nested-dissection ordering**.

source_lines.34: Draw one permutation uniformly from all $n!$ permutations of the distinct input sites. Initialize the fixed-universe supertriangle and current triangulation as in [[alg-incremental-planar-delaunay-edge-flips]], and maintain a directed acyclic graph (DAG) whose leaves correspond one-to-one with current triangulation triangles. Initially the DAG has one leaf for the supertriangle.
source_lines.36: For each next site $p$, start at the root. At each node, order its child triangles lexicographically by their sorted vertex identifiers and test each child by the same three signed-orientation containment tests used by `INSERT` in [[alg-incremental-planar-delaunay-edge-flips]]. Descend to the unique child containing $p$ until reaching a current leaf $T$. Under the augmented general-position condition, $p$ lies in the interior of a unique triangle at every stage; the located leaf therefore supplies the face certificate `face(T)`. Call `INSERT(p,face(T))` from [[alg-incremental-planar-delaunay-edge-flips]]. The update verifies that certificate, uses it without a triangle scan, and returns the ordered replacement events. Process those events in order: for a face split, replace the old leaf by pointers to its three new triangle leaves; for an interior-edge split, replace each of the two old leaves by pointers to the two new triangles whose interiors meet that old triangle; for a flip, point each of the two old leaves to both new triangle leaves. Each event names the triangles and overlap map as specified by the insertion procedure. A leaf replaced later is treated in the same way, so the graph remains acyclic and its current leaves correspond exactly to the current triangulation. The insertion procedure also accepts an interior-edge certificate from callers whose admissible inputs permit edge hits; this randomized variant's general-position condition excludes that case. Each internal node has at most three children. After construction, remove synthetic-vertex triangles for the returned Delaunay triangulation; the history DAG is the insertion-time point-location structure.

Then that finite-budget algorithm terminates in finite time after at most $N$ iterations and at most $N$ calls to each routine, returning \texttt{inconclusive}, \texttt{budget-exhausted}, or \texttt{certified}. source_lines.30: Input a bounded factorable optimization problem on a box $B$, its objective DAG $F$, a finite list of inequality-constraint DAGs $G_i$ representing $g_i(x)\le0$, a finite rule table, a precision $p\ge2$, and a dyadic interval format with fixed exponent bounds. For each non-product nonlinear node, the table must supply certified convex and concave graph bounds $\psi^-\le w\le\psi^+$ on its certified operand domain, with proof that they contain the exact graph and that the imposed epigraph/hypograph inequalities form a convex relation. The table must also supply a convex underestimator $\phi_B$ for the objective DAG's final value, verified to satisfy $\phi_B(\iota_B(x))\le f(x)$ for every exact input $x\in B$. All domain hypotheses and interval/coefficient enclosures must be certified. For each interval call, pass the same declared precision and format to [[alg-interval-dag-box-enclosure-and-bound]]. Traverse the union of the objective and constraint DAGs in topological order, using a lifted variable for each node. For an affine node, add its exact affine relation. For a product node $w=uv$, add the four McCormick inequalities from [[def-mccormick-bilinear-box-envelope]] using certified operand bounds; [[lem-mccormick-envelope-equals-graph-convex-hull]] proves this relation is a convex outer enclosure of the product graph. For every other nonlinear node, add its certified convex and concave graph bounds; if its domain hypotheses, interval bounds, graph containment, or convexity cannot be verified, return unsupported-relaxation or inconclusive. For each constraint DAG, require its final lifted value to be at most zero.

source_lines.40: Initialize $Q(s,a)=U(s,a)$, batch sum $B(s,a)=0$, sample count $\ell(s,a)=0$, batch start $b(s,a)=0$, learning flag $L(s,a)=\mathrm{true}$, and global last-update time $t^*=0$. For interaction times $t=1,2,\ldots$, in current state $s$, choose an action maximizing $Q(s,\cdot)$ under the fixed tie order, output and take that action $a_t$, then observe reward $r$ and next state $s'$. If $b(s,a)\le t^*$, set $L(s,a)=\mathrm{true}$. If $L(s,a)$ is true, set $b(s,a)=t$ when $\ell(s,a)=0$, increment $\ell(s,a)$ by one, and add $r+\gamma\max_{c\in A(s')}Q(s',c)$ to $B(s,a)$. When $\ell(s,a)=m$, set $\bar B=B(s,a)/m$. If $Q(s,a)-\bar B\ge2\epsilon_1$, replace $Q(s,a)$ by $\bar B+\epsilon_1$ and set $t^*=t$. Otherwise set $L(s,a)=\mathrm{false}$ exactly when $b(s,a)>t^*$. In either outcome reset $B(s,a)=0$ and $\ell(s,a)=0$ after a completed batch; if $L(s,a)$ remains false, make no sample or Q update on this visit. Leave all other entries unchanged. Use $s'$ as the current state in the next iteration.

Full horizon coverage means $P^\pi_H\ll P^\mu_H$, so every behavior-null trajectory event is also target-null. In this finite setting, the condition $\pi(a\mid s)>0\Rightarrow\mu(a\mid s)>0$ at every state-action pair reachable under $\pi$ before time $H$ is sufficient for full horizon coverage. source_lines.39: Assume AC and take horizon $H=1$, discount $\gamma=\tfrac12$, states $s_0,z$, actions $a,b$ at $s_0$, and action $c$ at $z$. Every action moves to $z$; action $a$ gives reward $0$, action $b$ gives reward $1$, and action $c$ gives reward $0$. The target policy chooses $b$ at $s_0$, and both policies choose $c$ at $z$. With behavior probabilities $\mu(a\mid s_0)=\mu(b\mid s_0)=\tfrac12$, full trajectory coverage holds: the single-trajectory ordinary importance-sampling score is $2$ when action $b$ is observed and $0$ when action $a$ is observed, and its expectation is the target value $1$. If instead $\mu(a\mid s_0)=1$, the target action has no behavior support. Two processes that agree on the logged action $a$ and its reward $0$, but give action $b$ rewards $1$ and $-1$, respectively, have identical logged-data laws and different target values; the behavior data cannot identify which value is correct.

source_lines.25: Let $m\ge1$ be an integer, let $n\ge2m+1$, and fix $0<\Delta<1$. In a two-arm $n$-round bandit, let every reward-stack entry of arm 1 equal $1$ and every reward-stack entry of arm 2 equal $1-\Delta$. Under explore-then-commit with exploration count $m$, the algorithm commits to arm 1 and has expected reward regret exactly $m\Delta$. The expected-regret theorem gives the upper bound $m\Delta+(n-2m)\Delta e^{-m\Delta^2/4}$ for this instance.

Choose an integer $C\ge1$ and set $N=\lceil CbQ\rceil$. Since $b\le2^Q$ and $Q\le2^Q$, $N\le(C+1)2^{2Q}$, so the least $q_N$ with $N\le2^{q_N}$ satisfies $q_N\le2Q+q_{C+1}$. By step 1.3 and $q_T\le Q$, the bracket is at most $1+\frac{4G^2}{\mu}(2Q+q_{C+1}+1)+k_\alpha(Q+2)$. Set $c=4G^2/\mu$, $a=2c+k_\alpha$, $b_0=c$, and $b_1=1+c+2k_\alpha$; the bracket bound equals $aQ+b_0q_{C+1}+b_1$. Choose an integer $r\ge2$ so large that $r(r-1)/2\ge a+b_0(r+1)+b_1$; such an $r$ exists because the left side is quadratic with positive leading coefficient and the right side is affine in $r$. The binomial theorem gives $C:=2^r\ge r(r-1)/2$, while $C+1\le2^{r+1}$ gives $q_{C+1}\le r+1$. Hence $C\ge a+b_0q_{C+1}+b_1$. Since $Q\ge1$ and $a,b_0,b_1\ge0$, $CQ\ge(a+b_0q_{C+1}+b_1)Q\ge aQ+b_0q_{C+1}+b_1$; as $b\ge B$, this gives $N\ge CbQ\ge B(aQ+b_0q_{C+1}+b_1)$. Thus $N\ge\bar uT$ times the bracket, which also implies the required inequality with $u$. Moreover $Q=O(\log(B+2))$, so $N=O(B\log(B+2))=\widetilde O(\bar uT)$. When $u\ge1$, this is $\widetilde O(uT)$; if $u<1$, replacing it by $\bar u=1$ is a valid upper-bound normalization for the iteration count. The estimate retains the hindsight optimum $\epsilon_N$ and assumes no realizability condition $\pi^*\in\Pi$. [A1, A3, A4, step 1.3, step 4.1, algebra] ∎

For each $a\in A(s)$, the point masses $p(s',\rho\mid s,a)$ on $S\times\mathcal R\subseteq E$ (and zero on the added dummy-reward points) define a probability measure $\mu_a$ on $E$: they are nonnegative and total $1$ by [F1]. To check countable additivity, fix a bijection $e:n\to E$. For any disjoint sequence $(B_j)$, each nonempty $B_j$ has a least index $i_j<n$ with $e(i_j)\in B_j$, by [F8]; disjointness makes these indices distinct, so only finitely many $B_j$ are nonempty. Its values are nonnegative and $K_\pi(x,E)=\sum_a\pi(a\mid s)=1$ by [F1]. For a disjoint countable family $(B_j)$, only finitely many $B_j$ are nonempty by the same argument; additivity of each $\mu_a$ and finite-sum interchange [F6] give $K_\pi(x,\bigcup_jB_j)=\sum_jK_\pi(x,B_j)$. Thus $B\mapsto K_\pi(x,B)$ is a probability measure. Every subset of $E$ is measurable and every function on the discrete source $E$ is measurable, so [F2] makes $K_\pi$ a probability kernel. source_lines.35: There are two finite one-step Markov decision processes with the same logged-data law under one behavior policy, but different target-policy values and different uniquely optimal actions. A finite one-step Markov decision process here has a finite state set, finite nonempty action sets, a finite reward set, and a probability mass on the next-state/reward pair for every state/action pair. Let the state set be $\{s_0,z\}$, the action sets be $A(s_0)=\{a,b\}$ and $A(z)=\{c\}$, the reward set be $\{-1,0,1\}$, and the horizon be $H=1$. In both processes, action $a$ at $s_0$ gives reward $0$ and moves to $z$, and action $c$ at $z$ gives reward $0$ and stays at $z$. In process $M_+$, action $b$ at $s_0$ gives reward $1$ and moves to $z$; in process $M_-$, it gives reward $-1$ and moves to $z$. The behavior policy chooses $a$ at $s_0$ with probability $1$, while the target policy chooses $b$ there with probability $1$; both policies choose $c$ at $z$ with probability $1$. Every behavior-generated logged trajectory is $(s_0,a,0,z)$ in both processes, so every sample size $n\ge1$ has the same logged-data law in $M_+$ and $M_-$. The target value is the expected one-step reward: it is $1$ in $M_+$ and $-1$ in $M_-$, and the unique value-maximizing initial action is $b$ in $M_+$ and $a$ in $M_-$. An estimator here is a real-valued function of the logged dataset; it is unbiased for a target value when its expectation under the logged-data law equals that value. Consequently, no such estimator can be unbiased for the target value in both processes, and no data-based action selector can identify the unique optimal initial action with certainty in both.

source_lines.50: $$T^*V(s)=\max_{a\in A(s)}\left[r(s,a)+\gamma\sum_{s'\in S}P(s'\mid s,a)V(s')\right]$$

source_lines.64: 2.1 First suppose $D\ge16$. In this branch, set $$k=\lfloor S/2\rfloor,\qquad b=\lfloor A/3\rfloor,\qquad B=A-b-1,\qquad K=kB,\qquad p=\frac8{3D},\qquad e=\frac7{20}\sqrt{\frac{pK}{T}}.$$ There are $k$ paired bad/good states $(x_i,y_i)$. If $S$ is odd, include one additional bare routing state. Arrange the bad states and the optional bare state into a breadth-first rooted $b$-ary tree of height $h$. At each bad state, $B$ useful actions have reward zero and move to its good partner with probability $p$, otherwise staying put. The remaining $b+1$ actions route deterministically toward the parent or one of the $b$ child slots, with missing slots giving self-loops; their rewards are zero. At each good state all $A$ actions have reward one and move to the paired bad state with probability $p$, otherwise staying put. At the optional bare state use the same routing actions and duplicate them to obtain exactly $A$ actions, all with reward zero. This uses exactly $S$ states and exactly $A$ actions per state. For each of the $K$ useful pairs $j$, environment $M_j$ changes just that pair's probability of entering its good state from $p$ to $p+e$. The baseline $M_0$ has no change. Fix the initial state at the bad root. Every environment is communicating. [given, step 1.1, F2, construct, algebra]

If $h=2$, breadth-first filling implies $n\ge b+2$, so $S\ge2b+3\ge2A/3\ge A^{4/5}$ and hence $h\le(5/2)\log_A S$. If $h\ge3$, it implies $S\ge2b^{h-1}$, so $$S\ge(2b^2)b^{h-3}\ge A^{6/5}A^{(2/5)(h-3)}=A^{2h/5}.$$ Thus always $h\le\max\{1,(5/2)\log_A S\}\le D/8$. source_lines.68: 4.1 In $M_j$ the optimal average reward is $$\rho^*=\frac{p+e}{2p+e}=\frac12+\frac{e}{4p+2e}.$$ To prove this, take the function $v$ equal to $1/(2p+e)$ at every good state and zero elsewhere. At every state-action pair, $r+Pv-v\le\rho^*$: equality holds at good states and the special useful pair, ordinary useful pairs give $p/(2p+e)$, and routes give zero. Summing this inequality in conditional expectation gives average reward at most $\rho^*$, because $v$ is bounded. Routing to the special bad state and then always using its special action realizes the two-state chain with transitions $p+e$ and $p$, whose invariant good-state mass is $(p+e)/(2p+e)$. Its convergence in Cesàro mean follows directly from the two-state recurrence; the finite expected routing/hitting transient changes no average reward. This proves the formula. Let $G_t$ be the indicator that the current state is good, let $U_t$ indicate a useful action at a bad state, and let $Q_t$ indicate a routing action (including every action at the bare state). Then $G_t+U_t+Q_t=1$ and $$\mathbb E_j[G_{t+1}-G_t\mid\text{history, action}]=pU_t+e\mathbf1\{j\text{ used at }t\}-pG_t.$$ Rewards equal $G_t$. Since $G_1=0$, summing the equality gives the exact identity $$\mathbb E_jR_T=\frac T2-\frac12\mathbb E_j\sum_{t=1}^TQ_t+\frac e{2p}\mathbb E_jN_j-\frac{\mathbb E_jG_{T+1}}{2p}.$$ In particular, $$\mathbb E_j[T\rho^*-R_T]\ge\frac{eT}{4p+2e}-\frac e{2p}\mathbb E_jN_j.$$ There is no adverse additive initial-transient term. In the baseline, the same identity with $e=0$ yields $$\sum_{j=1}^K\mathbb E_0N_j=\mathbb E_0\sum_tU_t=\frac T2-\frac12\mathbb E_0\sum_tQ_t+\frac{\mathbb E_0G_{T+1}}{2p}\le\frac T2+\frac1{2p}.$$ [given, step 2.1, step 3.1, F1, construct, algebra]
source_lines.72: 6.1 Now suppose $1\le D<16$, the remaining allowed diameter range. The parameter condition gives $A\ge S^{20/D}>S^{5/4}$, so $S/A<S^{-1/4}\le10^{-1/4}<3/5$. All rewards in the baseline are independent Bernoulli variables of mean $1/2$. For each of the $K$ self-loop pairs $j$, environment $M_j$ changes that pair's reward mean to $1/2+e$, where $$e=\frac15\sqrt{K/T}\le\frac15.$$ The last inequality follows from $K\le SA\le T$ because $D\ge1$. Rewards may be generated independently conditional on state-action history; transitions are the same deterministic transitions in all environments. Every environment has diameter one and exactly the required numbers of states and actions. Its optimal average reward is $1/2+e$: no reward mean exceeds this, and the learner can reach the special state in at most one step and then repeatedly use its special self-loop. Start at any fixed state. Here the testing calculation gives $$\operatorname{KL}(P_0\Vert P_j)\le\frac{10}{3}e^2\mathbb E_0N_j,\qquad \frac1K\sum_j\mathbb E_jN_j\le\frac TK+Te\sqrt{\frac{5T}{3K}},$$ because $1/2-e\ge3/10$ and $\sum_j\mathbb E_0N_j\le T$. It covers $C$: around any $x\in C$ take $B(x,\delta)\subset C$. By [F17], choose $m\ge1$ with $3/m<\delta$ and then $q\in\mathbb Q^n$ with $|q-x|<1/m$. Thus $x\in B(q,1/m)$ and $\overline{B(q,2/m)}\subset B(x,\delta)\subset C$. By steps 4.1 and 6.1, $u=c_C$ almost everywhere on each such inner ball. The exceptional sets are measurable and null; by [F19] their countable union is null. Hence $u=c_C$ almost everywhere on all of $C$. If $\Omega=\varnothing$, there is no component to consider. source_lines.64: 2.1 The three profiles are solutions. For $x_0\ne\tfrac12$ each $u_i$ is $C^1$ near $x_0$ with $|u_i'|=1$, so at any upper or lower test the spatial slope equals $u_i'(x_0)=\pm1$, and [F1] gives $F(\pm1)=0$ in both directions. At $x_0=\tfrac12$, only $u_3$ is non-differentiable: writing $h=x-\tfrac12$ we have $u_3(\tfrac12+h)=\tfrac12-|h|$. If $\phi$ is an upper test with slope $p=\phi_x(\tfrac12,t_0)$, then $u_3\le\phi$ near the point gives for $h>0$ the inequality $-h+o(h)\le ph+o(h)$, hence $p\ge-1$, and for $h<0$ the inequality $h+o(|h|)\le ph+o(|h|)$, hence $p\le1$; thus every upper-test slope lies in $[-1,1]$ and $F(p)\le0$. If $\phi$ were a lower test, $u_3\ge\phi$ would give for $h>0$ that $p\le-1$ and for $h<0$ that $p\ge1$, which is impossible; hence there is no lower test at the peak and the supersolution condition is vacuous. By step 1.1 the same reduction applies to $u_1$ and $u_2$ at every point. Hence all three profiles are viscosity solutions of $|u'|=1$ on $(0,1)$. [step 1.1, F1, F2, algebra]
source_lines.66: 3.1 Distinctness and boundary traces. At $x=\tfrac14$ the values are $(u_1,u_2,u_3)=(\tfrac14,\tfrac34,\tfrac14)$ and at $x=\tfrac34$ they are $(\tfrac34,\tfrac14,\tfrac14)$, which distinguishes every pair; also $u_1-u_2=2x-1$ changes sign on $(0,1)$. The continuous extensions to $[0,1]$ have boundary values $u_1(0)=0,\ u_1(1)=1$; $u_2(0)=1,\ u_2(1)=0$; and $u_3(0)=u_3(1)=0$. Thus the equation with no prescribed boundary data admits at least three distinct viscosity solutions, and the displayed candidates carry different endpoint traces. [step 2.1, algebra] ∎

source_lines.35: Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $c>0$ and let $u$ be a free solution constructed by the formulas of [[thm-kirchhoff-formula-for-the-three-dimensional-wave-equation]], [[thm-poisson-formula-for-the-two-dimensional-wave-equation]], [[thm-odd-dimensional-wave-formula-by-spherical-means]] or [[thm-even-dimensional-wave-formula-by-descent]] from compactly supported admissible data. Then for every $(x,t)$ with $t>0$ the value $u(x,t)$ is determined by the data restricted to $\overline B_{ct}(x)$: two admissible data pairs agreeing there produce the same value at $(x,t)$. For the forced solution of [[thm-forced-three-dimensional-kirchhoff-duhamel-formula]], the value is determined by the source on the backward cone $\{(y,s):0\le s\le t,\ |y-x|\le c(t-s)\}$; two sources agreeing there produce the same value at $(x,t)$.
source_lines.57: 2.1 Forced case and conclusion. The retarded potential of the forced three-dimensional formula is an integral of the source over the backward cone $|y-x|\le c(t-s)$, $0\le s\le t$; sources agreeing there give equal integrals, hence equal values at $(x,t)$. This proves the local determination of the constructed solutions by the stated data or source; no uniqueness claim for arbitrary $C^2$ solutions is made, that being the energy statement of the wave-energy page. [F1, given] ∎

source_lines.51: [L3] On any open star-shaped domain $U\subseteq\mathbb C$, the integral of a holomorphic scalar- or Banach-valued function over a closed piecewise $C^1$ contour in $U$ is zero ([[lem-banach-valued-cauchy-theorem-on-star-shaped-domains]]). In particular this applies to contours in the sector $S:=\{\lambda\ne0:|\arg\lambda|<\pi/2+\delta\}$; the improper keyhole integrals defining $T$ converge absolutely ([[lem-contour-definition-of-an-analytic-semigroup]]).
source_lines.61: 1.1 The double integral. Fix admissible contours $\Gamma_1=\Gamma(r_1,\theta_1)$ and $\Gamma_2=\Gamma(r_2,\theta_2)$ with $\pi/2+\delta_0<\theta_1<\theta_2<\pi/2+\delta$ and $r_2<r_1$; then every point of $\Gamma_1$ lies outside the interior of $\Gamma_2$ and every point of $\Gamma_2$ lies inside the interior of $\Gamma_1$. By [L1] and [L4] the product $T(z_1)T(z_2)$ is the norm limit of the truncated products, and for each truncation the finite double integral of $e^{\lambda_1z_1+\lambda_2z_2}R(\lambda_1)R(\lambda_2)$ equals its iterate, so $T(z_1)T(z_2)=\frac1{(2\pi i)^2}\int_{\Gamma_2}\int_{\Gamma_1}e^{\lambda_1z_1+\lambda_2z_2}R(\lambda_1)R(\lambda_2)\,d\lambda_1d\lambda_2$ with absolutely convergent iterated integrals. [L1, L4, given, algebra]
source_lines.63: 1.2 The finite-keyhole winding calculation. For $R>r$, let $C_R(r,\theta)$ be the closed contour obtained by appending to $\Gamma_R(r,\theta)$ the counterclockwise outer arc $Re^{i\alpha}$, $\theta\le\alpha\le2\pi-\theta$, through the left half-plane. Its interior is $D_R=\{\lambda:|\lambda|<R,\ |\lambda|<r\text{ or }|\arg\lambda|>\theta\}$, with $0$ included by the first alternative; it is star-shaped about $0$. For $p$ off $C_R$, the winding number is one when $p\in D_R$ and zero when $p$ is outside $\overline{D_R}$; equivalently $\oint_{C_R(r,\theta)}(\lambda-p)^{-1}d\lambda$ is $2\pi i$ or $0$, respectively. At $p=0$, the two radial integrals of $d\lambda/\lambda$ cancel, while the inner and outer arcs contribute $2i\theta$ and $i(2\pi-2\theta)$, so the index is $1$. Since $D_R$ is connected, [L5] gives the same index at every interior point. Every exterior point can move radially out beyond radius $R$ without meeting the trace, then along an outer circle, so it belongs to the unbounded component, where [L5] gives index $0$. If $z\in\Sigma_\delta$ and $\theta$ is admissible for $z$, then on the outer arc $\operatorname{Re}(\lambda z)\le-cR|z|$ for some $c>0$, so $\int_{A_R}e^{\lambda z}(\lambda-p)^{-1}d\lambda\to0$ for fixed $p$. Put $D_\infty:=\bigcup_{R>r}D_R$. If $p\in D_\infty$, then $p\in D_R$ for every sufficiently large $R$; writing $e^{\lambda z}(\lambda-p)^{-1}=e^{pz}(\lambda-p)^{-1}+G(\lambda)$ with entire $G$ having a global primitive shows that the open contour integral tends to $2\pi i e^{pz}$. If instead $p\notin\overline{D_\infty}$, then $p$ lies outside every $\overline{D_R}$ and, for each finite $R$, choose $0<\varepsilon_R<\operatorname{dist}(p,\overline{D_R})$ and set $U_{R,\varepsilon_R}=\overline{D_R}+B(0,\varepsilon_R)$. This is an open star-shaped neighborhood of $\overline{D_R}$ that avoids $p$; the integrand is holomorphic there, so its closed integral vanishes by [L3], and the outer arc tends to zero, giving an open contour integral equal to zero. The nested-contour cases evaluated below have $p$ either inside $D_\infty$ or outside $\overline{D_\infty}$, so no boundary-pole case is needed. [L3, L5, given, algebra]
source_lines.65: 2.1 The resolvent identity and the inner integrals. By [L2], $R(\lambda_1)R(\lambda_2)=\frac{R(\lambda_2)-R(\lambda_1)}{\lambda_1-\lambda_2}$, so the double integral of [step 1.1] splits as $A_2-A_1$, where $A_1$ is the term with $R(\lambda_1)$ and the inner $\Gamma_2$ integral, and $A_2$ is the term with $R(\lambda_2)$ and the inner $\Gamma_1$ integral. The two infinite contours are disjoint and have positive separation $d:=\operatorname{dist}(\Gamma_1,\Gamma_2)>0$: their finite arc pieces are disjoint compact sets, and their ray tails have distinct angles $\theta_1\ne\theta_2$, so the distance between tails tends to infinity. Thus $|\lambda_1-\lambda_2|^{-1}\le d^{-1}$; together with exponential decay along the rays and the sectorial resolvent bound, this gives absolute integrability of each split double-integral term and justifies Fubini. For each fixed $\lambda_1\in\Gamma_1$, the nesting in [step 1.1] puts $\lambda_1$ outside the closure of the full unbounded keyhole region $D_{\infty,2}:=\bigcup_{R_2>r_2}D_{R_2}(r_2,\theta_2)$, so it is outside every truncated interior. For each $R_2$, the scalar integrand $e^{\lambda_2z_2}/(\lambda_1-\lambda_2)$ is holomorphic on an open star-shaped neighborhood of $\overline{D_{R_2}}$ avoiding its pole, so the integral on $C_{R_2}(r_2,\theta_2)$ is zero by [L3]. Its outer arc contribution tends to zero by exponential decay, hence the open inner $\Gamma_2$ integral in $A_1$ vanishes. For each fixed $\lambda_2\in\Gamma_2$, the nesting puts it inside the unbounded keyhole interior of $\Gamma_1$, and therefore in $D_{R_1}$ for every sufficiently large $R_1$. On $C_{R_1}(r_1,\theta_1)$, the decomposition $e^{\lambda_1z_1}/(\lambda_1-\lambda_2)=e^{\lambda_2z_1}/(\lambda_1-\lambda_2)+[e^{\lambda_1z_1}-e^{\lambda_2z_1}]/(\lambda_1-\lambda_2)$ has an entire second term with a global primitive; by [step 1.2] the first term integrates to $2\pi i e^{\lambda_2z_1}$. The outer arc of the original exponential integrand tends to zero for this fixed $\lambda_2$, so the open inner $\Gamma_1$ integral in $A_2$ is $2\pi i e^{\lambda_2z_1}$. These are pointwise evaluations of the inner improper integrals; no radius-limit is interchanged with the outer integration. [step 1.1, step 1.2, L2, L3, given, algebra]
source_lines.69: 3.1 The semigroup law. Substituting [step 2.1] into [step 1.1] gives $T(z_1)T(z_2)=\frac1{(2\pi i)^2}\int_{\Gamma_2}e^{\lambda_2z_2}2\pi i e^{\lambda_2z_1}R(\lambda_2,A)\,d\lambda_2=\frac1{2\pi i}\int_{\Gamma_2}e^{\lambda_2(z_1+z_2)}R(\lambda_2,A)\,d\lambda_2=T(z_1+z_2)$, the last equality by the independence of the contour [L1], since $\Gamma_2$ is admissible for $z_1+z_2\in\Sigma_{\delta_0}$ when $\theta_2>\pi/2+\delta_0$. [step 1.1, step 2.1, L1, given, algebra]

source_lines.62: 1.1 First use $h(u)=(1-|u|)_+$ as a density in the space variable u. It is nonnegative Borel and $\int h=2\int_0^1(1-u)\,du=1$, so it defines a probability. Its characteristic function q has vanishing imaginary part by the oddness of $h(u)\sin(su)$. For $s\ne0$, integration by parts with $1-u$ and $\sin(su)/s$ yields $$q(s)=2\int_0^1(1-u)\cos(su)\,du=\frac2s\int_0^1\sin(su)\,du=\frac{2(1-\cos s)}{s^2}.$$ All factors and derivatives are continuous on $[0,1]$, so FTC and the bridge apply. Density integration is applied to the real and imaginary positive/negative parts. At s=0, q(0)=1, and continuity follows from the characteristic-function lemma. Thus q is nonnegative everywhere and bounded by one, with $q(s)\le4/s^2$ for $|s|\ge1$. The primitive $-1/s$ on $[1,R]$, the bridge and monotone convergence give $\int_1^\infty s^{-2}\,ds=1$; reflection gives the other tail. Hence q is integrable. [F1, F3, F4, F5, F7, F8, F9, F10, F11]
source_lines.64: 2.1 Apply density inversion to that probability with characteristic function q. It supplies the continuous density $H(y)=(2\pi)^{-1}\int e^{-isy}q(s)\,ds$. This equals h everywhere: if the two continuous densities differed at y, continuity would give a small interval where their difference had one strict sign, contradicting that both densities integrate to the same interval mass. In particular $1=h(0)=H(0)=(2\pi)^{-1}\int q$. Therefore $f=q/(2\pi)$ is nonnegative and integrates to one, so defines a probability. It has exactly the displayed formula and the continuous value $1/(2\pi)$ at zero. [step 1.1, F2, F3]
source_lines.66: 3.1 Density integration and the identity in step 2.1 now give $$\varphi_f(t)=\frac1{2\pi}\int e^{itx}q(x)\,dx=H(-t)=h(-t)=(1-|t|)_+.$$ This includes t=0 and both endpoints t=±1, where the value is zero; outside the closed interval it is zero as well. The density value at x=0 was fixed by continuity, not division by zero. AC is inherited from the compact bridge and density inversion. The argument applied inversion only to the known law h before establishing that the triangle is a characteristic function. [step 2.1, F1, F6, F9] ∎

source_lines.26: Assume AC. Start with $r,g$ positive integers of red and green balls, and reinforce each drawn color by $c\ge1$. For integer $c$ this counts balls; the same construction works for real $c\ge1$ as color weights. If $R_n$ is the red count or weight after $n$ draws, then $R_n/(r+g+nc)$ is a bounded martingale for the draw-history filtration at every $n\ge0$.
source_lines.46: 1.1 Use $\Omega=(0,1]$ with the trace Lebesgue sigma-algebra and length probability. Restriction is a measure by [F2] (equivalently restrict its event formula to subsets of $\Omega$), and [F1] gives total mass one. Define intervals for finite color words recursively: $I_{\varnothing}=(0,1]$. If $h$ has length $n$, contains $j$ red letters, and $I_h=(a,b]$, put $T_n=r+g+nc$ and $p_h=(r+cj)/T_n$. Then $0<p_h<1$ because both $r+cj$ and $g+c(n-j)$ are positive. Set $I_{hR}=(a,a+p_h(b-a)]$ and $I_{hG}=(a+p_h(b-a),b]$. Both are positive-length half-open intervals [[def-half-open-box]], disjoint with union $I_h$. Induction gives a finite partition at every depth, and each point has exactly one compatible word of every finite length. Thus every draw is defined on this one space by the interval containing the point; no infinite-product existence is assumed. [given, F1, F2]
source_lines.48: 2.1 Let $\mathcal F_n$ consist of all unions of depth-n intervals. Complements and countable unions just select subsets of this finite partition, so it is a sigma-algebra. Refinement makes it a filtration. A word interval is exactly the intersection of the corresponding first n color events; conversely a color event up to n is a union of word intervals. Hence $\mathcal F_n$ is the draw-history sigma-algebra. On $I_h$ set $R_n=r+cj$ and $U_n=R_n/T_n$. These are finite-valued $\mathcal F_n$-measurable variables and $0<U_n<1$. If $J_{n+1}$ indicates the next red draw, then $\int_{I_h}J_{n+1}\,dP=P(I_{hR})=p_hP(I_h)=\int_{I_h}U_n\,dP$. Finite addition proves this identity for every event in $\mathcal F_n$. Both variables are bounded, so [F3] identifies $E[J_{n+1}\mid\mathcal F_n]=U_n$. [F1, F3, step 1.1]
source_lines.50: 3.1 The pathwise update is $R_{n+1}=R_n+cJ_{n+1}$. The bounded $\mathcal F_n$-measurable $R_n$ is its own conditional version, since its event identities are tautologies. Since $T_n+c$ is deterministic and positive, conditional linearity gives $E[U_{n+1}\mid\mathcal F_n]=(R_n+cU_n)/(T_n+c)=R_n(1+c/T_n)/(T_n+c)=R_n/T_n=U_n$. Thus the bounded adapted process is a martingale [[def-martingale-submartingale-and-supermartingale]]. For $r=g=c=1$, $U_0=1/2$ and the first two possible new proportions are $2/3$ and $1/3$, each with probability $1/2$; their mean is $1/2$. After the first red draw the next proportions are $3/4$ and $1/2$ with probabilities $2/3$ and $1/3$, whose mean is $1/2+1/6=2/3$. AC supplies the countable choice assumed in Lebesgue construction and CE existence; the interval recursion itself makes no selections. [F3, F4, F5, step 1.1, step 2.1] ∎

For $t\ge0$, compact attainment and rational approximation give $$\{H\le t\}=\bigcap_{m\ge1}\bigcup_{q\in(\mathbb Q\cap[0,t])\cup\{t\}}\{a_q<\varepsilon+1/m\ \text{or}\ a_q>R-1/m\}.$$ The reverse inclusion follows since the continuous nonnegative distance of $a_s$ to the closed set $(-\infty,\varepsilon]\cup[R,\infty)$ then has minimum zero on $[0,t]$. On the common probability-one event $Z_0=x$, the initial radius is strictly between the boundaries. Continuity and the intermediate value theorem give $H=S_\varepsilon\wedge T_R$, the boundary value $|Z_H-y|\in\{\varepsilon,R\}$ when $H<\infty$, and $|Z_s-y|\in(\varepsilon,R)$ for $s<H$. source_lines.30: Let $R$ be a commutative unital ring, let $q,\rho\in R^\times$, put $z=q-q^{-1}$, and choose $\delta\in R$ with $z(\delta-1)=\rho-\rho^{-1}$. For $n\ge2$, the BMW algebra $BMW_n(R;q,\rho,\delta)$ is the unital associative $R$-algebra generated by invertible $g_i$ and elements $e_i$ for $1\le i<n$, subject to the following relations (an adjacent relation is imposed only when both indices exist):
source_lines.32: - braid and distant braid: $g_i g_{i+1}g_i=g_{i+1}g_i g_{i+1}$ and $g_i g_j=g_jg_i$ for $|i-j|\ge2$;
source_lines.36: - loop: $e_i^2=\delta e_i$.
source_lines.40: If $z$ is invertible, the parameter relation reads $\delta=1+(\rho-\rho^{-1})/z$. If $z$ is not invertible, the presentation uses the universal coefficient relation $z(\delta-1)=\rho-\rho^{-1}$ and does not divide by $z$. The quotient by the two-sided ideal generated by all $e_i$ is the cup-cap-zero Hecke quotient; this definition does not assert a BMW diagram-basis theorem or a BMW quantum-centralizer theorem.

source_lines.40: Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]) for this norm-completion construction, and let $H$ be a complex Hilbert space. Order its finite-dimensional complex subspaces by inclusion. This is a directed system because the span $F+G$ of any two finite-dimensional subspaces is finite-dimensional. To each such $F$, assign the finite-dimensional CAR C*-algebra of [[thm-finite-dimensional-car-algebra-is-matrix-algebra]], with the generator-preserving maps of [[lem-car-finite-subspace-inclusions-are-isometric]]. Identify each stage with its image under these injective maps and let $\mathsf{CAR}_{\mathrm{loc}}(H)$ be their algebraic union.
source_lines.42: The common finite-stage norm is well defined on this union because every inclusion is isometric. Under Countable Choice, [[thm-metric-completion-exists]] supplies a metric completion and [[thm-metric-completion-carries-a-unique-banach-space-structure]] equips it with the compatible Banach-space structure; this is the norm completion of [[def-completion-of-a-normed-space]]. Define the **CAR C*-algebra over $H$**, $\mathsf{CAR}(H)$, to be this norm completion of $\mathsf{CAR}_{\mathrm{loc}}(H)$. Addition, multiplication, scalar multiplication, and involution are the compatible finite-stage operations; submultiplicativity and isometry of the involution make them extend continuously to the completion, and the C*-identity passes to limits. The identity is nonzero because the zero-dimensional stage is $\mathbb C$ and every inclusion preserves its unit. For $f\in H$, write $c(f)$ for the image of the generator in the stage $\operatorname{span}\{f\}$; the universal inductive-limit property and its norm are proved in [[thm-general-car-has-universal-inductive-limit-norm]].

source_lines.36: For $n\ge0$, let $\iota_n:\mathsf{CAR}_n\to\mathsf{CAR}_{n+1}$ be the unique unital $*$-homomorphism sending each of the first $n$ annihilation and creation generators to the generator with the same index. Here $\mathsf{CAR}_n$ is the universal finite-mode C*-algebra of [[thm-finite-mode-car-algebra-is-full-matrix-algebra]]. Then $\iota_n$ is isometric and injective. Under the occupation-basis identifications $\mathcal F_{n+1}\cong\mathcal F_n\otimes\mathbb C^2$, it is represented by $A\mapsto A\otimes I_2$.
source_lines.41: [F1] The finite-mode C*-algebra is universal for the finite CAR relations and is represented faithfully on $\mathcal F_n$ as $M_{2^n}(\mathbb C)$ ([[thm-finite-mode-car-algebra-is-full-matrix-algebra]]).
source_lines.43: [F2] In the occupation basis, the first $n$ annihilation and creation operators act by the toggle formulas in the finite-mode matrix-unit construction ([[lem-finite-mode-car-occupation-matrix-units]]).
source_lines.49: 1.1 The first $n$ generators in $\mathsf{CAR}_{n+1}$ satisfy the $n$-mode CAR relations. The quotient universal property in [F3], followed by the finite-mode C*-completion in [F1], therefore gives the unique unital $*$-homomorphism $\iota_n$ with the stated generator values. [given, F1, F3, construct]
source_lines.51: 1.2 Identify $e_S\otimes e_\varepsilon$ with $e_{S\cup(\{n+1\}\text{ if }\varepsilon=1)}$, where $S\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}$ and $\varepsilon\in\{0,1\}$. For $j\le n$, the number of occupied indices below $j$ is unchanged by the last occupation bit. The formulas in [F2] therefore give $c_j^{(n+1)}=c_j^{(n)}\otimes I_2$ and $(c_j^\dagger)^{(n+1)}=(c_j^\dagger)^{(n)}\otimes I_2$. By multiplication and linearity, the representation of $\iota_n(x)$ is $\pi_n(x)\otimes I_2$ for every $x\in\mathsf{CAR}_n$. [given, F2, algebra]
source_lines.53: 2.1 For any $A\in M_{2^n}(\mathbb C)$ and $(x_0,x_1)\in\mathbb C^{2^n}\oplus\mathbb C^{2^n}$, $\|(A\otimes I_2)(x_0,x_1)\|_2^2=\|Ax_0\|_2^2+\|Ax_1\|_2^2\le\|A\|^2(\|x_0\|_2^2+\|x_1\|_2^2)$, so $\|A\otimes I_2\|\le\|A\|$. Conversely, vectors $(x,0)$ with $\|x\|_2\le1$ give $\|A\otimes I_2\|\ge\|A\|$. By [F1] and step 1.2, $\|\iota_n(x)\|=\|\pi_n(x)\otimes I_2\|=\|\pi_n(x)\|=\|x\|$. Thus $\iota_n$ is isometric and therefore injective; the argument includes $n=0$. [given, F1, step 1.2, algebra] ∎

source_lines.26: Put $A=\mathbb Z[a^{\pm1},s,d^{\pm1}]/(s(d-1)-(a-a^{-1}))$. This ring is an integral domain and embeds in $\mathbb Q(i)(a,s)$ by $d\mapsto1+(a-a^{-1})/s$, where $i^2=-1$. A link diagram means a finite generic immersion of circles in the oriented plane with over/under data at its double points. Regular isotopy is generated by planar isotopy and Reidemeister moves II and III. A positive curl is a one-crossing curl whose oriented self-crossing has sign $+1$; its sign is independent of the direction chosen on its component. There is a unique function $P$ from link diagrams, including the empty diagram, to $A$ with $P(\varnothing)=1$, unchanged by regular isotopy, satisfying the following local rules: a positive or negative curl multiplies $P$ by $a$ or $a^{-1}$; a disjoint trivial circle multiplies $P$ by $d$; and $P(L_+)-P(L_-)=s(P(L_0)-P(L_\infty))$. Here in an oriented disk with four cyclically labelled endpoints $1,2,3,4$, $L_+$ connects $1$ to $3$ over the strand from $2$ to $4$, and the two smoothings are chosen so that the oriented smoothing for any orientation making this crossing positive is $L_0$; $L_-$ reverses the crossing and $L_\infty$ is the other smoothing. Rotating the disk interchanges both differences and preserves the rule. In particular the empty diagram freely generates the quotient of the free $A$-module on closed diagrams by these rules.
source_lines.30: **Given:** Finite link diagrams, the Reidemeister moves, and the indicated crossing, curl and smoothing conventions.
source_lines.32: [F1] Crossings can be switched independently. Switching changes only over/under data, and smoothing a crossing removes that crossing. Operations in disjoint crossing disks commute.
source_lines.50: 4.1 The multi-component switch set for lifting a fixed component is independent of point and direction, so step 2.1 makes its expansion independent of these choices. For a knot, moving the point past one encounter with a crossing toggles exactly that crossing in the descending switch set. The two terminal descending diagrams differ by switching this crossing, which is the first or last encounter from the new point. Their terminal values satisfy the required sum-skein equation: if their writhes are $v+1,v-1$, the two smoothings have values $b^v$ and $hb^v$. To see this, the smoothing that separates the traversed initial portion produces two descending unknots with one over the other; the other is their connected sum with possibly one direction reversed. Their total self-writhe is $v$, since the mutual crossing-sign sum of the two separated portions is zero: one lies over the other, and their algebraic planar intersection number is zero. Both diagrams reduce by pulling these overlying arcs away, followed by removing curls, so their evaluations follow from lower-crossing invariance and curl factors. The equation is $b^{v+1}+b^{v-1}=t(1+h)b^v$. By commuting the toggled switch to the beginning of the expansion, this terminal equality makes $Q(D,p)$ unchanged. Moving the point around all arcs proves point independence. Averaging the two directions makes direction independence explicit. Agreement with the terminal scalar on descending diagrams is deferred until after regular-isotopy invariance; point independence alone does not identify the two directed expansions. [F1, step 2.1, step 3.1, algebra]
source_lines.58: 8.1 For move III, label the three local arcs by their height order. First give them the height order in which they are first encountered in a chosen traversal or component-lift expansion. There are then no local switches, and corresponding switches outside the disk produce identical terminal values and lower-crossing smoothing terms related by the same move, giving invariance by induction. The six possible height orders are connected by exchanging adjacent heights. Such an exchange switches one corresponding crossing on both sides of the move. Apply the sum-skein equation at those crossings: each sum of the old and switched evaluations is $t$ times a pair of smoothing evaluations. The two pairs agree. One smoothing cancels the two remaining crossings by move II or identifies them by planar isotopy; the other slides a cup past them. Here is an endpoint description of the cup slide, independent of any BMW presentation. In the following diagram words the factors are stacked from top to bottom in their written left-to-right order. In a three-strand rectangle let $e_j$ denote the actual crossing-free cup and cap joining adjacent positions $j,j+1$, and $x_j$ the actual crossing at those positions. The diagrams $e_1x_2x_1$ and $x_2x_1e_2$ both reduce to the diagram with upper cup $(1,2)$, lower cap $(2',3')$, and an untwisted strand from $3$ to $1'$. Slide the arc attached to the cup across the two crossing disks; the two successive over/under encounters then bound a bigon and cancel by move II. Likewise $x_1x_2e_1$ and $e_2x_1x_2$ reduce to upper cup $(2,3)$, lower cap $(1',2')$, and the strand from $1$ to $3'$. Reflecting the crossing data gives the same cancellations for $x_1^{-1},x_2^{-1}$. These are identities of the smoothed diagrams by planar deformation and move II, concerning at most $N-1$ crossings, rather than assumed identities in an abstract algebra. Thus the equality of old evaluations is equivalent to equality of switched evaluations. The adjacent-height exchanges reach every type III configuration, proving move III invariance for every traversal, component choice and outside diagram. Consequently a descending knot $U$ now has $L(U)=b^{w(U)}$: pull its descending arc away by nonincreasing moves II and III until only curls remain, then use step 6.1. This uses the just-proved invariance at $N$, not a direct prescription in step 3.1. Finally expand the established skein equation along the switches for any directed point $p$. The terminal value is now $L(U_p)=b^{w(U_p)}$, so step 2.1 gives $Q(D,p)=L(D)$, for both directions. Thus the average agrees with every directed expansion, including on descending knots. This closes the simultaneous crossing-number induction over $F$. [step 2.1, step 5.1, step 6.1, step 7.1, induction]

source_lines.61: [F5] $\iota_n$ appends one rightmost vertical strand and $E_n$ is $\delta^{-1}$ times the right closure; for real $\delta$, the involution is conjugate-linear reflection across a horizontal line. ([[def-temperley-lieb-diagram-tower-and-right-closure]])
source_lines.67: 1.1 On a basis diagram, appending a rightmost vertical strand leaves all existing matching pairs unchanged. Distinct diagrams remain distinct after appending it, so freeness in [F1] makes $\iota_n$ injective. Stacking two such appended diagrams creates no new closed component and is the appended version of their original stack, so $\iota_n$ preserves products and the unit. When $\delta$ is real, horizontal reflection also commutes with appending, so it preserves the involution. Right-closing the newly appended vertical strand creates exactly one circle, so $c_n(\iota_n(D))=\delta D$ and $E_n\iota_n(D)=D$. Linearity gives $E_n\iota_n=\mathrm{id}$. [F1, F2, F5, construct]
source_lines.69: 2.1 For basis diagrams $a,b$ on $n$ strands and $x$ on $n+1$ strands, stack the three diagrams and attach the right closure arc at the right boundary. Every path or cycle in this finite graph is unchanged if the left $n$-strand stacks are performed before the right closure: the closure arc meets only the two rightmost boundary endpoints, and the factors $a,b$ attach only to the left $n$ interfaces. The exterior matching is therefore the product $a c_n(x)b$, with the same number of removed cycles and the same powers of $\delta$. Thus $c_n(\iota_n(a)x\iota_n(b))=a c_n(x)b$. Multiplication by $\delta^{-1}$ proves bimodularity on basis diagrams; bilinearity extends it. [F1, F2, F5, step 1.1, algebra]
source_lines.73: 4.1 Right-closing $\iota_n(x)d_n$ connects the last cap and cup to the exterior closure arc; the result is the diagram $x$ on the first $n$ strands, with no new circle. Thus $c_n(\iota_n(x)d_n)=x$, so $E_n(\iota_n(x)d_n)=\delta^{-1}x$. Trace preservation and [F4] give $\tau_{n+1}(\iota_n(x)d_n)=\tau_n(E_n(\iota_n(x)d_n))=\delta^{-1}\tau_n(x)$. [F1, F4, F5, step 3.1, algebra]

source_lines.34: Let $K$ be any field, $\delta\in K$, and let $0\le r\le n$ with $n-r$ even. Assume $r>0$ or $\delta\ne0$ or $n=r=0$. Put $A_n=\mathrm{TL}_n(K,\delta)$, use the right modules $W_{n,t}$ of [[def-temperley-lieb-link-state-standard-modules]], and put $D_{n,t}=W_{n,t}/\operatorname{rad}\phi_{n,t}$. There are $y,z:n\to r$ with $y\circ z^*=1_r$, and for $r>0$ both may be chosen as basis monic diagrams. There is an idempotent $e\in A_n$ with $eA_ne\cong A_r$ such that $M\mapsto Me$ is exact, sends $W_{n,t}$ to $W_{r,t}$, and sends $D_{n,t}$ to $D_{r,t}$, with value zero when $t>r$.
source_lines.54: 1.1 We construct $y,z:n\to r$ with $y\circ z^*=1_r$. Write $n=r+2k$. If $k=0$, take identities. If $r>0$, take $y$ with bottom cups $(1,2),(3,4),\ldots,(2k-1,2k)$ and all remaining sites propagating; take $z$ with cups $(2,3),(4,5),\ldots,(2k,2k+1)$ and all remaining sites propagating. In $y\circ z^*$, the first through strand follows the single alternating chain through sites $1,2,\ldots,2k+1$, while each remaining through strand is straight. There is no closed component, and the exterior matching is $1_r$. If $r=0$ and $\delta\ne0$, choose the same adjacent perfect matching $y=z_0$ on $n=2k$ sites and put $z=\delta^{-k}z_0$. Then $y\circ z^*=\delta^{-k}\delta^k1_0=1_0$. This also handles $n=r=0$ with the empty diagram and no scalar inversion. [F1, given, construct, algebra]
source_lines.56: 2.1 Set $e=z^*\circ y\in A_n$. Step 1.1 gives $e^2=e$. The map $A_r\to eA_ne$ sending $a$ to $z^*\circ a\circ y$ is multiplicative because $y\circ z^*=1_r$, and its inverse is $b\mapsto y\circ b\circ z^*$. Indeed the first composite is identity, and the second is $b\mapsto ebe=b$ on the corner. Thus it is an algebra isomorphism with identity $1_r$ mapping to $e$. [F1, step 1.1, algebra]
source_lines.60: 3.2 For every label $t$, the map $W_{n,t}e\to W_{r,t}$ sending $xe$ to $x\circ z^*$ is well-defined, since diagrams of propagation less than $t$ remain such after composition. Its inverse sends $u:r\to t$ to $u\circ y$, which lies in $W_{n,t}e$. Their composites are identity by $y\circ z^*=1_r$ and $xe=x\circ z^*\circ y$. They respect right $A_r$ action under the corner identification in step 2.1. If $t>r$, every diagram $r\to t$ has propagation less than $t$, so both spaces vanish. [F1, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra]

source_lines.36: Fix $n\ge0$, a commutative ring $R$, and $\delta\in R$. For $1\le i<n$, let $d_i\in\mathrm{TL}_n(R,\delta)$ be the elementary cup-cap diagram of [[def-temperley-lieb-diagram-category]]. Then
source_lines.38: $$d_i^2=\delta d_i\ (1\le i<n),\qquad d_i d_{i+1}d_i=d_i,\quad d_{i+1}d_i d_{i+1}=d_{i+1}\ (1\le i\le n-2),\qquad d_i d_j=d_jd_i\ (1\le i,j<n,\ |i-j|>1).$$
source_lines.48: [F1] $d_i$ has a cap joining top points $i,i+1$, a cup joining bottom points $i,i+1$, and vertical through strands at all other positions. ([[def-temperley-lieb-diagram-category]])
source_lines.50: [F2] Stacking removes each closed cycle with one coefficient $\delta$ and leaves the exterior matching. ([[def-temperley-lieb-diagram-category]])
source_lines.52: [F3] Products $xy=x\circ y$ stack the left factor above the right factor; composition is associative and bilinear. ([[def-temperley-lieb-diagram-category]], [[thm-temperley-lieb-diagram-category-laws]])
source_lines.58: **Proof technique:** direct.
source_lines.60: 1.1 In the stack $d_i^2$, all strands outside positions $i,i+1$ pass straight through. In the two affected positions, the cup of the upper copy joins to the cap of the lower copy to form exactly one closed cycle; the remaining exterior path connections are the same cap and cup as in $d_i$. The stack rule [F2] therefore gives $d_i^2=\delta d_i$. [F1, F2, F3]
source_lines.62: 1.2 Restrict to positions $i,i+1,i+2$ in the stack with upper factor $d_i$, middle factor $d_{i+1}$ and lower factor $d_i$. The upper cap and lower cup are the exterior cap and cup of the result. The remaining path starts at the exterior top point $i+2$: it follows the upper through strand to the first interface, the middle cap to position $i+1$, the upper cup to position $i$, the middle through strand to the second interface, the lower cap to position $i+1$, the middle cup to position $i+2$, and the lower through strand to exterior bottom point $i+2$. Thus the two remaining exterior endpoints are joined exactly as in $d_i$, and all six interface points lie on this path; no closed component is formed. The product is therefore $d_i d_{i+1}d_i=d_i$. Reflecting this three-position stack horizontally about its middle strand preserves stacking and loop counts while interchanging $d_i$ and $d_{i+1}$, so it gives $d_{i+1}d_i d_{i+1}=d_{i+1}$. [F1, F2, F3]

source_lines.35: Let $R$, $\delta$, $n$, $t$ and $W_{n,t}(R,\delta)$ be as in [[def-temperley-lieb-link-state-standard-modules]]. For link states $x,y$, let $x^*$ denote reflection across a horizontal line. The diagram $y\circ x^*:t\to t$ is either $\delta^c1_t$ for some $c\ge0$ or has fewer than $t$ propagating components. Define $\phi_{n,t}(x,y)=\delta^c$ in the first case and $0$ in the second, and extend $R$-bilinearly. Then $\phi_{n,t}$ is symmetric and satisfies
source_lines.37: $$\phi_{n,t}(x\cdot a,y)=\phi_{n,t}(x,y\cdot a^*)$$
source_lines.39: for all $x,y\in W_{n,t}(R,\delta)$ and $a\in\mathrm{TL}_n(R,\delta)$. Here $a^*$ is reflection across a horizontal line. The matrix of $\phi_{n,t}$ in the link-state basis is the Gram matrix obtained by reflecting and capping two link states, with one factor $\delta$ for each closed loop.
source_lines.53: 1.1 For basis link states $x$ and $y$, the composite $y\circ x^*$ is a diagram from $t$ to $t$. If all $t$ boundary points propagate, planarity forces them to connect in their order, so after removing $c$ closed loops the result is $\delta^c1_t$ for a unique $c$. Otherwise it has fewer than $t$ propagating components. Thus the stated value is determined by the matching and loop count, and it extends uniquely to an $R$-bilinear form on the free link-state basis [F1, F2]. [F1, F2, given, construct]
source_lines.57: 3.1 For basis states $x,y$ and a basis diagram $a\in\mathrm{TL}_n$, reflection gives $(x\circ a)^*=a^*\circ x^*$. Both form values are therefore the coefficient of $1_t$ in the same associative composite $y\circ(x\circ a)^*=y\circ a^*\circ x^*=(y\circ a^*)\circ x^*$. They have the same exterior matching and number of removed loops, so their coefficients of $1_t$ agree. If an intermediate term has fewer than $t$ propagating components, it remains lower-propagating after further stacking and contributes zero on both sides. This proves the invariance identity for basis states and basis diagrams; bilinearity proves it for all $x,y,a$. [F1, F2, step 1.1, step 2.1] ∎

source_lines.30: Let $R$ be a commutative ring with unit, $\delta\in R$, $n\ge1$, and let $t$ be allowed for $W_{n,t}(R,\delta)$. Include $\mathrm{TL}_{n-1}(R,\delta)$ into $\mathrm{TL}_n(R,\delta)$ by adding a rightmost vertical strand, and restrict the right action along this inclusion. Set $W_{m,s}=0$ when $s<0$, $s>m$, or $m-s$ is odd. Then there is a short exact sequence of right $\mathrm{TL}_{n-1}(R,\delta)$-modules
source_lines.32: $$0\longrightarrow W_{n-1,t-1}\longrightarrow \operatorname{Res}^{TL_n}_{TL_{n-1}}W_{n,t}\longrightarrow W_{n-1,t+1}\longrightarrow0.$$
source_lines.34: The sequence gives a two-step filtration; it is not asserted to split.
source_lines.40: [F1] Link states are basis half-diagrams; the right action stacks the state above the algebra diagram and kills lower-propagating terms ([[def-temperley-lieb-link-state-standard-modules]], [[lem-temperley-lieb-link-state-module-action-is-well-defined]]).
source_lines.42: [F2] The inclusion $\mathrm{TL}_{n-1}\to\mathrm{TL}_n$ is horizontal juxtaposition with the identity strand, and composition is associative ([[def-temperley-lieb-diagram-category]], [[thm-temperley-lieb-diagram-category-laws]]).
source_lines.54: 1.1 Let $U$ be the span in $W_{n,t}$ of link states in which the rightmost bottom site $n$ is a defect. Removing that defect and its top endpoint gives a link state in $W_{n-1,t-1}$; conversely, adding a new rightmost bottom site joined to a new rightmost top defect gives the inverse map. These basis maps define an $R$-module isomorphism $W_{n-1,t-1}\to U$. [F1, given, construct]
source_lines.56: 2.1 Under the inclusion in [F2], the rightmost strand of every diagram from $\mathrm{TL}_{n-1}$ is vertical and does not meet the other $n-1$ sites. Stacking such a diagram below a link state in $U$ leaves the external site $n$ connected to its same defect. Thus $U$ is a $\mathrm{TL}_{n-1}$-submodule, and the isomorphism in step 1.1 intertwines the restricted action. [F1, F2, step 1.1]
source_lines.58: 2.2 The quotient by $U$ has basis the link states in which $n$ is paired to a site $m<n$. Cut the arc $(m,n)$ and turn $m$ into a defect. Noncrossing forces every defect to lie outside this arc, so this new defect is the rightmost one; the result is a link state with $n-1$ sites and $t+1$ defects. The inverse attaches a new site $n$ to the rightmost defect. These operations are inverse bijections of bases, so they give an $R$-module isomorphism of the quotient's underlying module with $W_{n-1,t+1}$. [F1, step 1.1, construct]
source_lines.60: 3.1 Check the quotient map on a basis state whose rightmost site $n$ is paired to $m<n$. A generator $d_i$ with $i\notin\{m-1,m\}$ does not meet the endpoint $m$; stacking and cutting therefore give the same exterior matching and the same loop count. If $i=m-1$, the site $m-1$ is either a defect or is paired to a site $k<m-1$ (it cannot be paired to a site inside $(m,n)$, since that would cross the arc $(m,n)$). In the paired case, stacking joins the distinct arcs $(k,m-1)$ and $(m,n)$ and replaces them by the bottom arc $(m-1,m)$ and the arc $(k,n)$; cutting either result at the arc ending at $n$ gives the same link state, with no loop removed. In the defect case, stacking makes $n$ a defect, so the result lies in $U$ and is zero in the quotient. Cutting first makes $m-1$ and $m$ two defects; stacking $d_{m-1}$ joins their two top endpoints, leaving fewer than $t+1$ propagating strands, so its class in $W_{n-1,t+1}$ is also zero. If $i=m$, then $m+1$ lies inside the arc $(m,n)$ and must be paired to some $k$ with $m+1<k<n$. Stacking joins the distinct arcs $(m,n)$ and $(m+1,k)$, replacing them by $(m,m+1)$ and $(k,n)$; cutting at the arc ending at $n$ before or after this operation gives the same state, again with no loop removed. These cases exhaust generators touching $m$; hence the quotient map intertwines every $d_i$. By [F3] it intertwines the whole $\mathrm{TL}_{n-1}$-action. The basis descriptions in step 1.1 and step 2.2 give exactness at every term. [F1, F2, F3, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 2.2]

source_lines.40: **Given:** $\delta\in\mathbb C^\times$, the trace-pairing radicals, and the maps from [[def-temperley-lieb-diagram-tower-and-right-closure]].
source_lines.42: [F1] The diagram tower maps $\iota_n$ and $E_n$ are bimodular and trace-preserving. ([[lem-temperley-lieb-diagram-tower-conditional-expectation-identities]])
source_lines.54: 2.1 If $x\in J_n$ and $z\in\mathrm{TL}_{n+1}$, trace preservation and right bimodularity yield $\tau_{n+1}(z\iota_n(x))=\tau_n(E_n(z\iota_n(x)))=\tau_n(E_n(z)x)=0$, because $E_n(z)\in\mathrm{TL}_n$. Hence $\iota_n(x)\in J_{n+1}$. [F1, step 1.1, algebra]
source_lines.56: 3.1 If $x\in J_{n+1}$ and $a\in\mathrm{TL}_n$, then $\tau_n(aE_n(x))=\tau_n(E_n(\iota_n(a)x))$ by left bimodularity, and trace preservation makes this $\tau_{n+1}(\iota_n(a)x)=0$ by the definition of $J_{n+1}$. source_lines.51: Put $k=\ell-2$ and quotient the diagram category by the tensor ideal generated by $p_{k+1}$. A retained path of length $n$ is $a=(a_0,\ldots,a_n)$ with $a_0=0$, $0\le a_i\le k$ and $|a_i-a_{i-1}|=1$. There are inclusions $i_a:p_{a_n}\to n$ and retractions $r_a:n\to p_{a_n}$ such that $r_ai_b=0$ for distinct paths, $r_ai_a=p_{a_n}$, and $\sum_a i_ar_a=1_n$. Consequently the $E_{a,b}=i_ar_b$ at a common endpoint form complete matrix units, with
source_lines.53: $$E_{a,b}E_{c,d}=\delta_{b,c}E_{a,d},\qquad \operatorname{Tr}_n(E_{a,b})=\delta_{a,b}[a_n+1]_q.$$
source_lines.75: 1.2 For $1\le a\le k$ set $f_a=p_a\otimes1$, $X_a=f_aU_af_a$ and $\lambda_a=[a+1]/[a]$. Define $\alpha_a=f_a(1_{a-1}\otimes\cup)p_{a-1},\qquad \beta_a=p_{a-1}(1_{a-1}\otimes\cap)f_a.$ Absorption of $p_{a-1}$ next to $p_a$ gives $\alpha_a\beta_a=X_a$: insert the cup/cap and remove the absorbed lower projector. Closing the other composite is exactly the right partial trace of $p_a$ in its lower corner, so [F1] gives $\beta_a\alpha_a=\lambda_ap_{a-1}$. Thus $X_a^2=\lambda_aX_a$. The JW recursion gives $f_a=p_{a+1}+\lambda_a^{-1}\alpha_a\beta_a.$ The two terms are orthogonal because $p_{a+1}$ kills the joining turnback. The down maps are inclusion $\alpha_a$ and retraction $\lambda_a^{-1}\beta_a$; the up maps are the tautological inclusion/retraction of $p_{a+1}$. For $a=0$ there is only $p_1$. Every denominator here has index at most $\ell-1$ and is nonzero. [F1, F2, F3, construct, algebra]
source_lines.81: 3.1 Start with the single rank-zero path and tensor its identity decomposition by $1$. Inductively split each endpoint summand $p_a\otimes1$ by steps 1.2 and 2.1 and compose its up/down maps with the preceding path maps. Cross-composites of the new up/down terms vanish by turnback annihilation; the equal down composite is $\lambda_a^{-1}\beta_a\alpha_a=p_{a-1}$ and the up composite is $p_{a+1}$. Different preceding paths have zero composite by induction. Their new projections sum to the old projection tensored with $1$, because the split is complete; at the boundary only the down term remains. This proves simultaneously $r_ai_b=0$ for distinct paths, $r_ai_a=p_{a_n}$ and $\sum_a i_ar_a=1_n$ for every rank. [F1, F2, step 1.2, step 2.1, induction, construct, algebra]
source_lines.83: 4.1 For paths with equal endpoint put $E_{a,b}=i_ar_b$. The composites in step 3.1 give their matrix-unit multiplication. Insert the complete path identity on each side of any morphism and use the corners of step 1.3: these units span all endomorphisms, and the same argument describes unequal-degree Hom spaces. They are independent because multiplying a putative relation by $r_a$ and $i_b$ isolates its coefficient times the nonzero endpoint projector. Closing $i_ar_b$ has the same finite component graph as closing $r_bi_a$, even though the cut occurs at a different object. Thus the trace is zero off the diagonal and $[a_n+1]$ on it. Each matrix block has nonzero weighted ordinary trace pairing, detected by its transposed matrix units. This proves completeness and nondegeneracy at every rank. Together with step 1.1 it proves all assertions without a recoupling division at the boundary. [F1, F2, F3, step 1.1, step 3.1, step 1.3, algebra] ∎

source_lines.39: Let $(V,B)$ be a finite-dimensional nondegenerate real quadratic space, $Q(v)=B(v,v)$, and let $\Gamma$ and $\rho_x(v)=\alpha(x)vx^{-1}$ be as in [[def-real-clifford-group-and-normalized-pin-spin]]. For anisotropic $u$, $\rho_u=r_u$. Every $x\in\Gamma$ acts by an element of $O(V,B)$, is homogeneous, and is a nonzero scalar times a product of anisotropic vectors. The kernel of $x\mapsto\rho_x$ on $\Gamma$ is exactly $\mathbb R^\times 1$; consequently the unrestricted normalizer in the definition is a group and agrees with its homogeneous part.

source_lines.33: Let $\Lambda_0=\mathbb Z[\lambda^{\pm1},z_0,\delta^{\pm1}]/(\lambda^{-1}-\lambda-z_0(\delta-1))$ and map it to $R$ by $\lambda\mapsto\rho$, $z_0\mapsto-z$, and $\delta\mapsto\delta$. A framed $(n,n)$ tangle is an isotopy class, fixing the boundary, of pairwise disjoint embedded ribbons in a rectangle times an interval, with $n$ prescribed ribbon intervals at each end. An ordinary $(n,n)$ tangle diagram is a generic immersed collection of arcs and circles in the rectangle with those $2n$ fixed endpoints, with each transverse double point marked over/under. Regular isotopy means planar isotopy fixing the boundary together with Reidemeister moves II and III, but not move I; this is the framed-diagram convention of Goodman–Hauschild, §§2.1–2.2. Multiplication is vertical stacking, and the identity is the diagram of $n$ vertical strands. Define $KT_n(R)$ as the quotient of the free $R$-module on regular-isotopy classes by the local rules of Goodman–Hauschild, Definition 2.6, after the displayed parameter substitution: the crossing skein relation is $L_+-L_-=z(L_{\mathrm{id}}-L_{\mathrm{cup-cap}})$, the two opposite single-crossing curls evaluate to $\rho^{-1}$ and $\rho$ times the straight strand, and an isolated unknotted, untwisted circle is removed with coefficient $\delta$. Here $L_+$ and $L_-$ differ by the crossing, while $L_{\mathrm{id}}$ and $L_{\mathrm{cup-cap}}$ are its identity and cup-cap smoothings; all four diagrams agree outside a small disk. Order the $2n$ boundary labels by $1<\cdots<n<n'<\cdots<1'$. The standard orientation of a diagram orients each nonclosed strand from its lower-ordered endpoint to its higher-ordered endpoint and traverses the nonclosed strands by increasing initial endpoint. Such an oriented diagram is totally descending if every crossing is first met as an over-crossing in this traversal. For every perfect matching of the $2n$ boundary points there is a unique regular-isotopy class with that matching which is totally descending, has no strand self-crossings, and has no closed component. The universal BMW-to-tangle isomorphism over $\Lambda_0$ of Goodman–Hauschild, Theorem 5.41, base-changes along $\Lambda_0\to R$ to an isomorphism $BMW_n(R;q,\rho,\delta)\to KT_n(R)$ in the convention of [[def-bmw-algebra-with-fixed-kauffman-skein-convention]]. Both algebras are free over $R$ on these classes, so their rank is $(2n-1)!!$.

source_lines.49: 1.1 Work first over $\Lambda_0$ and write $s=-z_0$, so $s(\delta-1)=\lambda-\lambda^{-1}$, where $z_0$ denotes the skein variable called $z_0$ in the statement. The coefficient ring is the domain $A$ of [F3], under $a=\lambda,s=-z_0,d=\delta$; the coefficient injection and its factorization arguments were proved in that supplier. The scalar evaluation of [[lem-framed-kauffman-link-evaluation]], with $a=\lambda$, $s=-z_0$ and $d=\delta$, identifies the closed-diagram skein module with $\Lambda_0$. Its positive crossing is the usual positive braid crossing, with identity smoothing first. A positive braid closed as a two-strand braid gives a positive self-curl with factor $\lambda$; if the same crossing is followed by a cup-cap, the cup forces opposite strand directions, giving a negative self-curl with factor $\lambda^{-1}$. Thus the helper's framing rules give exactly $G_iE_i=\lambda^{-1}E_i$ and the displayed source convention. [given, F3, algebra]
source_lines.51: 2.1 Choose a direction, order and initial point on every closed component as well as the standard directions and order of the boundary strands. A crossing is incorrect if first encountered underneath. The skein relation replaces an incorrect crossing by its reversal and two diagrams with one fewer crossing. Induct first on the total crossing number and, for the unchanged-crossing term, on incorrect crossings of this fixed traversal. Reversal changes no component or traversal and removes exactly that incorrect crossing. Smoothing terms use the outer induction, with newly chosen traversals if needed. Hence the quotient is spanned by descending diagrams. A descending component is unknotted; successively lifting its traversed portion above its remaining portion and pulling that initial arc away leaves only framing curls. Earlier components lie above later ones, so closed components can be separated and removed. Removing curls multiplies by powers of $\lambda$, and removing circles by $\delta$. The surviving diagrams are descending with no closed components and no self-crossings. [F1, step 1.1, induction]
source_lines.53: 3.1 For a fixed connector, draw simple arcs in separate height layers ordered by their initial endpoints and join them to the fixed boundary intervals. This gives a descending, loop-free, self-crossing-free representative $T_c$. Any two such representatives can be put in those same layers: each earlier strand is over every later strand, so changing its height introduces no intersection. Within its layer, a simple arc with specified endpoints in a disk deforms to any other such arc, while other arcs are in different layers. Its framing has no self-curl. These deformations give framed isotopy, equivalently regular isotopy of the diagrams. Thus the class $T_c$ is unique. Step 2.1 proves that these classes span. [F2, step 2.1, construct]
source_lines.55: 4.1 Close all boundary strands outside the rectangle without new crossings and evaluate by step 1.1, multiplying by $\delta^{-n}$; call the resulting linear functional $\epsilon$. Let $*$ reflect a diagram top to bottom. For any choice of diagrams $U_c$ with connector $c$, form $B=(\epsilon(U_cU_d^*))_{c,d}$. Specialize $\lambda=1,z_0=0$ to $\mathbb Z[\delta^{\pm1}]$. Switching crossings and deleting curls then have no effect, so the entry becomes $\delta^{k_c+k_d+\ell(c,d)-n}$, where $k_c$ is the number of closed components of $U_c$ and $\ell(c,d)$ counts the alternating cycles in the union of the two matching edge sets on the same $2n$ vertices. This is at most $n$, and equals $n$ precisely when every cycle has two vertices, that is, $c=d$. Factor the units $\delta^{k_c}$ from row $c$ and $\delta^{k_d}$ from column $d$. The remaining matrix has diagonal $1$ and off-diagonal terms of strictly negative $\delta$-degree. The determinant of this remaining matrix has constant term $1$, because every nonidentity permutation uses an off-diagonal entry. Therefore the specialized determinant is nonzero. Therefore $\det B\ne0$ in the domain $\Lambda_0$. A relation among the $U_c$, paired with every $U_d^*$, has zero coefficient vector over $\operatorname{Frac}(\Lambda_0)$ and hence over $\Lambda_0$. This proves independence of any representatives with distinct connectors, in particular the $T_c$. [step 1.1, step 3.1, algebra]

source_lines.49: 3.1 The local reduction used below is the following cup-train calculation. Start with a cup at position $a$ and successively cross its right leg past $s$ strands: $T_s=X_{a+s}\cdots X_{a+1}U_a$; all subscripts denote positions at the appropriate intermediate object. A cap at position $j$ outside $[a-1,a+s+1]$ commutes below this train. Within that interval it shortens the expression, except that $s=0,j=a$ removes a loop and gives $\delta$. Here are the reductions covering the interval. At $j=a+s$, use $AX=A$ to remove the last crossing. At $j=a+s+1$, use the slide relation to move the cap left across the last crossing, commute that crossing below the other disjoint factors, and repeat; after $s$ repetitions the cap is next to the cup at position $a+1$, and the snake relation deletes that cap and cup. At $a\le j<a+s$, commute the cap down to the first crossing meeting it, use the slide relation, and cancel the two resulting equal adjacent crossings with $X^2=1$ (when the crossing meets the cup use $XU=U$ instead). At $j=a-1$, commute down to the cup and apply the reflected snake relation. Each operation replaces a word with strictly fewer elementary factors, apart from the loop factor which is retained as a scalar. [step 2.1, algebra]
source_lines.51: 4.1 A crossing outside the same interval commutes below $T_s$. For $a+1\le j<a+s$, commute it to the two consecutive crossings it meets, apply the braid relation, and commute the resulting crossing below the cup; this writes $X_jT_s$ as a train followed by one crossing. At the right endpoint $j=a+s$, cancel the repeated last crossing. At $j=a$, commute towards the cup, use the cup-slide relation and then cancel repeated crossings, or use $XU=U$ when $s=0$. At $j=a+s+1$, the expression is the train $T_{s+1}$. At $j=a-1$, the reflected cup-slide relation moves the starting cup one position left: the expression is a reflected train or shortens by crossing cancellation. Apply the same calculation after reflection whenever the moving leg travels left. Thus a cap or crossing applied to a train either shortens the word (possibly extracting $\delta$), passes below the train, or extends its moving leg by one strand. These calculations use only the listed relations, not an isotopy or a representation. [step 3.1, algebra]

source_lines.34: Let $A=A^0\oplus A^1$ be a $\mathbb Z/2$-graded unital associative algebra over a field, and suppose it contains an invertible homogeneous element $u\in A^1$. For left modules, the rule $M\mapsto M^0$ gives a bijection between isomorphism classes of graded-simple $A$-modules (with even isomorphisms) and isomorphism classes of simple $A^0$-modules. An inverse sends a left $A^0$-module $N$ to the induced graded module $A\otimes_{A^0}N$.
source_lines.50: 1.1 Write $u^{-1}=x_0+x_1$ with $x_i\in A^i$. From $1=uu^{-1}=ux_0+ux_1$, the odd component $ux_0$ and even component $ux_1$ must be $0$ and $1$, respectively. Since $u$ is invertible, $x_0=0$ and $u^{-1}=x_1\in A^1$. Consequently $A^1=uA^0$: inclusion follows from [F1], and for $a\in A^1$, $u^{-1}a\in A^0$ gives $a=u(u^{-1}a)$. [given, F1, construct, algebra]
source_lines.54: 3.1 Define $\mu:A\otimes_{A^0}M^0\to M$ by $\mu(a\otimes m)=am$. The multiplication map is balanced over $A^0$, so [F3] makes $\mu$ well defined; associativity makes it $A$-linear. Its even part $A^0\otimes_{A^0}M^0\to M^0$ is an isomorphism with inverse $m\mapsto1\otimes m$, by the balancing relation. By step 1.1, the map $M^0\to A^1\otimes_{A^0}M^0$, $m\mapsto u\otimes m$, is an isomorphism: its inverse is $a_1\otimes m\mapsto(u^{-1}a_1)m$, which is well defined because $u^{-1}a_1\in A^0$ and respects balancing. Under this identification, the odd part of $\mu$ is $m\mapsto um$, bijective by step 2.1. Hence $\mu$ is a graded $A$-module isomorphism. [given, F1, F3, step 1.1, step 2.1, construct]
source_lines.56: 3.2 If $L\subseteq M$ is a graded submodule, then $L^1=uL^0$ by invertibility of $u$ and the grading. Conversely, for any $A^0$-submodule $N\subseteq M^0$, the subspace $N\oplus uN$ is graded and is stable under $A$: for $a\in A^0$, $u^{-1}au\in A^0$, so $a(un)=u(u^{-1}au)n\in uN$; for $b\in A^1$, step 1.1 writes $b=ua_0$ with $a_0\in A^0$, whence $bN\subseteq uN$ and $b(uN)\subseteq N$ because $ua_0u\in A^0$. Thus it is an $A$-submodule. By the definition of graded-simple in [F2], $M$ has a proper nonzero graded submodule exactly when $M^0$ has a proper nonzero $A^0$-submodule. [given, F1, F2, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra]
source_lines.58: 4.1 For any left $A^0$-module $N$, the induced module $A\otimes_{A^0}N$ splits as $A^0\otimes_{A^0}N\oplus A^1\otimes_{A^0}N$: the map $(a_0+a_1)\otimes n\mapsto(a_0\otimes n,a_1\otimes n)$ is well defined by balancing and has inverse given by addition. This is a grading because left multiplication respects the parity of $A$, while the balancing relations use only even elements. Its degree-zero part is isomorphic to $N$ by $a_0\otimes n\mapsto a_0n$, with inverse $n\mapsto1\otimes n$. If $N$ is simple, step 3.2 makes the induced module graded-simple. Conversely, step 3.1 identifies any graded $M$ with the module induced from $M^0$, and step 3.2 says $M$ is graded-simple exactly when $M^0$ is simple. Restriction to degree zero and induction are therefore inverse on isomorphism classes: even $A$-isomorphisms restrict to $A^0$-isomorphisms, and $A^0$-isomorphisms induce even $A$-isomorphisms. [F2, F3, step 3.1, step 3.2, algebra] ∎
