source_lines.46: 2.1 Regard a cap on consecutive positions as one symbol $C$ occupying two positions and a through endpoint as a symbol $T$ occupying one. In each maximal interval with no through endpoints, replace the noncrossing cap matching by consecutive adjacent caps; do the corresponding operation on the bottom cups. This gives a flat diagram with the same through endpoints and the same order-preserving through strands. The baseline product $d_1d_3\cdots d_{2p-1}$ has $p$ adjacent caps and cups followed by $t$ through strands, with $p,t$ as in step 1.1. Whenever a top cap at $(i-1,i)$ is followed by a through strand at $i+1$, stacking $d_i$ above that diagram changes the top symbols $CT$ to $TC$: tracing the glued endpoints sends the former through strand to $i-1$ and makes the cap occupy $(i,i+1)$. The cap of the generator and the old through component join into a path meeting the exterior boundary, so no cycle is created. Thus left multiplication by these generators performs each adjacent $CT\mapsto TC$ top swap and leaves the bottom cap/cup pairing unchanged. Sorting from $C^pT^t$ to the prescribed top pattern takes finitely many swaps. For the bottom, if a cup at $(i-1,i)$ is followed by a through endpoint at $i+1$, stack $d_i$ below; its top cap joins the old cup path to the through path, moving the through endpoint to $i-1$ and placing the bottom cup at $(i,i+1)$. These are distinct paths, so no cycle forms. Right multiplication therefore performs the corresponding bottom $CT\mapsto TC$ swaps while leaving the top pairing unchanged. Sorting the bottom pattern is finite as well. The resulting flat diagram has both prescribed patterns and the same order-preserving through strands. [F1, F2, F3, step 1.1, construct]
source_lines.48: 3.1 It remains to restore each nested cap or cup in the flat diagram of step 2.1. A cap island is the matching on a consecutive interval $i,i+1,\ldots,i+2q-1$ whose endpoints are all paired internally and whose outermost cap joins $i$ to $i+2q-1$; the cup version is defined analogously. In the flat diagram those points have simple caps $(i,i+1),(i+2,i+3),\ldots,(i+2q-2,i+2q-1)$. For $q=1$ no generator is needed. For $q>1$, stacking $d_{i+1}d_{i+3}\cdots d_{i+2q-3}$ above them creates the outer cap $(i,i+2q-1)$ and leaves $q-1$ simple caps on the interior endpoints. To verify this, start with the rightmost factor: its glued bottom cup meets endpoints belonging to two distinct cap paths, so their union is a path with exterior endpoints rather than a cycle; it replaces those two adjacent simple caps by one outer cap and one interior simple cap. Each preceding factor performs the same merge with the next simple cap to the left, extending the outer cap by two endpoints while preserving the remaining interior simple caps. Thus no closed component is created at any stage. The reflected product below restores the corresponding bottom cup island by the same path check. [F1, F2, F3, step 2.1, induction, construct]
source_lines.50: 4.1 The cap intervals of a noncrossing matching are nested or disjoint, because interlacing pairs are excluded by [F1]. Thus they form a finite nesting forest. Every generator monomial in $P_n(R,\delta)$ is equal either to $0$ or to $\delta^sN$ for some $s\ge0$ and $N\in\mathcal N_n$. The set $\mathcal N_n$ is in bijection with Dyck paths of semilength $n$; consequently it has $C_n$ elements and spans $P_n(R,\delta)$. source_lines.57: 1.2 Encode $N(j,k)$ by a grid path from $(0,0)$ to $(n,n)$: move east to $x=j_1$, north to $y=k_1$, east to $x=j_2$, north to $y=k_2$, and continue through $(j_r,k_r)$, then move east to $x=n$ and north to $y=n$. For the empty word use east from $(0,0)$ to $(n,0)$ and then north to $(n,n)$. The inequalities $k_i\le j_i$, $j_i<j_{i+1}$ and $k_i<k_{i+1}$ say exactly that this path stays in $y\le x$. Conversely, in any path from $(0,0)$ to $(n,n)$ using east and north steps and staying in $y\le x$, record each positive vertical run whose $x$-coordinate is less than $n$ by its endpoint $(j_i,k_i)$; omit the forced final vertical run at $x=n$. There is no vertical run at $x=0$, every recorded run is preceded by a positive horizontal run, and consecutive recorded coordinates strictly increase in both coordinates. The path condition gives $k_i\le j_i$, while $j_i<n$ and $k_i<n$ by construction. Thus the corners recover exactly one admissible parameter list; if there are no recorded runs, it is the empty word. The parameterization itself has no duplicate formal words: within each block the indices decrease consecutively, while at every block boundary the next index $j_{i+1}$ is strictly greater than the preceding endpoint $k_i$; hence the block boundaries are exactly the strict ascents in the index sequence and uniquely recover all $(j_i,k_i)$. Mapping east to up and north to down sends $x-y$ to the height, so these paths are exactly the Dyck paths in [F2]. This also covers $n=0$, where the path and word are empty. [F2, given, construct]

source_lines.58: 1.1 Let f:D_f→{0,1} be a nonconstant Boolean function on N bits and g:D_g→{0,1} a nonconstant Boolean function on m bits. The composed partial function h=f∘g^N has domain D_h={ (x_1,…,x_N)∈D_g^N : (g(x_1),…,g(x_N))∈D_f }. This domain is nonempty: choose one z∈D_f and fixed preimages in D_g of 0 and 1, which exist because g is nonconstant, then lift the coordinates of z blockwise. Choose optimal matrices Γ_f,Γ_g normalized so max_i||Γ_f∘Δ_i||=max_j||Γ_g∘Δ_j||=1; write a=||Γ_g||=Adv±(g). [given, F1, F2, F3, F6]
source_lines.60: 1.2 Decompose each adversary matrix by output classes, Γ_g=[[0,B_g],[B_g^T,0]]. For a,b∈{0,1}, let G^{ab} be the (a,b) block of Γ_g when a≠b and let G^{aa}=a I on D_g^a. For x,y∈D_h put \tilde x=(g(x_1),…,g(x_N)) and define (Γ_h)_{xy}=(Γ_f)_{\tilde x,\tilde y}\prod_{j=1}^N G^{\tilde x_j,\tilde y_j}_{x_j,y_j}. This matrix is real symmetric and vanishes whenever h(x)=h(y); if Γ_f,Γ_g are entrywise nonnegative, so is Γ_h. [given, F1, F2, F3, construct]
source_lines.62: 2.1 By [F4,F5], choose a singular-vector basis of the cross block B_g. Pair its positive singular vectors across the two output classes, and pair equal numbers of left and right null vectors with singular value zero. If the null-space dimensions differ, each leftover null vector is a one-dimensional component supported on just one output class; its equal-output patch is aI and its cross-output action is zero. For a paired singular value s≤a, the four restrictions G^{00},G^{01},G^{10},G^{11} act as a times C_s=[[1,s/a],[s/a,1]], which is positive semidefinite with unit diagonal. A leftover singleton is represented by C_0=diag(1,0) or diag(0,1), a positive semidefinite matrix with diagonal entries at most one. For each tuple of child components, the corresponding invariant subspace is indexed by the compatible outer output labels b∈D_f, and the restriction of Γ_h is a^N times the compression of Γ_f∘C, where C_{b,b′} is the product of the selected two-output factors. The tensor-product factor C is positive semidefinite with diagonal entries at most one. Write C_{b,b′}=⟨c_b|c_{b′}⟩ with ||c_b||≤1; then V|b⟩=|b⟩⊗|c_b⟩ is a contraction and V^*(Γ_f⊗I)V=Γ_f∘C, so ||Γ_f∘C||≤||Γ_f||. The SVD components span every child input space, proving ||Γ_h||≤||Γ_f||a^N. [given, F4, F5, step 1.2, algebra]
source_lines.64: 3.1 Choose top singular pairs (u_f,v_f) and (u_g,v_g) for the cross blocks of Γ_f and Γ_g. The bipartite block form makes α_f=(u_f,v_f)/√2 and α_g=(u_g,v_g)/√2 eigenvectors with eigenvalues ||Γ_f|| and a. For a fixed outer output tuple b, each child factor G^{b_j,b′_j} sends the restricted α_g component in class b′_j to a times the corresponding component in class b_j, whether b_j=b′_j (the patched aI block) or b_j≠b′_j (the singular-vector equation for B_g). Substitution in the definition of Γ_h therefore shows α_h(x)=α_f(tilde x)∏_jα_g(x_j) is an eigenvector with eigenvalue ||Γ_f||a^N. Together with step 2.1 this gives ||Γ_h||=||Γ_f||a^N. [given, F1, F4, F5, step 1.2, step 2.1, algebra]
source_lines.66: 3.2 Fix an input bit q in block j and put d=||Γ_g∘Δ_q||. If d=0, then every entry of Γ_g∘Δ_q is zero, the equal-output patch dI is zero, and the masked composed block is zero. Suppose d>0. In Γ_h∘Δ_{j,q}, if the outer block outputs agree at j, its factor Γ_f∘Δ_j is zero; equivalently, the patched equal-output child block is diagonal in x_j and is killed by the inner mismatch Δ_q. If the outer outputs differ at j, the child cross block is exactly the corresponding block of Γ_g∘Δ_q. Thus the masked composite has the same entrywise construction as step 1.2 with outer matrix Γ_f∘Δ_j, child j cross block from Γ_g∘Δ_q patched by dI on equal-output blocks, and every other child patched by aI. Repeating the invariant-subspace and correlation-compression argument of step 2.1 bounds its norm by ||Γ_f∘Δ_j|| d a^{N−1}. The paired, zero-singular, and singleton components are handled as in step 2.1; the outer and inner filtered norms are at most one by normalization, so ||Γ_h∘Δ_{j,q}||≤a^{N−1}. [given, F3, F4, F5, step 1.2, step 2.1]
source_lines.68: 4.1 Therefore max_{j,q}||Γ_h∘Δ_{j,q}||≤a^{N-1}, while ||Γ_h||=Adv±(f)a^N by step 3.1. Its ratio is at least Adv±(f)a, proving Adv±(f∘g^N)≥Adv±(f)Adv±(g). If Γ_f and Γ_g are nonnegative, step 1.2 makes Γ_h nonnegative, so the identical argument proves Adv(f∘g^N)≥Adv(f)Adv(g). If either function is constant, the asserted lower bound is the trivial zero bound. [given, F1, F2, step 1.2, step 3.1, step 3.2] ∎

If $N=M$, identify $A_M$ with the raw address register. If $N<M$, supply a separate clean $N$-level raw-address register $Q_N$ initialized to $|0\rangle$, together with clean comparator and routing workspace.
source_lines.39: **Output:** The zero-completed query action $|j,b\rangle\mapsto|j,b\oplus\widetilde x_j\rangle$ on $A_M$ and the response bit, where $\widetilde x_j=x_{j+1}$ for $j<N$ and $\widetilde x_j=0$ for $j\ge N$, with every added register restored to its specified computational-basis zero state.

For each $j=1,\ldots,N-1$, apply the basis transposition $(0\ j)$ to $Q_N$ conditioned on $A_M=j$ and $v=1$; apply no transposition for other control values. These mutually disjoint controlled permutations define a finite input-independent unitary $R_{N,M}$, with

source_lines.30: Let $B(0,r)\subseteq K\subseteq B(0,R)$ be a closed convex body in $\mathbb R^n$, $n\ge2$. The grid has $(d+1)^2$ vertices, of which the two rough sides contain $2(d+1)$ distinct vertices; hence $Q_0$ has $(d-1)(d+1)=d^2-1$ coordinates. There are $d^2$ faces. [F1, given, algebra]
source_lines.86: 1.2 The columns of $\partial_2$ are independent. If a face combination $b\in Q_2$ has zero boundary, its coefficient on each top horizontal physical edge is the coefficient of the unique face immediately below that edge, so all top-row face coefficients vanish. On the next horizontal row, each boundary coefficient is the sum of the face coefficients immediately above and below; the already-zero top row forces the next row to vanish. Repeating downward gives $b=0$. Hence $\operatorname{rank}\partial_2=d^2$. [F1, given, algebra]
source_lines.88: 1.3 A self-avoiding left-to-right path starts with one of the $d+1$ horizontal edges from a left rough vertex into the patch. At each subsequent vertex the square grid has at most four incident edges, and the edge just used cannot be immediately traversed backwards, leaving at most three choices. Thus for length $\ell\ge1$ there are at most $(d+1)3^{\ell-1}\le(d+1)3^\ell$ such paths. [F1, algebra]
source_lines.98: 5.1 For a relative cycle $z$, let $q_i(z)$ be the parity of its selected horizontal edges between columns $i$ and $i+1$, for $i=0,\ldots,d-1$. Summing the relative vertex-boundary equations over columns $1,\ldots,i$ cancels every interior edge twice and leaves only the two cut sets, so $q_0(z)=q_i(z)$. Each face boundary has either zero or two horizontal edges in a given column strip, so $q_i$ vanishes on $\operatorname{im}\partial_2$. The straight horizontal row $z_0$ has $q_i(z_0)=1$ for every $i$, and is therefore not a relative boundary. Since the quotient in step 4.2 is one-dimensional, every nonzero Z logical class has all $q_i=1$; it must contain at least one horizontal edge in each of the $d$ disjoint strips. Thus its weight is at least $d$, and $z_0$ attains $d$. [F1, F3, step 4.2, algebra]
source_lines.100: 6.1 In the edge subgraph of a relative cycle, every vertex outside $R$ has even degree, so all odd-degree vertices lie in $R$. The handshake identity $\sum_v\deg(v)=2|E|$ shows there are an even number of them. Add one dummy vertex joined to each odd boundary vertex; every degree in the augmented finite graph is now even. Starting with any unused edge, follow unused edges: at a vertex other than the start, the number of used incident edges is odd, so its even total degree leaves an unused edge. Finiteness therefore closes the trail at its start. Removing this closed trail preserves even degrees; repeating decomposes all edges into closed trails. Deleting dummy edges leaves cycles and paths with endpoints in $R$. Across any vertical cut, a cycle crosses evenly and a path crosses oddly exactly when its endpoints lie on opposite sides. Since $q_i=1$, at least one path joins the left and right rough sides. Removing repeated-vertex loops leaves a self-avoiding such path contained in the support. It crosses each of the $d$ disjoint vertical cuts, so its length is at least $d$. [step 5.1, construct, algebra]
source_lines.102: 6.2 For X-type supports, use the dual graph with one vertex per face and top and bottom exterior vertices, and one dual edge crossing each physical primal edge. The normalizer condition makes each face vertex even-degree, and X checks are the dual boundaries around vertices outside $R$. Their quotient has dimension $\dim(C_1/C_2)=1$ by step 4.1. A straight dual path from top to bottom is in the normalizer because it enters and leaves each face, and it crosses the straight Z logical row once. Since that Z cycle commutes with every X check, this odd intersection shows the dual path is not an X check; it represents the nonzero class. [F1, F2, F3, F6, step 4.1, step 4.2, step 5.1, algebra]
source_lines.104: 7.1 For an X support $x$, let $q'_j(x)$ be the parity of selected horizontal primal edges in row $j$, for $j=0,\ldots,d$. Each X stabilizer has either zero or two such edges in each row, so every $q'_j$ vanishes on the X stabilizer space. The straight dual path from step 6.2 has $q'_j=1$ for all $j$. Since the X logical quotient is one-dimensional, every nontrivial class has $q'_j=1$ in each of the $d+1$ disjoint rows. Its weight is therefore at least $d+1$. In the dual support graph every face vertex has even degree, so the finite even-degree decomposition from the path argument in step 6.1, now with top and bottom exterior vertices as boundary vertices, splits it into cycles and paths ending at those exterior vertices. A cycle and a path with both endpoints at the same exterior vertex cross each horizontal cut evenly; since every $q'_j=1$, at least one path joins top to bottom. Every such path has length at least $d+1$, and the straight dual path attains this bound. [F1, F3, step 6.1, step 6.2, algebra]

source_lines.36: (A) For $\mathfrak g=\mathfrak{sl}_2$, let $B(1)=\{v_0\xrightarrow{1}v_1\}$ with $wt(v_0)=\lambda_1,\ wt(v_1)=-\lambda_1$ and $\varepsilon_1(v_0)=0,\varphi_1(v_0)=1,\varepsilon_1(v_1)=1,\varphi_1(v_1)=0$ (as in [[ex-tensor-crystal-b-one-tensor-b-one-for-sl-two]]). Then $B(1)^\vee=\{v_0^\vee,v_1^\vee\}$ has the single arrow $v_1^\vee\xrightarrow{1}v_0^\vee$, weights $wt(v_0^\vee)=-\lambda_1,\ wt(v_1^\vee)=\lambda_1$, and $(\varepsilon_1,\varphi_1)$ equal to $(1,0)$ at $v_0^\vee$ and $(0,1)$ at $v_1^\vee$. Hence $B(1)^\vee\cong B(1)$ as crystals, realized with the highest vertex $v_1^\vee$.
source_lines.38: (B) For $\mathfrak g=\mathfrak{sl}_3$, let $B(\lambda_1)=\{u_1\xrightarrow{1}u_2\xrightarrow{2}u_3\}$ be the standard crystal of [[ex-highest-components-in-a-small-type-a-two-tensor-crystal]]. Then $B(\lambda_1)^\vee=\{u_1^\vee,u_2^\vee,u_3^\vee\}$ has the arrows $u_2^\vee\xrightarrow{1}u_1^\vee$ and $u_3^\vee\xrightarrow{2}u_2^\vee$, weights $-\lambda_1,\ -\lambda_2+\lambda_1,\ \lambda_2$ at $u_1^\vee,u_2^\vee,u_3^\vee$, and $\varepsilon/\varphi$ exchanged; this is the crystal $B(\lambda_2)$ of the dual three-dimensional module, so $B(\lambda_1)^\vee\cong B(\lambda_2)$.
source_lines.40: (C) On the tensor square of (A), $(B(1)\otimes B(1))^\vee\cong B(1)^\vee\otimes B(1)^\vee$ under $(b_1\otimes b_2)^\vee\mapsto b_2^\vee\otimes b_1^\vee$; both sides split as $B(2)\sqcup B(0)$ because each of $B(2),B(0)$ is self-dual along the chain reversal (weights $2\lambda_1,0,-2\lambda_1$ are symmetric).

source_lines.66: 1.1 (A) Apply $\tilde f_1(b^\vee)=(\tilde e_1b)^\vee$ and $\tilde e_1(b^\vee)=(\tilde f_1b)^\vee$ of [F1] to $b=v_0,v_1$: $\tilde e_1v_0=0$ gives $\tilde f_1(v_0^\vee)=0$; $\tilde e_1v_1=v_0$ gives $\tilde f_1(v_1^\vee)=v_0^\vee$; $\tilde f_1v_0=v_1$ gives $\tilde e_1(v_0^\vee)=v_1^\vee$; $\tilde f_1v_1=0$ gives $\tilde e_1(v_1^\vee)=0$. So the only arrow is $v_1^\vee\xrightarrow{1}v_0^\vee$ and the values $(\varepsilon_1,\varphi_1)=(\varphi_1,\varepsilon_1)$ are $(1,0)$ at $v_0^\vee$ and $(0,1)$ at $v_1^\vee$; weights are negated by [F1]. Comparing with [F2], the map $v_1^\vee\mapsto v_0$, $v_0^\vee\mapsto v_1$ preserves arrows, weights and $\varepsilon/\varphi$, so $B(1)^\vee\cong B(1)$ with highest vertex $v_1^\vee$. [given, F1, F2]
source_lines.68: 1.2 (B) By [F1] the arrows become $u_3^\vee\xrightarrow{2}u_2^\vee\xrightarrow{1}u_1^\vee$, with weights $\lambda_2,\lambda_1-\lambda_2,-\lambda_1$ along that chain. The pairs $(\varepsilon_1,\varphi_1)$ at $(u_1^\vee,u_2^\vee,u_3^\vee)$ are $(1,0),(0,1),(0,0)$, and the color-two pairs are $(0,0),(1,0),(0,1)$. Construct a module on $w_1,w_2,w_3$ with these successive weights: set $F_2w_1=w_2$, $F_1w_2=w_3$, $E_2w_2=w_1$, $E_1w_3=w_2$, all other $E_i,F_i$ images zero, and $K_hw_j=q^{\langle wt(w_j),h\rangle}w_j$. These maps satisfy [F6]: the weight shifts give the toral relations, the same-color commutators have diagonal entries $(0,1,-1)$ and $(1,-1,0)$, matching $(K_i-K_i^{-1})/(q_i-q_i^{-1})$, and the cross-color commutators vanish. Each $E_i^2,F_i^2$ and each alternating triple $E_iE_jE_i,F_iF_jF_i$ with $i\ne j$ vanishes, proving both $A_2$ Serre relations. The module is nonzero, integrable and generated by its highest vector $w_1$ of dominant weight $\lambda_2$, so [F6](ii) identifies it with $V(\lambda_2)$. Each color has one length-one string and one trivial string; [F7] therefore makes the canonical lattice $\bigoplus_jA_0w_j$ with residue crystal $B(\lambda_2)$. The map $u_3^\vee\mapsto w_1$, $u_2^\vee\mapsto w_2$, $u_1^\vee\mapsto w_3$ preserves all crystal data. To check the module-dual description as well, realize the standard module by $F_1u_1=u_2$, $F_2u_2=u_3$, $E_1u_2=u_1$, $E_2u_3=u_2$, the given weights and zero remaining images. The same relation check with colors exchanged identifies this cyclic integrable module with $V(\lambda_1)$ by [F6]. For its linear dual basis $u_j^*$, [F8] gives the displayed $w$-actions on $w_1=u_3^*$, $w_2=-q_1u_2^*$, $w_3=q_1^2u_1^*$ (here $q_1=q_2$). Thus $V(\lambda_2)$ is the dual three-dimensional module, without a crystal-component uniqueness or AC premise. [F1, F3, F6, F7, F8, algebra]
source_lines.70: 2.1 (C) The swap sends $(v_j\otimes v_k)^\vee$ to $v_k^\vee\otimes v_j^\vee$. On the right the three-element lowering chain is $(v_1^\vee\otimes v_1^\vee)\to(v_0^\vee\otimes v_1^\vee)\to(v_0^\vee\otimes v_0^\vee)$, with weights $2\lambda_1,0,-2\lambda_1$; each next raising reverses the preceding arrow by [F4]. The remaining vertex $v_1^\vee\otimes v_0^\vee$ has weight zero and both operators vanish there: the tie $\varphi_1(v_1^\vee)=\varepsilon_1(v_0^\vee)=1$ selects the bottom second factor for lowering and the top first factor for raising. This is the image of the isolated dual vertex $(v_0\otimes v_1)^\vee$. The reversed three-element chain is $B(2)$ and the isolated vertex is $B(0)$ by [F5], so both sides have the claimed decomposition. [step 1.1, F1, F2, F4, F5]

source_lines.36: Compute the tensor crystal $B(1)\otimes B(1)$ of [[def-tensor-product-of-crystals]] with the two-case rule of [[thm-crystal-basis-tensor-product-rule]]. Writing the four vertices as $v_j\otimes v_k$ with $j,k\in\{0,1\}$, the rule gives
source_lines.38: $$\tilde f_1(v_j\otimes v_k)=\begin{cases}v_{j+1}\otimes v_k,&1-j>k,\\ v_j\otimes v_{k+1},&1-j\le k,\end{cases}\qquad \tilde e_1(v_j\otimes v_k)=\begin{cases}v_{j-1}\otimes v_k,&1-j\ge k,\\ v_j\otimes v_{k-1},&1-j<k.\end{cases}$$
source_lines.40: Consequently: $v_0\otimes v_0$ is the unique highest vertex of weight $2\lambda_1$ and generates the chain $v_0\otimes v_0\to v_1\otimes v_0\to v_1\otimes v_1$; the remaining vertex $v_0\otimes v_1$ has weight $0$, is killed by $\tilde e_1$ and by $\tilde f_1$, and forms a one-element component; and $\varepsilon_1,\varphi_1$ of the four vertices are $(0,2),(1,1),(2,0),(0,0)$ at $(0,0),(1,0),(1,1),(0,1)$ respectively. Hence $B(1)\otimes B(1)=B(2)\sqcup B(0)$, matching the classical decomposition $V(1)\otimes V(1)=V(2)\oplus V(0)$ of dimensions $4=3+1$; here $B(2)$ is the three-element $1$-chain of weights $2\lambda_1,0,-2\lambda_1$ and $B(0)$ the one-element crystal of weight $0$.

source_lines.34: **Assume the axiom of choice** ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $M$ be a chosen $P$-graded type-one quantum weight module that is integrable, has finite-dimensional label-weight spaces and weight set contained in a finite union of cones $\lambda-Q_+$ ([[def-quantum-weight-module-and-integrability]]), and let $(L,B)$ be a crystal basis of $M$ ([[def-crystal-lattice-and-crystal-basis]]).
source_lines.36: (i) **Splitting along the top isotypic part.** Let $\lambda$ be a maximal weight of $M$, put $N_0:=U_q(\mathfrak g)M_\lambda$ and let $N_1$ be the sum of the remaining simple constituents, so that $M=N_0\oplus N_1$ and $N_0\cong V(\lambda)^{\oplus m}$ with $m=\dim M_\lambda$. Then $L=(L\cap N_0)\oplus(L\cap N_1)$, $B=\bigl(B\cap(L\cap N_0)/q(L\cap N_0)\bigr)\sqcup\bigl(B\cap(L\cap N_1)/q(L\cap N_1)\bigr)$, and both pairs are crystal bases of $N_0$ and $N_1$.
source_lines.38: (ii) **Uniqueness.** There is a locally weight-finite indexed family $(\lambda_j)_{j\in J}$ in $P^+$ and an isomorphism of $U_q(\mathfrak g)$-modules $\Phi:M\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }\bigoplus_{j\in J}V(\lambda_j)$ with $\Phi(L)=\bigoplus_j\mathcal L(\lambda_j)$ and $\Phi$ inducing a bijection $B\to\bigsqcup_j\mathcal B(\lambda_j)$ of crystals. The multiset $\{\lambda_j:j\in J\}$ is the multiset of highest weights of the simple integrable constituents of $M$: the number of $j$ with $\lambda_j=\lambda$ equals the multiplicity $[M:V(\lambda)]$.
source_lines.40: (iii) **Components.** Through $\Phi$ the connected components of the crystal $B$ are exactly the canonical highest weight crystals $\mathcal B(\lambda_j)$; each component has a unique highest weight element $b$, of dominant weight $\lambda$, and equals the lowering-generated subcrystal $F(b)$ of [[def-highest-weight-element-and-connected-highest-weight-crystal]]. In particular the crystal graph of any crystal basis of $M$ is determined up to isomorphism by $M$, and no other highest weight elements occur.

source_lines.28: Let $P$ have counterclockwise vertices $(0,0),(4,0),(5,2),(2,4),(0,3)$. It is a convex simple pentagon with Jordan content $15$.
source_lines.42: 1.1 Write the vertices as $v_0,\ldots,v_4$ in the displayed order. The five supporting-line calculations $$\det(v_{i+1}-v_i,v_j-v_i)>0\qquad(j\notin\{i,i+1\})$$ give respectively the positive lists $(8,16,12)$, $(8,8,11)$, $(16,8,7)$, $(6,10,7)$, and $(12,15,6)$, with indices modulo five. Thus every other vertex lies strictly to the left of every directed boundary edge. The intersection of these five closed left half-planes is convex, has exactly the displayed boundary chain, and contains both diagonals from $v_0$; hence the chain is simple and counterclockwise and those diagonals triangulate it. The three triangle determinants are $8$, $16$, and $6$, so [L1] gives content $(8+16+6)/2=15$. [L1, algebra]
source_lines.44: 1.2 The cyclic shoelace sum is $(0+8+20+6+0)-(0+0+4+0+0)=30$, so [L2] gives content $30/2=15$. [L2, algebra]

source_lines.36: **Given:** A cylinder of radius $r>0$ and height $H>0$; integers $n\ge2$ and $m\ge1$; and the Schwarz lantern with $m$ horizontal bands, $n$ vertices per ring, and successive rings staggered by angle $\pi/n$.
source_lines.48: 1.1 Every vertex lies on the cylinder. Parametrize each triangular face affinely over the standard parameter triangle. Its constant parameter tangents are two edge vectors, so [L1] makes its area one half of their cross-product norm. Each of the $m$ bands contains $2n$ congruent triangles; expanding those edge-vector cross products gives total area $$A_{m,n}=2rn\sin(\pi/n)\sqrt{H^2+m^2r^2(1-\cos(\pi/n))^2}.$$ [given, L1, algebra]
source_lines.50: 1.2 Take $m=n^3$. The maximum edge length is bounded by the sum of the vertical step $H/n^3$ and a circular chord of angle at most $2\pi/n$, so the mesh tends to zero by [L2]. [given, L2, algebra]
source_lines.52: 2.1 By [L1], $n^2(1-\cos(\pi/n))=2(n\sin(\pi/(2n)))^2\to\pi^2/2$ using [L2]. Hence $n^3(1-\cos(\pi/n))$ grows like $(\pi^2/2)n$ and diverges by [L3]. [step 1.2, L1, L2, L3, algebra]
source_lines.54: 3.1 Also $n\sin(\pi/n)\to\pi$ by [L2]. Substitution in step 1.1 and step 2.1 shows $A_{n^3,n}\to+\infty$. [step 1.1, step 2.1, L2, L3, algebra]

source_lines.96: 2.1 Fix the trisection rule. Let $(u,v) \in I$ and $y \in \mathbb{R}$. Put $d = v - u > 0$, $s = u + d/3$ and $t = s + d/3$; then $u < s < t < v$ by step 1.2 and [L4], since $s - u = t - s = v - t = d/3 > 0$. The three pairs $(u,s)$, $(s,t)$, $(t,v)$ all lie in $I$ and their intervals are contained in $[u,v]$. Moreover $[u,s]$ and $[t,v]$ are disjoint, because $x \le s < t \le x$ is impossible; so $y$ fails to lie in at least one of the three. Define $T(u,v,y)$ to be the **first** of $(u,s)$, $(s,t)$, $(t,v)$, in that fixed order, whose interval does not contain $y$. This is a definition by cases on the three conditions $y \in [u,s]$, $y \in [s,t]$, $y \in [t,v]$, so $T : I \times \mathbb{R} \to I$ is a function and no choice is made. [step 1.2, L4, construct]
source_lines.102: 5.1 Apply [L5] with $X = \mathbb{N} \times I$, $x_0 = (0, (p,q))$, which lies in $X$ because $p < q$ by step 3.1, and $F(n, (u,v)) = (\sigma(n), T(u, v, f(n)))$: this yields $h : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N} \times I$ with $h(0) = x_0$ and $h(\sigma(n)) = F(h(n))$. An induction using [L6] shows the first coordinate of $h(n)$ is $n$, so we may write $h(n) = (n, (a_n, b_n))$ with $a_n < b_n$, $a_0 = p$, $b_0 = q$ and $(a_{\sigma(n)}, b_{\sigma(n)}) = T(a_n, b_n, f(n))$ for every $n$. By step 2.1 this gives $a_n \le a_{\sigma(n)}$, $b_{\sigma(n)} \le b_n$ and $f(n) \notin [a_{\sigma(n)}, b_{\sigma(n)}]$. [step 2.1, step 3.1, step 4.1, L4, L5, L6, construct]
source_lines.104: 6.1 For $m \le n$ one has $a_m \le a_n$ and $b_n \le b_m$, by induction on $n$ using step 5.1 and transitivity; consequently $a_m \le b_n$ for all $m, n$: if $m \le n$ then $a_m \le a_n < b_n$, and if $n \le m$ then $a_m < b_m \le b_n$, and any two naturals are comparable by [L6]. source_lines.106: 7.1 The set $S = \{\, a_n : n \in \mathbb{N} \,\}$ is nonempty and bounded above by $b_0$ by step 6.1, so [L1] gives its least upper bound $x = \sup S$, unique by [L2]. [step 5.1, step 6.1, L1, L2]

Hence $x \in [a_n, b_n]$ for every $n$. [step 6.1, step 7.1, L1, L3, L4]
source_lines.110: 9.1 Taking $n = 0$ in step 8.1 gives $x \in [a_0, b_0] = [p, q]$, and $[p,q] \subseteq (a,b)$ by step 3.1, so $x \in (a,b)$. Fix $n \in \mathbb{N}$: by step 8.1 applied to $\sigma(n)$, $x \in [a_{\sigma(n)}, b_{\sigma(n)}]$, whereas $f(n) \notin [a_{\sigma(n)}, b_{\sigma(n)}]$ by step 5.1, so $x \ne f(n) = g(n)$. As $n$ was arbitrary, the element $x$ of $(a,b)$ is not a value of $g$, contradicting the surjectivity of $g$ obtained in step 4.1. So no such pair $a < b$ exists: for every $a < b$ both $[a,b]$ and $(a,b)$ fail to be at most countable, that is, both are uncountable by [L7]. source_lines.33: An **elementary solid region** is a compact set $E\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ supplied with a simple description in each of the three coordinate directions ([[def-simple-solid-region-in-a-coordinate-direction]]) together with one compatible finite patch presentation of $\partial E$ that is adapted to a simple description of $E$ in each of the three coordinate directions ([[def-adapted-outward-boundary-presentation-of-a-simple-solid-region]], [[def-finitely-patched-regular-surface-and-integrals]]).
source_lines.35: Explicitly, the data are: three simple descriptions $(x,D_x,\gamma^x_1,\gamma^x_2)$, $(y,D_y,\gamma^y_1,\gamma^y_2)$ and $(z,D_z,\gamma^z_1,\gamma^z_2)$, each describing the same set $E$; one compatible finite patch presentation $\Sigma=\bigl((D_1,\varphi_1),\ldots,(D_P,\varphi_P)\bigr)$ whose patch images cover $\partial E$ and are contained in $\partial E$; and, for each of the three directions $k$, a partition of $\{1,\ldots,P\}$ into sublists $\Sigma^{+}_k,\Sigma^{-}_k,\Sigma^{0}_k$ making $\Sigma$ adapted to the $k$th description. The boundary is that of [[def-metric-interior-closure-boundary]].
source_lines.37: **One presentation, three partitions.** The patch list is the same in all three directions; only the sorting of its indices into upper, lower and lateral changes with $k$. That is what makes the three single-direction flux identities statements about one and the same boundary integral, and it is the whole content of the word "elementary" here.
source_lines.43: - **A patch may be lateral in one direction and a face in another.** The six faces of a box illustrate both: the top and bottom faces are the upper and lower sublists for $k=z$ and lateral for $k=x$ and $k=y$. What cannot happen is a patch lateral in all three directions, and that is [[cor-every-face-of-an-elementary-solid-region-is-outward-oriented]].

source_lines.80: 3.1 Parametrize $\partial B$ by $\psi(\phi,\theta)=(\sin\phi\cos\theta,\sin\phi\sin\theta,2+\cos\phi)$ on $D=[0,\pi]\times[0,2\pi]$. Direct differentiation and the cross-product formula give $\psi_\phi\times\psi_\theta=\sin\phi(\sin\phi\cos\theta,\sin\phi\sin\theta,\cos\phi)$. On $D^\circ$ this is nonzero and points outward. Strict monotonicity of cosine on $[0,\pi]$ and [L11] make the parametrization injective on its interior; its only repeated boundary images lie at the seam or poles. source_lines.40: Let $S$ be the Smith-Volterra-Cantor set ([[def-fat-cantor-set]]). Then:
source_lines.62: **Given:** The lengths $(\lambda_n)$, the gaps $g_n = \lambda_n - \lambda_{n+1}$, the finite lists $(N_n, \ell^{(n)})$ with entries $e^{(n)}_j$, and the sets $S_n$, $S$ of [[def-fat-cantor-set]]. For $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and $j < N_n$ write $M^{(n)}_j := \big(e^{(n)}_j + \lambda_{n+1},\ e^{(n)}_j + g_n\big)$ for the open interval removed from the $j$-th piece at stage $n$.
source_lines.66: [L1] The construction: $N_0 = 1$, $e^{(0)}_0 = 0$, $\lambda_0 = 1$, $N_{n+1} = N_n + N_n$, $e^{(n+1)}_j = e^{(n)}_j$ for $j < N_n$ and $e^{(n+1)}_{N_n + j} = e^{(n)}_j + g_n$ for $j < N_n$; $S_n = \bigcup_{j<N_n}[e^{(n)}_j, e^{(n)}_j + \lambda_n]$; $S = \bigcap_n S_n \subseteq S_m \subseteq [0,1]$; $0 < \lambda_{n+1} < g_n < \lambda_n \le 2^{-n}$; $g_n + \lambda_{n+1} = \lambda_n$; $\lambda_n - 2\lambda_{n+1} = 4^{-n-1}$; and $\sum_{j<N_n} c = 2^{n}c$ for every real $c$ ([[def-fat-cantor-set]], [[def-interval]], [[def-integer-power]], [[lem-power-laws]]).
source_lines.100: 2.1 **The removed pieces.** Fix $n$ and $j < N_n$. By [L1] the pieces $[e^{(n)}_j, e^{(n)}_j + \lambda_{n+1}]$ and $[e^{(n)}_j + g_n,\ e^{(n)}_j + \lambda_n]$ both occur among the pieces of $S_{n+1}$, so a point $x$ of $[e^{(n)}_j, e^{(n)}_j + \lambda_n]$ outside $S_{n+1}$ satisfies $\lambda_{n+1} < x - e^{(n)}_j < g_n$, that is $x \in M^{(n)}_j$; hence $S_n \setminus S_{n+1} \subseteq \bigcup_{j<N_n} M^{(n)}_j$. Conversely $M^{(n)}_j \cap S_{n+1} = \varnothing$: a piece of $S_{n+1}$ coming from $i \ne j$ lies in $[e^{(n)}_i, e^{(n)}_i + \lambda_n]$, which is disjoint from $[e^{(n)}_j, e^{(n)}_j + \lambda_n] \supseteq M^{(n)}_j$ by step 1.3, while the two pieces coming from $j$ itself are disjoint from the open interval $M^{(n)}_j$ by [L10]. Finally each $M^{(n)}_j$ has length $g_n - \lambda_{n+1} = \lambda_n - 2\lambda_{n+1} = 4^{-n-1}$, so $\sum_{j<N_n} 4^{-n-1} = 2^{n} \cdot 4^{-n-1} = 4^{-1} \cdot 2^{-n}$ by [L1]. [step 1.3, L1, L10]
source_lines.114: - **Where the construction differs from the Cantor set, and where it does not.** Steps 1.2, 1.3, 1.4, 2.2 and 3.1 use only that the pieces shrink to $0$ in length, double in number and stay separated, which the middle-thirds construction also satisfies; so $S$ and $C$ are indistinguishable at that level. The difference is entirely in step 2.1: the removed length at stage $n$ is $4^{-1}2^{-n}$ here and $2^{n}3^{-n-1}$ there, and only the first is summable to less than $1$. The removed lengths are added up in [[ex-fat-cantor-measure-computed]], where they total exactly $2^{-1}$.

source_lines.43: 1.1 Choose a direction $e$ such that the scalar projections $\langle v_i,e\rangle$ of the finitely many boundary vertices are pairwise distinct. Such a direction exists because only finitely many directions perpendicular to a difference $v_i-v_j$ are forbidden. Use the projection onto $e$ as the horizontal coordinate and the perpendicular coordinate as the vertical one. No boundary edge is vertical in these coordinates. [given, choose, construct]
source_lines.45: 2.1 Between two consecutive vertex projections, every boundary edge that crosses the open vertical slab is the graph of an affine function, and disjoint boundary edges have a fixed vertical order throughout the slab. On a vertical line in the slab, the compact set $P$ can change between membership and nonmembership only at one of these boundary crossings. Near such a crossing the boundary is a single straight segment and, because the crossing point is not an interior point of $P$, the two local sides cannot both lie in $P$; since $P=\overline{\operatorname{int}P}$, exactly the side belonging to $P$ is filled. Starting below the bounded set and moving upward therefore expresses the part of $P$ in the slab as a finite union of closed bands between consecutive affine boundary graphs. [step 1.1, given]
source_lines.47: 3.1 Take the closures of all those bands in the finitely many closed slabs. Insert every boundary--wall intersection as a subdivision vertex and use their common finite refinement on each vertical wall. Before this common refinement, the closure of a nonempty band is a convex triangle or quadrilateral: it is bounded by two vertical segments and two affine graphs that retain their vertical order. The common refinement may add collinear vertices to a vertical side, so each resulting two-dimensional cell is a convex polygon whose boundary carries all wall-subdivision vertices. These cells cover $P$, and two distinct cells meet only in a union of full consecutive wall segments, a common vertex, or not at all. [step 2.1, construct]
source_lines.49: 4.1 Choose one interior point in each two-dimensional cell. Join it to every boundary vertex of that cell in cyclic order. Convexity keeps every joining segment in the cell, and each consecutive boundary pair with the interior point forms a nondegenerate triangle. These triangles cover the cell. On a shared vertical wall, both adjacent cells use the same refined boundary segments, so triangles from opposite sides meet in a full common refined segment, a common endpoint, or not at all; within one cell the fan triangles meet in a full radial edge, the chosen interior point, or not at all. The resulting finite family is therefore face-to-face, covers $P$, and is a triangulation by [L1]. [step 3.1, L1, discharge-construct: finite face-to-face triangulation] ∎

source_lines.52: 1.1 Since $\alpha_1=0$, [F1] gives $Z_1=(m,m)$ with probability one, independent of $X$. By [F2], conditioning on this state and reversing to $s=0$ returns $X$ exactly. source_lines.39: Fix integers $M,q\ge1$, set $[M]=\{1,\ldots,M\}$, and write the image space on a fixed patch grid as $\mathcal X=(\mathbb R^q)^M$. A measurable space is a set with a specified sigma-algebra; equip $\mathcal X$ and a finite-dimensional latent space $\mathcal Z$ with such structures. An image is $x=(x_1,\ldots,x_M)\in\mathcal X$, with $q$ real pixel values in each of its $M$ patches. Let $S=(x^{(1)},\ldots,x^{(n)})$ be a finite training set with $n\ge1$. For $u\in\mathbb R^q$, set $\|u\|_2^2=\sum_{r=1}^q u_r^2$. For $V\subseteq[M]$ let $\mathcal Z^V=\{(z_j)_{j\in V}:z_j\in\mathcal Z\}$. For unmasked reconstruction, the encoder and decoder are deterministic measurable maps $E_\phi:\mathcal X\to\mathcal Z$ and $D_\psi:\mathcal Z\to\mathcal X$. For masked reconstruction, the encoder is a measurable deterministic map $(V,(x_j)_{j\in V})\mapsto(z_j)_{j\in V}\in\mathcal Z^V$, and the decoder maps the ordered length-$M$ sequence of encoded visible tokens and mask tokens to an element of $\mathcal X$. Each mask token is one learned vector $m\in\mathcal Z$ reused at every masked position. All maps take finite real values; when implemented by feedforward neural networks, each is a finite computation graph evaluated in the layered order of its vertices.
source_lines.53: For masked autoencoding, fix an integer $k$ with $1\le k<M$ and let $\mathcal V_k=\{V\subseteq[M]:|V|=k\}$, a set with cardinality $\binom{M}{k}$. A mask $V$ is sampled uniformly from $\mathcal V_k$; the patches in $V$ are visible and the patches in $[M]\setminus V$ are masked. The encoder receives only the visible patches, with their positions, and no mask tokens. The decoder receives the encoded visible patches and a shared learned mask token at each missing position, with position information for all $M$ slots, and outputs predictions $\hat x_j(\phi,\psi;x,V)\in\mathbb R^q$ for every patch position.

source_lines.29: **Given:** ZFC. We construct a tree with nonempty countable levels $T_\alpha$ for $\alpha<\omega_1$ and a strictly increasing rational labeling $\ell$.
source_lines.55: 2.1 Start with the singleton root $T_0=\{(0,0)\}$ with label zero and its constant enumeration. At a successor stage, for each $x\in T_\alpha$ create a distinct immediate successor $(x,q)$ for every rational $q>\ell(x)$, with label $q$, then rename these pairs by level-tagged least indices as in step 1.1. Its predecessors are $x$ and all predecessors of $x$. The level is nonempty and countable, since it is an enumerated subset of $T_\alpha\times\mathbb Q$. Strict labeling persists. There are infinitely many successors below any $r>\ell(x)$: the distinct rationals $\ell(x)+(r-\ell(x))/(m+2)$ for $m<\omega$ lie strictly between the two bounds. In particular every old last-level node splits. [F5, F6, F9, step 1.1]
source_lines.57: 3.1 At every partial stage the small-successor condition is required only for nodes whose successor level has already been constructed. Maintain also the invariant that for $\operatorname{ht}(x)<\beta$ and rational $r>\ell(x)$ an extension at level $\beta$ has label less than $r$. It is vacuous at the root stage. At the successor level $\alpha+1$, if $x\in T_\alpha$, its successor of label $(\ell(x)+r)/2$ works. If $x$ lies below $\alpha$, use the earlier invariant with bound $s=(\ell(x)+r)/2$ to obtain $y\in T_\alpha$ above $x$ with $\ell(y)<s$, and extend $y$ by the successor of label $(\ell(y)+r)/2<r$. This verifies every request at the new level; all earlier requests persist. [F5, step 2.1]
source_lines.59: 4.1 At a nonzero limit $\delta<\omega_1$, the union of earlier levels is countable: enumerate its nodes by pairing $d_\delta(n)$ with the stored enumeration of that level. Its height is $\delta$, and its order and labeling satisfy all previous invariants, since every pair of old nodes and every request involving a level below $\delta$ occurs in an earlier stage. Every old node has infinitely many small successors, supplied at its successor stage, which is below $\delta$. The old union is normal: roots agree, extensions persist, and predecessor sets at each old limit level were fixed when that level was added. F1 gives at least one nonempty countable new level preserving strict labeling, bounded extensions and normality, and retaining the small-successor condition at old nodes. New tops have no successor requirement until the next stage. Injectively rename its nodes by tags $(\delta,n)$ and store a surjection from $\omega$ onto the renamed level. Let $E\subseteq C$ be the set of eligible codes for this history and take the new level record to be $c(E)$. Eligibility requires the old order and labels to be unchanged, the new nodes to have level tag $\delta$, and exactly the properties just obtained from F1. The set $E$ is nonempty by F1 and countability, so this selection is defined uniquely from the earlier history and the fixed $c$. All invariants, with the stage-relative successor requirement of step 3.1, and normality persist. [F1, F9, A1, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1]
source_lines.61: 5.1 Steps 2.1–4.1 prescribe the next level and its enumeration from the earlier history and the fixed parameters. Extend the rule arbitrarily, say by the empty record, on histories not satisfying the invariants. F2 then defines all levels for $\alpha<\omega_1$. Their union is a set by Replacement and Union, with height $\omega_1$ and nonempty countable levels. Normality and splitting follow from their stagewise verification: any requested extension, limit-level comparison, or immediate successor appears at some stage. The labeling is strictly increasing because every comparison already appears at one stage. [F2, F9, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 4.1]
source_lines.63: 6.1 On any chain the labeling is injective into $\mathbb Q$, because distinct comparable nodes have strictly different labels. F4 makes the chain countable. Its height image is countable and hence not cofinal in $\omega_1$ by F7, whose choice hypothesis follows from A1. No branch is cofinal. Thus the constructed $\omega_1$-tree is Aronszajn, and the increasing rational labeling makes it special by F8. [F4, F7, F8, A1, step 5.1]
source_lines.65: 7.1 The tree is uncountable: its height map is onto $\omega_1$ since every level is nonempty, whereas the image of a countable set is countable. For each rational $q$, the fiber $\ell^{-1}(\{q\})$ is an antichain by strict increase. If all these fibers were countable, F4 would index them countably and F3, using the countable choice supplied by A1, would make their union $T$ countable, a contradiction. At least one fiber is an uncountable antichain; by F8 the tree is not Suslin. [F3, F4, F8, A1, step 5.1, step 6.1] ∎

source_lines.29: In a finite DAG, a **route** is a finite sequence of vertices with consecutive vertices adjacent by an arrow in either direction; repeated vertices are allowed. Collider and noncollider status is assigned to each internal occurrence using its two incident route arrows. A route is **active given $C$** if each noncollider occurrence is outside $C$ and each collider occurrence is an ancestor of $C$, including membership in $C$. If an active route joins vertices $x,y\notin C$ with $x\ne y$, then an active distinct-vertex path joins $x$ and $y$ given $C$.
source_lines.41: 1.1 Among active routes with these endpoints choose one of minimum length. If a repeated vertex occurs at an endpoint, discard the initial segment through the later occurrence of $x$, or the terminal segment from the earlier occurrence of $y$. Endpoints are outside $C$, and all retained internal occurrences have their old incidences, so the shortened route is active. Consequently any repetition in a minimum route consists of two internal occurrences of a vertex $v$. Delete the segment between two such occurrences and identify them. Only the two incidences at the joined occurrence of $v$ change. If $v\in C$, its old occurrences were both colliders, so the joined occurrence is still a collider. If $v\notin C$ and the joined occurrence is a noncollider, it is allowed; if it is a collider and $v$ is an ancestor of $C$, it is also allowed. [given, F1, choose, construct]
source_lines.43: 2.1 The sole remaining possibility is that the join makes $v$ a collider although $v$ is not an ancestor of $C$. Both original occurrences were then noncolliders. The retained edge before the first occurrence points into $v$, so its deleted departure edge must point out of $v$; likewise the deleted arrival edge at the second occurrence points out of $v$, since its retained departure edge points into $v$. Traverse the deleted segment starting with its arrow out of $v$. There must be a first place where its arrows cease to point forward: the final arrow points backward, and an entirely forward return to $v$ would also contradict acyclicity. At that first change is a collider $w$, reached from $v$ by a directed segment. A directed segment in a DAG has no repetitions. Activity of the original route makes $w$ an ancestor of $C$, hence $v$ an ancestor of $C$, a contradiction. Thus every loop deletion above is active and strictly shorter, contradicting minimality. The minimum route is therefore a path. [F1, step 1.1, construct] ∎

source_lines.58: 1.1 Suppose an active path joins $X$ to $Y$. From any noncollider follow an outgoing path edge forward until reaching an endpoint or a collider. The reached endpoint is in $X\cup Y$, while a reached collider is an ancestor of $C$ by activity. Thus every path vertex is in $H=\operatorname{An}_G(X\cup Y\cup C)$. Replace each collider segment $u\to w\leftarrow v$ by its moral edge $u-v$; colliders cannot be consecutive along a path. The resulting walk avoids $C$, since all retained internal vertices were noncolliders and the endpoints are outside $C$. Loop deletion in this undirected graph yields a moral path avoiding $C$. [F1, F2, construct]
source_lines.60: 1.2 Conversely suppose a moral path avoiding $C$ joins $X$ to $Y$. Keep its skeleton edges, and expand each remaining moral edge $u-v$ using a common child $w\in H$ as $u\to w\leftarrow v$. This is a finite route; its inserted occurrences are colliders and all its other occurrences are outside $C$. Every collider is in $H$. Call a collider occurrence bad if its vertex is not an ancestor of $C$. Among routes joining $X$ to $Y$ with every vertex in $H$ and every noncollider outside $C$, minimize the number of bad collider occurrences; the expanded route makes the class nonempty. If $w$ is a bad occurrence, it is an ancestor of some $s\in X\cup Y$. A directed path from $w$ to $s$ avoids $C$, since otherwise $w$ would be an ancestor of $C$. If $s\in X$, replace the whole prefix up to this occurrence of $w$ by that directed path traversed backward; if $s\in Y$, replace the suffix by the path traversed forward. If $w=s$, simply terminate at that occurrence. Otherwise the retained incident arrow points into $w$ and the new incident arrow points out of $w$, making it an allowed noncollider. All new internal chain occurrences are noncolliders outside $C$, and other retained occurrences have their original incidences. Intersections of the chain with the retained segment cause repetitions only; no loops are deleted in this step, and activity is defined occurrence by occurrence. At least the selected bad occurrence disappears and no new bad occurrence is introduced, contradicting minimality. Thus the minimum route is active. Its endpoints are distinct because $X,Y$ are disjoint, and [F3] gives an active path with those endpoints. [F1, F2, F3, construct, choose]

source_lines.42: [F1] A **covering map** is a continuous surjection $p:E\to B$ such that every $b\in B$ has an open neighbourhood $U$ for which $p^{-1}(U)$ is a disjoint union of open sets $V_j$, called **sheets**, and each restriction $p|_{V_j}:V_j\to U$ is a homeomorphism (def-continuous-map-top, def-homeomorphism-and-open-maps, def-disjoint-union-topology). Such a $U$ is **evenly covered**, and $p^{-1}(b)$ is the **fibre** over $b$. A covering is **trivial** when it is isomorphic over $B$ to a product projection $B\times F\to B$ with $F$ discrete. ([[def-covering-map-and-evenly-covered-neighbourhoods]]).
source_lines.44: [F2] Let $(X, \mathcal{T})$ be a topological space (def-topological-space). An **open cover** of $(X,\mathcal T)$ is a family $\mathcal U\subseteq\mathcal T$ of open sets with $X=\bigcup\mathcal U$; a **subcover** of $\mathcal U$ is a subfamily that is itself an open cover; and $(X,\mathcal T)$ is **compact** when every open cover of it has a finite subcover. ([[def-compact-space]]).
source_lines.46: [F3] Let $(X, \mathcal{T}_X)$ and $(Y, \mathcal{T}_Y)$ be topological spaces (def-topological-space), and let $\mathbb{R}$ carry its usual topology, the metric topology of $d_{\mathbb{R}}(s,t) = |s-t|$ (lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space, def-metric-topology, def-metrizable-space). Then: 1. **Continuous images.** If $f : X \to Y$ is continuous (def-continuous-map-top) and $(X, \mathcal{T}_X)$ is compact (def-compact-space), then $f[X]$ is a compact subset of $Y$. More generally, if $K \subseteq X$ is a compact subset of $X$ then $f[K]$ is a compact subset of $Y$. 2. **Extreme values.** If $(X, \mathcal{T}_X)$ is compact and nonempty and $g : X \to \mathbb{R}$ is continuous, then $g[X]$ has a maximum and a minimum (def-max-min): there are $x_{\max}, x_{\min} \in X$ with $$g(x_{\min}) \;\le\; g(x) \;\le\; g(x_{\max}) \qquad \text{for every } x \in X .$$ 3. **Compact to Hausdorff.** If $(X, \mathcal{T}_X)$ is compact, $(Y, \mathcal{T}_Y)$ is Hausdorff (def-hausdorff-space) and $f : X \to Y$ is a continuous bijection, then $f$ is a homeomorphism (def-homeomorphism-and-open-maps). Nonemptiness in claim 2 is a hypothesis and not an oversight: for $X = \varnothing$ the image is empty and has neither a maximum nor a minimum. **No choice principle is used**: the one selection made below is over a finite index set, where lem-finite-choice is a theorem of ZF. ([[thm-compactness-under-continuous-maps]]).

source_lines.47: [F2] Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space (def-metric-space). $(X,d)$ is **complete** if every Cauchy sequence in $(X,d)$ converges to a point of $X$; a subset $A\subseteq X$ is called complete when the metric subspace $(A,d_A)$ is complete. ([[def-complete-metric-space]]).
source_lines.49: [F3] Throughout, $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field (def-real-numbers) and a **sequence of reals** is a function $a : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ (def-sequence), written $(a_k)$; recall that $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$. The **sequence of partial sums** of a sequence $(a_k)$ of reals is $s_n:=\sum_{k<n}a_k$, so that $s_0=0$ and $s_{n+1}=s_n+a_n$; the **series** $\sum a_k$ **converges** when $(s_n)$ converges, and its **sum** is then that limit. ([[def-series]]).
source_lines.51: [F4] Let $r \in \mathbb{R}$ and let $r^k$ be the integer power (def-integer-power), so that $r^0 = 1$ for every $r$, including $r = 0$. 1. If $|r| < 1$ then the series $\sum r^k$ converges (def-series) and $$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} r^{k} \;=\; \frac{1}{1-r} .$$ 2. If $|r| \ge 1$ then $\sum r^k$ diverges. The series starts at $k = 0$ and its first term is $r^0 = 1$; in particular $\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} 2^{-k} = 2$, while the series starting at $k = 1$ sums to $1$. Which starting index is meant has to be said, and it is said here. ([[thm-geometric-series]]).

source_lines.96: 2.1 Both equal-exponent pairings preserve boundary direction: their formulas in step 1.1 use matching boundary parameters. Choose collars around paired interior points of the $a$-sides, with $t$ increasing along the boundary and $r\geq0$ pointing inward. These coordinates give the same face orientation on the two collars. A chart across the paired edge uses $(t,r)$ on the first collar and $(t,-r)$ on the second, so its generator has opposite signs relative to the face generators on the two sides. The sign is the local-homology sign of a reflection, which reverses the cyclic orientation of the boundary of a small disk, exactly as in the seam calculation for [L4]. A path through the open face joining the collar interiors, closed by one crossing of the seam, therefore transports its generator to its negative. A continuous orientation is unchanged by loop transport [L5], which is impossible for a generator of an infinite cyclic group. Hence $Y\cong K$ is nonorientable. The two equal-exponent pairs are crosscap blocks, and [L4] identifies the single block with $\mathbb{RP}^2$. [L1, L4, L5, step 1.1, step 1.2]
source_lines.98: 3.1 The cell counts of step 1.1 give $\chi(Y)=V-E+F=1-2+1=0$ by [L6], and this value is that of the Klein bottle by step 1.2. source_lines.98: 1.1 The pairing is the parameter reversal $s_1(t)\sim s_2(1-t)$, so the corner $v_0=s_1(0)$ is paired with $s_2(1)=v_0$ and the corner $v_1=s_1(1)$ with $s_2(0)=v_1$: each corner forms its own vertex class, the two sides form one edge class, and the disk interior is the one face. Hence the realization $Y$ has $V=2$, $E=1$, $F=1$, and these are the cells of its finite CW structure. [L1]
source_lines.100: 1.2 First replace the bigon by a round-disk representative. A disk homeomorphism takes its two corners to two points of the unit circle; a circle homeomorphism carrying these to antipodal points extends radially, $ru\mapsto r\varphi(u)$, with radial inverse. Composing gives a disk homeomorphism taking the two corners to opposite ends of a diameter. Conjugate the side pairing by this homeomorphism; it induces a quotient homeomorphism by [L2], using the inverse to obtain the inverse quotient map. We may now cut the round representative along that diameter $\gamma$, whose interior lies in the disk interior; the pieces are two bigons, $B_1$ with sides $s_1$ and one copy of $\gamma$, and $B_2$ with sides $s_2$ and the other copy $\gamma'$. By the split identity of [L3] the quotient $Y$ is homeomorphic to the quotient of $B_1\sqcup B_2$ by the pair $s_1\sim s_2$ together with the pair $\gamma\sim\gamma'$; since $\partial B_1=s_1\cup\gamma$ and $\partial B_2=s_2\cup\gamma'$ and the two pairings match at the common endpoints $v_0,v_1$, they combine into a single homeomorphism $h:\partial B_1\to\partial B_2$ that identifies the whole boundary circle of $B_1$ with the whole boundary circle of $B_2$. [L1, L3]
source_lines.102: 2.1 Fix homeomorphisms $\alpha_1:B_1\to\overline B_2(0,1)$ and $u_2:B_2\to\overline B_2(0,1)$ onto the closed unit disk, which exist because bigons are closed disks, and let $\varphi=\alpha_1\circ h^{-1}\circ u_2^{-1}$ on the unit circle; extending $\varphi$ radially by $\kappa(tu)=t\,\varphi(u)$ and putting $\alpha_2=\kappa\circ u_2$ gives a homeomorphism $\alpha_2:B_2\to\overline B_2(0,1)$ with $\alpha_2\circ h=\alpha_1$ on $\partial B_1$. Here $\kappa^{-1}(tu)=t\,\varphi^{-1}(u)$ and $\alpha_2^{-1}=u_2^{-1}\circ\kappa^{-1}$. Define $\Phi$ on the class of $x\in B_1$ as $(\alpha_1(x),\sqrt{1-\lVert\alpha_1(x)\rVert_2^2})$ and on the class of $x\in B_2$ as $(\alpha_2(x),-\sqrt{1-\lVert\alpha_2(x)\rVert_2^2})$: the two formulas agree on the glued boundary circle because $\alpha_2\circ h=\alpha_1$ there, so $\Phi$ is a well-defined continuous map out of the quotient by [L2]. It is surjective onto $S^2_+\cup S^2_-=S^2$ and injective because the two formulas are homeomorphisms onto the closed upper and lower hemispheres, which meet exactly in the equator. The quotient is compact as a continuous image of the compact disk $D$ [L2], while $S^2$ is Hausdorff [L4], so $\Phi$ is a homeomorphism by the compact-to-Hausdorff criterion [L4], and $Y\cong S^2$. [L2, L4, step 1.2]
source_lines.104: 3.1 The single pair has opposite exponents, so by [L1] it is orientation compatible; by step 2.1 the realization $Y$ is a boundaryless surface, and the generator carried by the oriented face continues unchanged across the single edge class, its locally constant generator classes over face and vertex charts supplying a continuous generating section as in [L6]. Hence $Y$, and by step 2.1 the sphere $S^2$, is orientable. [L1, L6, step 1.1, step 2.1]

source_lines.88: 1.1 The bottom and top sides of $Q$ form one paired class and the left and right sides form a second; the four corners are all identified, since the horizontal pairing gives $(0,0)\sim(0,1)$ and $(1,0)\sim(1,1)$ while the vertical pairing gives $(0,0)\sim(1,0)$ and $(0,1)\sim(1,1)$, so the four corner sectors join in the single cyclic link $(0,0)$–$(1,0)$–$(1,1)$–$(0,1)$–$(0,0)$. The square schema is therefore a connected surface schema with $V=1$, $E=2$, $F=1$, and its realization $Y$ is a nonempty compact connected boundaryless surface. [L1]
source_lines.90: 1.2 The map $f:Q\to T^2$, $f(s,t)=(p(s),p(t))$, is continuous because its two components $p\circ\mathrm{pr}_1$ and $p\circ\mathrm{pr}_2$ are continuous, and $f(s,t)=f(s',t')$ holds exactly when $s-s'\in\mathbb Z$ and $t-t'\in\mathbb Z$; for $s,s'\in[0,1]$ this means $s=s'$ or $\{s,s'\}=\{0,1\}$, and likewise in the second coordinate, so the fibres of $f$ are precisely the classes of the relation on $Q$ generated by the two side pairings. Since $f$ is constant on those classes, it induces a continuous bijection $\bar f:Y\to T^2$ out of the quotient. [given, L2, L3, L4]
source_lines.92: 2.1 The realization $Y$ is compact by [L1] and $T^2$ is Hausdorff by [L4], so the continuous bijection $\bar f$ is a homeomorphism by [L5]; hence the word $a\,b\,a^{-1}b^{-1}$ realizes the torus $T^2$. [L1, L4, L5, step 1.2]
source_lines.94: 3.1 The cell counts of step 1.1 give $\chi(Y)=V-E+F=1-2+1=0$ by [L6], and this is the Euler characteristic of $T^2$ by step 2.1. [L1, L6, step 1.1, step 2.1]

source_lines.36: For the quotient by integer translation, $q:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ is a covering map, and every deck transformation is a unique translation $x\mapsto x+n$ with $n\in\mathbb Z$.
source_lines.42: [F1] For a covering-space action of $G$ on $E$, the orbit map $E\to E/G$ is a covering. If $E$ is path-connected, the deck group of this covering consists exactly of the transformations supplied by $G$. ([[thm-orbit-map-of-a-covering-space-action-is-a-covering]]).
source_lines.56: 1.1 By [F5] the integers sit inside $\mathbb R$ as a subgroup under the ordered-field operations, so $x\sim y$ iff $x-y\in\mathbb Z$ is an equivalence relation on $\mathbb R$; [F4] supplies only the abstract construction of $\mathbb Z$ and not its copy in $\mathbb R$, so the embedding of [F5] is what makes the relation and the translations below meaningful. Take the quotient topology of [F3] on $\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$. [given, F3, F4, F5]
source_lines.58: 2.1 For an **open** interval $I$ of length below $1$ the translates $I+k$, $k\in\mathbb Z$, are pairwise disjoint, since two points of $I$ differ by less than $1$ while distinct integer translates differ by at least $1$ in the order of [F5]; the preimage $q^{-1}(q[I])=\bigcup_{k\in\mathbb Z}(I+k)$ is then a union of open sets, so $q[I]$ is open and evenly covered. Openness of $I$ is required and not cosmetic: for $I=[0,\tfrac12]$ the preimage $\bigcup_{k\in\mathbb Z}[k,k+\tfrac12]$ is not open, so $q[I]$ is not even a neighbourhood. [step 1.1, F3, F4, F5]
source_lines.60: 3.1 Each integer translation $\tau_n(x)=x+n$ is a homeomorphism satisfying $q\tau_n=q$. The intervals in step 2.1 show that this is a covering-space action of $\mathbb Z$ on $\mathbb R$. Since $\mathbb R$ is path-connected by straight-line paths, [F1] identifies the entire deck group with these translations. More explicitly, a deck transformation $h$ has $h(0)\in q^{-1}(q(0))=\mathbb Z$; the translation $\tau_{h(0)}$ agrees with $h$ at $0$, and the one-point determination used in [F1] makes them equal. Distinct integers give distinct translations. [step 2.1, F1, F2, F3]

source_lines.136: 1.3 **Crosscut claim.** Let $J$ be a Jordan curve with complementary regions $U$ (bounded) and $O$ (unbounded), let $p\ne q$ be points of $J$, and let $P$ be a simple polygonal arc from $p$ to $q$ whose remaining points all lie in one region $V$ of $\mathbb R^2\setminus J$; write $W$ for the region of $\mathbb R^2\setminus J$ different from $V$. Let $J_1,J_2$ be the two closed arcs of $J$ from $p$ to $q$ and put $D_i=J_i\cup P$. First, each $D_i$ is a Jordan curve: pasting parametrizations of $J_i$ and $P$ at their common endpoints gives a continuous bijection from the unit circle onto $D_i$, which is a homeomorphism because the unit circle is compact metric and $D_i$ carries the subspace topology and restricted metric of the plane; hence $D_i$ is compact and closed in the plane. [L7, L8] By [F1] if $J$ is a polygon, and otherwise by [A1, F2], each $D_i$ has exactly two complementary regions, and each of them has frontier $D_i$. Let $Z_i$ be the region of $\mathbb R^2\setminus D_i$ containing $W$, which is well defined because $W$ is connected and disjoint from $D_i$, and let $Y_i$ be the other region. Every point of $J\setminus J_i$ lies in $Z_i$: such a point $x$ has a ball $B$ about it disjoint from $D_i$, and $B$ meets $W$ because $x$ lies in the frontier of $W$, which is $J$; since $B$ is connected and contained in $\mathbb R^2\setminus D_i$, it lies in $Z_i$. Consequently $Y_i$ is disjoint from $J$, as it misses $J_i\subseteq D_i$ and misses $J\setminus J_i\subseteq Z_i$; being connected, $Y_i$ lies in one region of $\mathbb R^2\setminus J$, and since $W\subseteq Z_i$ it is not $W$, so $Y_i\subseteq V$. Next $Y_2\subseteq Z_1$: the set $Y_2$ misses $P\subseteq D_2$ and misses $J$, so it is contained in $\mathbb R^2\setminus D_1$; and $Y_2$ has points arbitrarily close to each point of the open arc $J_2\setminus\{p,q\}$, because the frontier of $Y_2$ is $D_2$; that arc is contained in $J\setminus J_1\subseteq Z_1$, and $Z_1$ is open, so $Y_2$ meets $Z_1$ and therefore lies in $Z_1$. Symmetrically $Y_1\subseteq Z_2$, so $Y_1\cap Y_2=\varnothing$. Now fix $x\in P\setminus\{p,q\}$. Because $P$ is a finite simple polygonal arc, choose a sufficiently small ball $B\subseteq V$ about $x$ that misses every nonlocal segment of $P$; then $B\cap P$ is just the one segment germ through $x$, or the two adjacent germs when $x$ is a polygonal vertex. Since $V$ misses $J$, we have $B\cap D_i=B\cap P$, so $B\setminus D_i=B\setminus P$ has exactly two connected local sides: two half-disks in the straight case and two sectors at a bend. Each local side is connected and contained in $\mathbb R^2\setminus D_i$, so it lies in $Z_i$ or in $Y_i$; as $x$ lies in the frontier of both $Z_i$ and $Y_i$, the ball $B$ meets both, so the two local sides receive opposite labels for each $i$; and no local side lies in both $Y_1$ and $Y_2$, because those sets are disjoint. Hence one local side lies in $Y_1$ and the other in $Y_2$. Finally let $N$ be a component of $V\setminus P$. It is open in the plane and closed in $V\setminus P$. Its closure in $V$ meets $P\setminus\{p,q\}$: otherwise it would be closed in $V$, and it is also open in $V$, so it would equal the connected set $V$, although the nonempty set $P\setminus\{p,q\}$ lies in $V$ and misses $V\setminus P$. So a ball $B\subseteq V$ about a point of that closure meets $N$, and $N$ misses $P$, so $N$ meets $B\setminus P$ and hence meets $Y_1\cup Y_2$. Since each $Y_i$ is open and has frontier $D_i$, which is disjoint from $V\setminus P$, each $Y_i$ is also closed in $V\setminus P$; the connected set $N$, meeting $Y_1\cup Y_2$, therefore lies in $Y_1$ or in $Y_2$. Hence $V\setminus P=Y_1\sqcup Y_2$ is exactly the decomposition into components, while $W$ remains a region of $\mathbb R^2\setminus(J\cup P)$ with frontier $J$. Therefore $\mathbb R^2\setminus(J\cup P)$ has exactly three regions, with frontiers $J,D_1,D_2$. The polygonal case of this claim is choice-free, and the arbitrary-Jordan case uses AC exactly through [F2]. [A1, F1, F2, L6, L7, L8]
source_lines.138: 2.1 **Polygonal face induction.** Let now $G$ be $2$-connected and polygonally drawn. Build it by the ear decomposition of step 1.2 from any cycle, and induct on the number of added ears, with the invariant: every face of the current drawing has a simple cycle as its facial boundary walk, and the drawing satisfies $V-E+F=2$. For the initial cycle $C_0$, which is a polygon, [F1] gives exactly two regions with frontier $C_0$, so each facial boundary walk traverses the cycle once, and $V-E+F=|V|-|V|+2=2$. Assume the invariant for a drawing $H$, and let $Q$ be the next ear, a polygonal arc with distinct endpoints $u\ne v$ on the drawing of $H$ and with relative interior disjoint from that drawing. The relative interior of $Q$ is connected and lies in the complement of the drawing of $H$, so it is contained in a single face $F$; let $J$ be the boundary cycle of $F$ and let $V$ be the region of $\mathbb R^2\setminus J$ containing $F$. By [L4] the frontier of $F$ meets the drawing $X_H$ of $H$ exactly in $J$. Since a face is a component of the open complement of $X_H$, its frontier lies in $X_H$; hence $\operatorname{Fr}(F)=J$. If $F$ were a proper subset of $V$, [L6] would give a polygonal path in $V$ from a point of $F$ to a point of $V\setminus F$. The first point at which that path leaves the open set $F$ would lie in $\operatorname{Fr}(F)\cap V=J\cap V=\varnothing$. Thus $F=V$. Apply step 1.3 to the polygonal Jordan curve $J$, the distinct points $u,v\in J$ and the polygonal arc $Q$, whose relative interior lies in $V$: the two arcs $J_1,J_2$ of $J$ from $u$ to $v$ give graph cycles $D_i=J_i\cup Q$ of the new drawing, and $F\setminus Q=Y_1\sqcup Y_2$, where $Y_i$ is the region of $\mathbb R^2\setminus D_i$ that does not contain the region of $\mathbb R^2\setminus J$ different from $V$, and the frontier of $Y_i$ is $D_i$. Every other face $F'$ of $H$ is disjoint from $Q$, because the relative interior of $Q$ lies in $F$ and the endpoints of $Q$ lie in the drawing of $H$; so $F'$ is a connected subset of the complement of the new drawing, and it is closed there because its frontier lies in the drawing of $H$ and misses the relative interior of $Q$, which lies in the open face $F$. Distinct faces of $H$ remain distinct regions, and every point of the complement of the new drawing belongs either to an old face other than $F$ or to $F\setminus Q=Y_1\cup Y_2$. Hence the regions of the new drawing are exactly the faces of $H$ other than $F$, together with $Y_1$ and $Y_2$; their frontiers are the old boundary cycles together with $D_1$ and $D_2$, so the invariant passes to the new drawing. An ear with $k\ge1$ edges contributes $k-1$ new vertices, $k$ new edges and one new region, so $V-E+F$ is unchanged. Induction over the finitely many ears proves the facial-cycle and Euler claims for $G$. [F1, L4, L6, L7, step 1.2, step 1.3]
source_lines.144: 4.1 **Hybrid induction.** Let now $G$ be $2$-connected, so $|V(G)|\ge3$ by [L2], and drawn as in the hybrid hypothesis: the cycle $C$ is drawn as a Jordan curve, and every other edge arc has its relative interior in the bounded region $U$ of $\mathbb R^2\setminus C$. Build $G$ by the ear decomposition of step 1.2 from the specified cycle $C$, and induct on the number of added ears, with the invariant: the exterior region of $C$ is a face with boundary cycle $C$, and every other face has a Jordan curve as frontier, that frontier being a graph cycle of the current drawing. For the initial drawing $C$, [F2] gives exactly two regions, the bounded $U$ and the exterior, each with frontier $C$, so both facial boundaries are the cycle $C$, and $V-E+F=|V|-|V|+2=2$. Let the next ear $Q$ with $k\ge1$ edges be added, with distinct endpoints $u\ne v$ on the drawing of $H$ and relative interior disjoint from it; by hypothesis that relative interior lies in $U$. It is connected, so it lies in a single face $F$ of $H$, and $F$ is not the exterior region, which is disjoint from $U$. Hence $F$ is a bounded face with a Jordan graph cycle $J$ as its frontier. Let $V$ be the region of $\mathbb R^2\setminus J$ containing $F$. If $F$ were a proper subset of $V$, [L6] would give a polygonal path in $V$ from a point of $F$ to a point of $V\setminus F$. The first point at which it leaves $F$ would lie in $\operatorname{Fr}(F)\cap V=J\cap V=\varnothing$. Thus $F=V$, and $V$ is the bounded region because $F\subseteq U$. In this AC-qualified hybrid argument, invoke [F2] for Jordan separation in the crosscut proof of step 1.3 even when $J$ happens to be polygonal; the optional [F1] choice-free branch of that earlier proof is not used here. Apply the bounded case of step 1.3 to $J$, $u,v$ and the polygonal arc $Q$: the curves $D_i=J_i\cup Q$ are Jordan curves and graph cycles of the new drawing, $F\setminus Q=Y_1\sqcup Y_2$, and the frontier of $Y_i$ is $D_i$. Every old face $F^{\prime}\ne F$ misses the relative interior of $Q$, so it remains connected and open in the complement of the new drawing. Its old frontier is a Jordan graph cycle contained in the old graph and hence in the new graph, so $F^{\prime}$ is also closed in that new complement. It therefore remains one component with the same frontier; the exterior region of $C$ is among these unchanged faces. Hence the invariant passes to the new drawing, and an ear with $k$ edges contributes $k-1$ vertices, $k$ edges and one region, so $V-E+F$ is unchanged. Induction over the finitely many ears proves both hybrid conclusions. All selections here are finite, and AC enters only through [F2], used for every Jordan crosscut in this hybrid argument. [A1, F2, L2, L6, L7, step 1.2, step 1.3] ∎

source_lines.38: [F1] A left action of a group $G$ on a space $E$ **by homeomorphisms** is a **covering-space action** when every $e\in E$ has an open neighbourhood $U$ such that $gU\cap U=\varnothing$ for every nonidentity $g\in G$ (def-group-action, def-homeomorphism-and-open-maps). Acting by homeomorphisms means that each map $e\mapsto g\cdot e$ is a homeomorphism of $E$; the underlying set action alone would not make the translates $gU$ open. This condition implies freeness (def-free-group-action) and makes the translates of $U$ pairwise disjoint. ([[def-covering-space-action]]).
source_lines.40: [F2] A **covering map** is a continuous surjection $p:E\to B$ such that every $b\in B$ has an open neighbourhood $U$ for which $p^{-1}(U)$ is a disjoint union of open sets $V_j$, called **sheets**, and each restriction $p|_{V_j}:V_j\to U$ is a homeomorphism (def-continuous-map-top, def-homeomorphism-and-open-maps, def-disjoint-union-topology). Such a $U$ is **evenly covered**, and $p^{-1}(b)$ is the **fibre** over $b$. A covering is **trivial** when it is isomorphic over $B$ to a product projection $B\times F\to B$ with $F$ discrete. ([[def-covering-map-and-evenly-covered-neighbourhoods]]).
source_lines.42: [F3] **The quotient topology.** Let $(X, \mathcal{T})$ be a topological space (def-topological-space), let $Y$ be a set and let $q : X \to Y$ be a surjection (def-injection-surjection-bijection). The **quotient topology** on $Y$ induced by $q$ is the final topology of the one-element family $(q)$ (def-initial-and-final-topology): $$\mathcal{T}_q \;:=\; \{\, V \subseteq Y : q^{-1}[V] \in \mathcal{T} \,\} .$$ That this is a topology is discharged in def-initial-and-final-topology, where every final topology is verified to satisfy (T1), (T2) and (T3). Dually, $C \subseteq Y$ is closed in $\mathcal{T}_q$ exactly when $q^{-1}[C]$ is closed in $X$, because $q^{-1}[Y \setminus V] = X \setminus q^{-1}[V]$. ([[def-quotient-topology]]).
source_lines.44: [F4] For a covering $p:E\to B$, a **deck transformation** is an isomorphism $h:E\to E$ over $B$, so $p\circ h=p$ (def-map-and-isomorphism-of-covering-spaces). Deck transformations form the **deck group** $\operatorname{Deck}(p)$ under composition, and this group acts on $E$ by evaluation (def-group, def-group-action). ([[def-deck-transformation-and-deck-group]]).
source_lines.54: 1.1 Let $U$ be a neighbourhood whose nonidentity translates are disjoint. Each $g$ acts by a homeomorphism of $E$ by [F1], so every translate $gU$ is open, and the full preimage of the orbit image of $U$ is $\bigcup_{g\in G}gU$, a disjoint union of open sets. That preimage being open makes the orbit image open in the quotient topology of [F3], and the orbit map is then an open continuous surjection, so [F6] applies to it. [given, F6, F3, F2, F1]
source_lines.56: 2.1 Each translate maps homeomorphically onto that quotient neighbourhood. [step 1.1, F6, F2, F3]
source_lines.60: 4.1 If the total space is path-connected, compare any deck transformation at one point with the unique group translate taking that point to its image; one-point determination then proves equality with that translate. [step 3.1, F4, F5, F1]

source_lines.32: For $n\ge1$, put $P=\mathbb R^n\setminus\{0\}$ and define
source_lines.34: $$H:P\times[0,1]\to P,\qquad H(x,t)=\bigl((1-t)+t/\lVert x\rVert_2\bigr)x.$$
source_lines.36: Then $H$ is continuous, $H(x,0)=x$, $H(x,1)=x/\lVert x\rVert_2$, $H(s,t)=s$ for $s\in S^{n-1}$, and $H(x,t)\ne0$.
source_lines.56: 1.1 The scalar $c(x,t):=(1-t)+t/\lVert x\rVert_2$ is positive, since $1-t\ge0$, $t\ge0$, and $\lVert x\rVert_2>0$. [L3]
source_lines.60: 1.3 Substituting $t=0$ and $t=1$ gives $H(x,0)=x$ and $H(x,1)=x/\lVert x\rVert_2$. If $s\in S^{n-1}$, then $\lVert s\rVert_2=1$ and $H(s,t)=s$. [L3]
source_lines.62: 2.1 Since $c(x,t)>0$ and $x\ne0$, $H(x,t)\ne0$. Hence $H$ takes values in $P$, and [L5] makes it continuous as a map $P\times[0,1]\to P$. [step 1.1, step 1.2, L5]

source_lines.27: Running Robinson-Schensted row insertion on the six permutations of $\{1,2,3\}$ gives
source_lines.28: $$123\mapsto(3),\quad 132\mapsto(2,1),\quad 213\mapsto(2,1),\quad 231\mapsto(2,1),\quad 312\mapsto(2,1),\quad 321\mapsto(1^3);$$
source_lines.45: 1.1 Explicit insertions: applying [F1] to each word, one letter at a time, gives the following tableaux (written as the list of their rows): $123\rightsquigarrow((1,2,3))$, shape $(3)$; $132$: $(1)$, then $(1,3)$, then $2$ bumps the $3$, giving rows $(1,2)$ and $(3)$, shape $(2,1)$; $213$: $(2)$, then $1$ bumps $2$ giving rows $(1)$ and $(2)$, then $3$ is appended in the first row, shape $(2,1)$; $231$: $(2)$, then $(2,3)$, then $1$ bumps $2$, giving rows $(1,3)$ and $(2)$, shape $(2,1)$; $312$: $(3)$, then $1$ bumps $3$ giving rows $(1)$ and $(3)$, then $2$ is appended in the first row, shape $(2,1)$; $321$: $(3)$, then $2$ bumps $3$, giving rows $(2)$ and $(3)$, then $1$ bumps $2$ and the expelled $2$ bumps $3$, giving rows $(1)$, $(2)$, $(3)$, shape $(1^3)$. Each bumping step is the deterministic rule of [F1] applied to the displayed entries. [given, F1]
